paragraphs.text:
OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, THE BISHOP OF NYSSA: AN EXACT EXPOSITION OF THE SONG OF SONGS

You laid a request before us [?] by letter about the Song of Songs, and I welcomed it as fitting for your venerable life, [?] and for your pure soul. You asked that a suitable contemplative reading should bring to light the philosophy hidden in the words, once the surface meaning of the text has been purified into undefiled thoughts. So I gladly took up this task. I did not do it because it would be of any use for your own character. I am persuaded that the eye of your soul is clean of every passionate and defiled thought, and that through these divine words it looks without hindrance toward the undefiled grace. I did it so that those [?] of a more fleshly disposition might receive some guidance toward the [?] spiritual and immaterial state of the soul, which this book leads to through the wisdom hidden in it. But some churchmen think we should hold to the letter of holy Scripture in everything. They do not accept that Scripture says anything for our benefit through riddles and hidden meanings. So I think I must first answer those who accuse us of such things. I must show that we do nothing improper when we try in every way to hunt out what is profitable from the divine and inspired Scripture. If the text is of some benefit when understood as it is spoken, we have what we seek ready to hand. But if something is said with concealment, in hidden meanings and riddles, and it would be useless

for our benefit if taken in its obvious sense, then we must turn such words over in our minds. The Word that teaches us through Proverbs guides us to understand what is said either as a parable, or as a dark saying, or as a saying of the wise, or as a riddle. Someone may wish to call the contemplative reading of these things by way of anagogy "tropology", or "allegory", or some other name. We will not quarrel over the name, so long as it holds profitable thoughts. When the great Apostle says that the law is spiritual, he includes the historical narratives under the name of the law. So all inspired Scripture is law to those who read it. It teaches those who listen attentively [?], not only through its plain precepts but also through its historical narratives, and leads them to knowledge of the mysteries and to a pure way of life. He uses interpretation as it suits him, with an eye to what is profitable, and does not worry about what name the kind of interpretation should be given. In one place he says he is now changing his tone, because he is about to turn the history into a demonstration of God's plan concerning the Covenants. Then he mentions Abraham's two children, born to him from the slave woman and the free woman, and he calls the contemplative reading of them "allegory". Again, after recounting certain events of the history, he says: "These things happened to them as types, but they were written for our instruction." And again, after saying that the ox treading out the grain must not be muzzled, he adds that God is not concerned about oxen, but that it was written [?] entirely for our sake. In one place he calls our dimmer understanding and partial knowledge "a mirror" and "a riddle". And again he calls the passage from bodily things to things of the mind a "turning to the Lord" and a "removal of the veil". In all these different ways and names of spiritual contemplation, he teaches us one kind of lesson. We must not by any means stay with the literal fact, since the obvious appearance of the words often harms us in our pursuit of a virtuous life. We must pass on to an immaterial and spiritual contemplation, so that our more bodily notions are changed into mind and understanding, and the more fleshly appearance of the words is shaken off like dust. That is why he says: "The letter kills, but the spirit gives life." Often [Scripture, that is,] the history does not give us examples of a good life if we stop at the bare facts. What does it do for the virtue of someone who hears that Hosea the prophet fathered children by harlotry, or that Isaiah went in to the prophetess, if the reading stops at the letter? Or what do the narratives about David contribute to a virtuous life (Hosea 1:2; [?])

when adultery and murder ran together in them into one single pollution? But suppose some account is found that shows what was brought about through these events to be blameless. Then the Apostle's saying will be shown true: "The letter kills" (for it holds examples of wicked deeds), "but the spirit gives life." For the spirit turns an unseemly and discredited sense into meanings more worthy of God. We know, too, that the Word himself, whom all creation worships, uncovered the meanings of the law for us in this way when he delivered the divine mysteries in the flesh, in human likeness and form. He said that the two men whose testimony is true are himself and the Father. He applied the bronze serpent, which was lifted up on high and protected the people against deadly bites, to what God accomplished for us through the cross. He also trained the sharpness of his own disciples through veiled and hidden words: in parables, in likenesses, in dark sayings, in maxims spoken in riddles. He explained these to them privately and cleared up their obscurity. And sometimes, when they did not grasp the meaning of what was said, he rebuked them for being slow and dull of understanding. When he ordered them to keep away from the leaven of the Pharisees, they looked anxiously at their bags, in which they had brought no supply of bread. Then he reproached them for not understanding that the leaven stood for teaching. Again, when the disciples set a table before him, he answered: "I have food to eat that you do not know about." They supposed he was speaking of bodily food that someone else had brought him. So he explained his own words: the food fitting and proper for him is to carry out the saving will. Countless such examples can be gathered from the sayings of the Gospels. In them the obvious sense is one thing, and what the meaning of the words points to is another. Take the water he promised to the thirsty, through which believers become springs of rivers; the bread that comes down from heaven; the temple that is destroyed and raised up in three days; the way; the door; the stone rejected by the builders and fitted into the head of the corner; the two in one bed; the mill; the women grinding; the one taken; the one left; the carcass; the eagles; the fig tree growing tender and putting out branches. All these and others like them should urge us to search the divine sayings, to pay attention to our reading, and to track down in every way whether some meaning can be found

that rises above the obvious sense and leads the mind by the hand toward things more divine and bodiless. This is why we are convinced that the tree whose fruit was forbidden as food was not a fig tree, as some have declared, nor any other fruit tree. If the fig had been deadly then, it would surely not be edible now. We have also learned from the Lord's own voice, which laid down as a doctrine that nothing that goes in through the mouth can defile a person. So we look for some other meaning in the law, one worthy of the majesty of the Lawgiver. When we hear that paradise is the work of God's planting, and that a tree of life was planted in the middle of paradise, let us seek to learn from the one who reveals hidden mysteries what kind of plants the Father farms and tends. Let us ask how the two trees, one of salvation and one of destruction, can both be in the very center of paradise. In the outline of a circle, the exact middle is always at its single center. If another center were placed beside it at some point, the circle would have to move along with that center, so that the first would no longer be the middle. Paradise there is one. So how does the text say that each tree is to be seen separately, and yet both this one and that one are in the middle? And the same text declared that all the works of God are very good, so it teaches that the deadly tree is foreign to God's planting. Unless someone uses philosophy to look for the truth in these words, they will seem incoherent or mythical to the unreflecting. It would take long to gather every case from the prophets. Micah says that in the last days a manifest mountain will rise above the tops of the mountains, and by this name he means the mystery of godliness, revealed for the overthrow of the hostile powers. The lofty Isaiah says that a rod will spring up and a flower from the root, and by this he points to the Lord's appearing in the flesh. Then there is the curdled mountain in the great David: what sense does it have that is evident in the letter? Or the chariot ten-thousandfold? Or the herd of bulls let loose among the heifers of the peoples? Or the foot dipped in blood? Or the tongues of the dogs? Or Lebanon with its cedars, ground fine like a calf? Countless others besides these can be gathered from the rest of prophecy to show that we must read the words for their meaning. If someone rejects this, as some like to do, it seems to me as if he set raw crops on the table for people to eat. He would not have threshed the ears, nor separated the grain from the chaff with the winnowing fan, nor ground the wheat into flour, nor made bread in the proper way of baking. Unprocessed produce is food for cattle, not for people. In the same way one might say

that the inspired words, if they are not worked over by finer contemplation, are food for irrational rather than rational creatures. This is true not only of the Old Testament but also of much of the Gospel teaching: the winnowing fork that clears the threshing floor, the chaff blown away, the wheat that stays at the winnower's feet, the unquenchable fire, the good granary, the tree that bears evil fruit in plenty, the threat of the axe that fearfully shows [?] the trees' prime, the stones changed into human nature. Let this be written in haste, in this letter to your wisdom, as a kind of defense against those who urge us to seek nothing from the divine words beyond the obvious appearance of the text. Origen labored diligently on this book, and we too have been eager to commit our own labor to writing. Let no one blame us for this, but look to the Apostle's divine saying: "Each will receive his own reward according to his own labor." I did not compose this work for display. Some of those who are with me, out of love of learning, took notes of much of what was said in church. I took some material from them, as much as their notes held in proper order, and added some of my own where additions were needed. So I have put the dictation in the form of homilies, carrying the contemplation of the text forward in order, word by word, as far as time and circumstances gave me leisure for it during the days of the fasts. In those days the discourse on this book was delivered with care to a public audience. If God, the steward of our life, grants us more years of life and a peaceful opportunity, we may perhaps go through the rest as well. For now our discourse and contemplation have reached the halfway point. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with us all to the ages of ages. Amen.

"Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices. Your name is ointment poured out. That is why the maidens have loved you; they have drawn you. We will run after you toward the fragrance of your ointments. The king has brought me into his chamber. Let us rejoice and be glad in you. Let us love your breasts more than wine. Uprightness has loved you."

You have followed Paul's counsel and put off the old self, with its deeds and desires, like a filthy garment. Through purity of life you have clothed yourselves in the shining garments of the Lord, such as he showed at his transfiguration on the mountain. Or rather, you have put on our Lord Jesus Christ himself, together with his [?] robe, and have been conformed to him in freedom from passion and in what is more divine. You, then, hear the

mystery of the Song of Songs. Come inside the undefiled bridal chamber, dressed in white, in pure and unstained thoughts. Let no one bring in passionate and fleshly reasoning. Let no one lack the garment of conscience that befits the divine wedding, and so be bound by his own thoughts, dragging the undefiled words of the Bridegroom and the bride down to brutish and irrational passions. Such a person, clothed by these thoughts in shameful fantasies, would be cast out from those who rejoice at the wedding, and would exchange the joy of the bridal chamber for gnashing of teeth and tears. I give this solemn warning as I am about to take up the mystical contemplation of the Song of Songs. Through what is written here, the soul is in a sense escorted as a bride to a bodiless and spiritual union with God. For he who wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth here shows the most perfect and blessed way of salvation, I mean the way of love. For some, salvation comes through fear: we look at the threats of punishment in Gehenna and separate ourselves from evil. There are also some who achieve virtue through the hope of the reward stored up for those who have lived piously. They gain the good not by love but by expecting a return. But one who has run up in soul toward perfection drives out fear. Such a disposition is servile: it stays with its master not out of love, but because it is afraid of the whip if it runs away. He looks beyond even the rewards themselves, so that he may not seem to value the reward more than the one who gives the gain. He loves with all his heart and soul and strength, not any of the things that come from God, but God himself, who is the source of all good things. This, then, is the disposition that the one who calls us to share in himself lays down as law for the souls of those who hear. The one who confirms this law is Solomon. By divine testimony his wisdom has no measure. It is incomparable and unequaled by all alike, both those who came before and those yet to come, and nothing that exists escaped him. Do you think I mean this Solomon, the son of Bathsheba, who offered a thousand burnt offerings on the mountain, and who took the Sidonian woman as his counselor in sin? Another Solomon is signified through him. He too was born from the seed of David according to the flesh. His name is peace. He is the true King of Israel and the builder of God's temple. He has encompassed the knowledge of all things, and his wisdom is boundless; or rather, his very being is wisdom and truth, and every name and concept that is lofty and worthy of God. He used this Solomon as an instrument and speaks to us through him: first in Proverbs, then in Ecclesiastes, and after these in the philosophy of the Song of Songs now before us. In his word he shows, step by step and in order, the ascent toward perfection. (1 Timothy 2:4 [?])

In the life of the flesh, not every age is capable of every natural activity, and our life does not move through the same things at the different stages of age. The infant does not do the work of the grown man, and the grown man is not carried in the arms of a nurse. At each season of life, something different is fitting and suitable. In the same way one can see in the soul something like the ages of the body, and through them an order and sequence is found that leads a person by the hand toward the virtuous life. That is why Proverbs teaches in one way, Ecclesiastes speaks in another, and the philosophy of the Song of Songs surpasses both with loftier teachings. The teaching of Proverbs speaks to one who is still a child and suits its words to that age. "Hear, my son," it says, "your father's laws, and do not reject your mother's rules." You see from these words that the soul is still at a tender and unformed age. The text sees it still needing a mother's rules and a father's correction. And so that the child may listen more eagerly to his parents, it promises him that children's ornaments will come from his diligence in his lessons. For the ornament of children is a golden necklace gleaming around the neck, and a garland woven from lovely flowers. But we must certainly understand these things in whatever way the meaning of the riddle leads us toward what is better. So he begins to sketch Wisdom for him, describing the bloom of her inexpressible beauty in varied and many ways. He wants the child to rise up toward a share in good things, not through fear and compulsion, but through desire and longing. A description of beauty somehow draws the desire of the young toward what is shown, and fans their longing to share in its bloom. So he adorns the beauty of Wisdom with praises, so that the child's faculty of desire may grow stronger as it is moved from attachment to material things to an immaterial bond. He does not only set forth in words the beauty of her bloom. He also counts up her wealth, which the one who lives with her will surely come to own. For now her wealth is seen in her ornaments. The ornament on her right hand is whole ages, as the text says: "Length of life and years of living are in her right hand." On her left hand she wears the precious wealth of the virtues, shining together with the splendor of glory. For it says: "In her left hand are wealth and glory." Then it speaks of her mouth, which breathes out the sweet scent of the fine spice of righteousness, saying: "From her mouth comes righteousness." And on her lips, it says, law and mercy bloom instead of a natural blush. So that beauty may be found gathered from every side for such a bride, even her walk is praised. For it says: "In the paths of righteousness [?]

[?] walks. Nor is greatness missing from the praises of her beauty: her growth has shot up like some flourishing plant. And this plant, to which her height is compared, is, he says, the tree of life itself. It becomes food for those who hold fast to it, and a secure and unshakable pillar for those who lean on it. By both I understand the Lord, for he is both the life and the support. The text runs thus: "She is a tree of life to all who hold fast to her, [and secure for those who lean on her as on the Lord]." Her power is included along with her other praises, so that the praise of wisdom's beauty may be made complete through every good thing. For "God," he says, "founded the earth by wisdom, and prepared the heavens by understanding." He refers each of the things we see in creation to the power of wisdom, and varies the names he gives her, for he calls the same thing wisdom and understanding, perception and knowledge and understanding, and the like. After this he begins to dress the young man as a bridegroom for such a union, bidding him look already toward the divine bridal chamber. For he says: "Do not forsake her, and she will hold fast to you; love her passionately, and she will keep you; put a rampart around her, and she will exalt you; honor her, that she may embrace you, that she may give your head a crown of graces and shield you with a crown of delight." Having now adorned the bride with these wedding crowns, he bids him never be parted from her, saying: "Whenever you walk, lead her along and let her be with you; and when you sleep, let her guard you, so that when you wake she may talk with you." By these words and others like them he kindles the desire of one who is still young in the inner man. He shows Wisdom herself in the text describing her own qualities, by which she above all draws the hearers into a loving bond, saying among other things, "I love those who love me." For the hope of being loved in return makes the lover desire more vehemently. He adds to these the rest of his counsels in declarative and unqualified maxims, and so leads the young man to a more perfect state. Then, at the end of Proverbs, he pronounces this good union blessed in the passage where he recounts the praises of that valiant woman. After that he adds the philosophy of Ecclesiastes for the one who has been sufficiently introduced to the desire for the virtues by the training of the proverbs. In this book he denounces people's attachment to appearances and declares vain everything unstable and passing, where he says, "All that comes is vanity." So he sets our soul's natural impulse toward invisible beauty above everything grasped by the senses. And having thus purified the heart of its attachment to appearances, then, through the Song of Songs,

he leads the mind as an initiate into the divine sanctuary. In this book what is depicted is the arrangement of a wedding, but what is meant is the union of the human soul with the Divine. For this reason the one who in Proverbs is called "son" is named "bridegroom," and Wisdom moves over into the place of the bride, so that the human being may be betrothed to God as a pure virgin and, cleaving to the Lord, may become one spirit. Through union with what is undefiled and free of passion, he becomes pure thought instead of heavy flesh. Since, then, it is Wisdom who speaks, love her as much as you can, with all your heart and strength; desire her as much as you are able. And I boldly add to these words: "Be passionately in love." For in the case of incorporeal things this passion is blameless and free of passion, as Wisdom says in Proverbs when she lays down the law of love for the divine beauty. The present text too commands the same, yet it does not offer bare advice on the subject. It philosophizes through hidden meanings, setting before its thoughts an image of the pleasures of life as the framework for these teachings. The image is a wedding scene, in which longing is mediated by desire for beauty. Yet it does not follow human custom, in which the bridegroom is the first to desire. Instead the virgin anticipates the bridegroom, unashamedly making her longing public and praying that she may one day delight in the bridegroom's kiss. For the virgin's good matchmakers, the patriarchs, prophets and lawgivers, brought the divine gifts to the betrothed, which custom calls bride-gifts, the name it gives to gifts before a marriage. These were the forgiveness of transgressions, the forgetting of evils, the removal of sin, the transformation of nature, the change of the corruptible into incorruption, the delight of paradise, the dignity of the kingdom, and gladness without end. Having received these divine gifts from the noble gift-bearers, who brought them to her through the teaching of the prophets, the virgin confesses her desire and hastens the gift of grace, eager now to delight in the beauty of the one she longs for. Some companions of her own age listen to her and stir the bride to still greater desire. The bridegroom too arrives, bringing with him a band of friends dear to his heart. These would be the ministering spirits through whom human beings are saved, or else the holy prophets, who hear the bridegroom's voice and rejoice and exult as the undefiled union is joined, through which the soul that cleaves to the Lord becomes one spirit, as the Apostle says. So I will once more repeat the warning I gave in connection with Proverbs. Let no one who is passionate and carnal, still reeking of the dead stench of the old man, drag down the meanings of these divinely inspired thoughts and words to brutish irrationality. Instead let each one step outside himself, leave the material world behind, and return in a sense, through freedom from

passion, into paradise. Made like God through purity, let him in this way enter the sanctuary of the mysteries revealed to us in this book. But if someone's soul is unprepared for such a hearing, let him listen to Moses, who lays down the law that we must not dare to climb the spiritual mountain before we have washed the garments of our hearts and purified our souls with the fitting sprinklings of our thoughts. So now, for as long as we devote ourselves to this contemplation, we should forget all thoughts of marriage, according to the command of Moses, who ordered those being initiated to keep themselves pure from marriage. And I think we must take up the lawgiver's commands in every respect as we are about to approach the spiritual mountain of the knowledge of God, where the female sort of thoughts is left behind, together with our material baggage, to the life below. And any irrational thought that is seen near such a mountain is put to death by firmer thoughts, as if by stones. Only in this way could we barely take in the sound of this trumpet, which sounds something great and extraordinary, beyond the capacity of its hearers. It is sent forth by the very darkness of obscurity in which God is, who burns up with fire everything material on such a mountain. Let us now, then, come within the Holy of Holies, which is the Song of Songs. In the phrase "Holy of Holies" this superlative expression teaches us an abundance and intensification of holiness. So too, through the "Song of Songs," the lofty word promises to teach us mysteries of mysteries. In the divinely inspired teaching there are many songs through which we are taught great thoughts about God, from the great David, from Isaiah, from Moses and from many others. Yet from this title we learn that as far as the holy songs stand above the songs of outside wisdom, so far does the mystery in the Song of Songs surpass the holy songs. Beyond this [?], human hearing and nature can neither find nor take in anything more for understanding. For this reason he placed at the head of his exposition of the doctrines, in the form of a riddle, the most intense of all the things done for pleasure, namely erotic passion. Through it we are to learn that the soul gazing on the inaccessible beauty of the divine nature must love [?] it as intensely as the body is drawn toward what is akin to it and of its own kind, transforming passion into freedom from passion. Then, with every bodily disposition extinguished, our mind may burn with love by the spirit alone, warmed by that fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth. But on how the soul must be disposed when it hears mystical words, I say this is enough. It would now be time to bring the divine words of the Song of Songs themselves into our contemplation. And first let us consider the force of the title. For it was not idly, I think, that the book was ascribed in its title to

Solomon. It was done so that readers would expect something great and divine in what is said. Everyone holds his wisdom in unsurpassed admiration because of the testimony about him, and for this reason his name is mentioned at the very opening, so that readers may trust that this book offers something great and worthy of his reputation. In the art of painting, the material is entirely the various dyes that together complete the likeness of a living creature. Yet someone who looks at the image that the art has completed with colors does not linger over the dyes laid on the panel. He looks only at the form that the artist brought out through the colors. In the same way, with the present Scripture we ought not to look at the material of the colors in its words. Rather we should see in them, as it were, the form of the King [?], traced out through pure thoughts. For in their obvious sense these words are white or yellow or black or red or blue or some other color: mouth and kiss, perfume and wine, the names of the bodily members, bed, maidens, and the like. But the form produced through them is blessedness and freedom from passion, union with God [?], estrangement from evils, and assimilation to what is truly beautiful and good. These are the thoughts that bear witness that Solomon's wisdom surpassed the limits of human wisdom. For what could be more astonishing than to make nature itself the purifier of its own passions, laying down the law of freedom from passion and teaching it through words that are thought to be passionate? He does not say that we must be free of the passionate movements of the flesh, put to death our members that are still on the earth, and keep our mouths pure of passionate words. Instead he so disposed the soul that it looks toward purity through things that seem at odds with it, and he conveys an undefiled meaning through passionate expressions. Let the word, then, teach us this one thing through its opening: those who are led into the sanctuary of the mysteries of this book are no longer human beings. Their nature has been transformed into something more divine through discipleship to Christ. So the Word testifies of his own disciples that they were greater than human, for the distinction the Lord drew set them apart from human beings when he said: "Who do people say that I am? But who do you say that I am?" Truly, someone who hears such words, whose obvious sense points to carnal pleasures, and does not slip into filthy thoughts, but is led by these very words to the philosophy of divine things and to pure conceptions, shows that he is no longer a human being, and that his nature is no longer mixed with flesh and blood. He displays the life hoped for in the resurrection of the saints,

having become equal to the angels through freedom from passion. After the resurrection the body, transformed into incorruption, will be joined to the human soul. The passions that now trouble us through the flesh will not rise with those bodies, but a peaceful state will take over our life. The mind of the flesh will no longer rebel against the soul. No civil war waged through passionate impulses will fight against the law of the mind, taking the defeated soul captive and handing it over to sin. Our nature will then be pure of all such things, and flesh and spirit will share one mind, since every bodily disposition will have been wiped out of our nature. In the same way, the word in this book urges those who listen, even though we live in the flesh, not to turn back to the flesh in our thoughts but to look to the soul alone. It urges them to offer all the expressions of love in these words, pure and undefiled, to the God who is good and surpasses all understanding. He alone is truly sweet, desirable and lovely, and enjoying him, which never ceases, becomes the starting point of greater desire, intensifying longing through sharing in good things. So Moses loved God, and so did Elijah. So John loved the bridegroom, saying: "He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice." So Peter, asked whether he loved, confesses boldly, saying: "You know, Lord, that I love you." So did the other apostles. So Paul, once a persecutor, loved Christ whom he had not seen, and wrote: "I betrothed you, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." So now the Church, the bride, loved the bridegroom, like the virgin in the Song who says: "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth." So too the one to whom God spoke mouth to mouth came, as Scripture testifies, to a greater desire for such kisses after so many appearances of God, and asked to see the one he longed for as though he had never yet beheld him. So too all the others in whom the divine longing lay deep never came to a halt in their desire. Everything that came to them from God for the enjoyment of the one they desired they made into fuel and kindling for still more intense desire. And so now too the soul joined to God is insatiable in its enjoyment: the more abundantly it is filled with enjoyment, the more intensely its longing grows. For the words of the bridegroom are spirit and life, and everyone who cleaves to the spirit becomes spirit, and whoever is joined to the life passes from death into life, according to the Lord's word. For this reason she longs to bring her soul near to the spring of spiritual life:

the virgin soul, that is. The spring is the bridegroom's mouth, from which the words of eternal life gush out and fill the mouth that draws them in, as the Prophet did when he drew in the Spirit through his mouth. One who draws a drink from a spring must put his mouth to the water, and the Lord is the spring, who said, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." Therefore the soul wishes to bring her own mouth to the mouth that pours forth life, saying: "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth." And he who pours out life for all and wills all to be saved wants none of the saved to be without a share in such a kiss, for this kiss cleanses every stain. That is why, it seems to me, the Lord said reproachfully to Simon the leper, "You gave me no kiss." For he would surely have been cleansed of his disease had he drawn in purity with his mouth. But he was naturally without love: his disease had made him overgrown with flesh in his own desire [?], and he remained unemptied of his affliction. The purified soul, however, with no fleshly leprosy in the way, sees the treasury of good things, and the name of the treasury is the heart. The Prophet too prayed that a pure heart be created. From the heart comes the supply of divine milk to the breasts, and by it the soul is nourished, drawing in grace in proportion to its faith. For this reason she says, "Your breasts are better than wine," using the breasts to point to the heart because of where they lie. Certainly anyone who takes the heart to mean the hidden and ineffable power of the Godhead will not go wrong. And one might reasonably take the breasts to mean the good works of the divine power on our behalf, through which God nurses each person's life, granting each who receives it the food suited to him. In passing we also learn another doctrine from the philosophy of this book: that there is a twofold perception in us, one bodily and the other more divine, as the word of Proverbs says somewhere: "You will find divine perception." For there is a certain correspondence between the movements and activities of the soul and the sense organs of the body, and this we learn from the present oracles of the Spirit. Wine and milk are judged by taste; but since these are intelligible, the power of the soul that perceives them is certainly intelligible too. A kiss happens through the sense of touch, for the lips touch each other in a kiss. But there is also a touch of the soul that lays hold of the Word, brought about by an incorporeal and intelligible contact, as the one said who wrote, "Our hands have handled the Word of life." Likewise the scent of the divine perfumes is not a scent perceived by the nostrils but by an intelligible and immaterial power, which draws in the fragrance of Christ by drawing in the Spirit. For this is how the virgin's prayer continues at the beginning: "Your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes is better than all spices." And

these words reveal, as we have understood them, a thought that is neither small nor to be despised. For perhaps, when the milk of the divine breasts is ranked above the gladness that wine gives us, we learn from these words that all human wisdom and knowledge of what exists, and every power of contemplation and comprehending imagination, cannot be compared on equal terms with the simpler food of the divine teachings. Milk comes from the breasts, and milk is food for infants. Wine, by its strength and warmth, is the enjoyment of the more mature. Yet what is perfect in outside wisdom is less than the teaching of the divine Word given to infants. Therefore the divine breasts are better than human wine. And the scent of the divine perfumes is finer than all the fragrance of spices. From this it seems to show the following meaning. By spices we understand the virtues, such as wisdom, temperance, courage, prudence and the like. Each of us makes use of them according to his own capacity and choice, and so we become fragrant, one in one way and another in another: one from temperance or wisdom, another from justice or courage or some other virtue, and another perhaps has in himself a fragrance blended from all such spices. Yet none of these could be compared with that perfect virtue which, the prophet Habakkuk says, has encompassed the heavens: "His virtue covered the heavens." This virtue is wisdom itself, justice itself, truth itself, and every other such thing. The scent of the heavenly perfumes, she says, has a charm beyond comparison with these spices known to us. Again, in what follows, the soul, the bride, touches on a loftier philosophy, showing that the divine power is inaccessible and cannot be contained by human reasoning, when she says: "Your name is perfume poured out." This, it seems to me, is what the saying signifies: the boundless nature cannot be grasped precisely by the meaning of a name. Every power of thought, and every expression of words and thoughts, however great and worthy of God it may seem, is by nature unable to touch the reality itself. Instead our reason conjectures the Word as if from traces and glimmers, inferring the incomprehensible from what is comprehended by a kind of analogy. For whatever name we may devise to make known the perfume of your divinity, she says, we do not signify the perfume itself by what we say. With our names for God we point only to some slight remnant of the vapor of the divine fragrance. It is like vessels from which perfume has been poured out: the perfume emptied from them is unknown in its own nature, as to what it is, but from a faint

…from the quality left in the vessel by the vapours, we form some conjecture about the perfume that has been poured out. This, then, is what we learn from what has been said: the perfume of the Godhead itself, whatever it is in its essence, is beyond every name and every thought. But the wonders we observe in the universe supply the material for the names we give to God. By them we call him wise, powerful, good, holy, blessed and eternal, judge and saviour, and so on. All these point to some faint quality of the divine perfume, which the whole creation, like a perfumer's jar, has taken on as an impression in itself through the wonders observed within it. "Therefore," it says, "the maidens have loved you; they have drawn you." She has given the reason for this praiseworthy desire and loving disposition. For who could fail to love such beauty, if only he had an eye able to gaze on its loveliness? The beauty that is grasped is not great, but what is surmised by conjecture from what appears is infinitely greater. Yet just as bodily love does not touch those who are still infants (for infancy has no room for that passion), nor can it be seen in those worn out by extreme old age, so too with divine beauty: the one who is still an infant, tossed to and fro and carried about by every wind of doctrine, and the one who is old and aged and close to vanishing away, are both found unmoved toward this desire. Invisible beauty does not touch such people. Only the soul that has passed beyond the state of infancy and come to its prime through spiritual maturity, that has taken on no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that is neither insensible through infancy nor feeble through age—the soul the text calls a maiden—only she obeys the great and first commandment of the law, loving with all her heart and strength that beauty of which the human mind can find no sketch or likeness to express it. Such maidens, then, having grown up through the virtues and having now, at the ripe season of the divine mysteries, come within the divine bridal chamber, love the bridegroom's beauty, and through their love turn him toward themselves. For the bridegroom is such that he returns the longing of those who love him. It is he who spoke thus in the person of Wisdom: "I love those who love me," and, "I will give those who love me substance" (he himself is that substance), "and I will fill their treasuries with good things." So souls draw toward themselves the longing of the incorruptible bridegroom, walking, as it is written, after the Lord God. The cause of their love is the fragrance of the perfume, toward which they are always running, straining forward to what lies ahead and forgetting what lies behind. "After you," it says, "we will run toward the scent of your perfumes." But those who do not yet possess the perfection of virtue, and are still youthful in age, promise that they will run toward the goal pointed out by the scent of the perfumes. For they say, "We will run toward the scent of your per-

fumes." But the more perfect soul, straining more vigorously toward what lies ahead, already reaches the goal for which the race is run, and is counted worthy of the treasures in the storerooms. For she says, "The king has brought me into his chamber." She who longed to touch the good with the tips of her lips, and had laid hold of the beauty only so far as the power of her prayer could show, prayed to be granted something like a kiss through the illumination of the Word. Now, through what she has obtained, having penetrated in thought to the inner part of the hidden things, she cries out that her race is no longer only at the doorway of good things. By the firstfruits of the Spirit, through whose grace, as through a kiss, she has been counted worthy to search the depths of God, she says that in the inner sanctuary of paradise, like the great Paul, she sees what cannot be seen and hears words that cannot be spoken. The next saying reveals in its words the ordering of the Church. For those who were first made disciples by grace, and became eyewitnesses and servants, did not keep the good confined within themselves, but by handing it on made the same grace available to those who came after them. That is why the maidens say to the bride—who first, by coming face to face with the Word, was filled with good things and counted worthy of the hidden mysteries—"Let us rejoice and be glad in you." Your gladness is our common joy, for just as you love the breasts of the Word more than wine, so we too love yours. Let us imitate your breasts, through which you give milk to drink to those who are infants in Christ. Let us love them more than human wine. To bring the thought out more clearly, what is said amounts to this. John, who leaned on the Lord's breast, loved the breasts of the Word. He laid his own heart like a sponge against the fountain of life, and through some ineffable impartation was filled with the mysteries hidden in the heart of Christ. Now he offers us the nipple filled by the Word, and fills us with the good things placed in him by the fountain, proclaiming with a loud voice the Word who always is. So we too will rightly say to him, "Let us love your breasts more than wine"—if indeed we have become such as to be maidens, neither childish in mind through the youth that is yoked to vanity, nor wrinkled by sin in an old age that ends in vanishing away. We love the flow of your teachings for this reason: because "Uprightness has loved you." For this is the disciple whom Jesus loved, and Jesus is Uprightness. This text names the Lord in a finer and more fitting way than the prophet David does. For David says, "The Lord God is upright," but this text calls him [?]

Uprightness itself, by which every crooked thing is made straight. May every crooked thing in us too become straight, and the rough places smooth ways, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon. Do not look at me, because I have been darkened, because the sun has looked askance at me. My mother's sons fought against me; they made me keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep. Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where do you pasture your flock, where do you make it rest at noon, lest I become like a veiled woman among the flocks of your companions. If you do not know yourself, you who are beautiful among women, go out in the tracks of the flocks, and pasture the kids by the tents of the

In the holy tabernacle of witness, what showed on the outside was not equal in honour to the beauty hidden within. The outer adornment of the tabernacle consisted of a curtain of linen fabric, coverings made of goats' hair, and wrappings of red-dyed skins, and to those who saw the outside nothing great or precious appeared beyond these. But inside, the whole tabernacle of witness shone with gold and silver and precious stones: the pillars, the bases, the capitals, the altar of incense, the altar of sacrifice, the ark, the lampstand, the mercy seat, the basins, and the veils of the entrances. In these the beauty was blended from every kind of bright-coloured dye: thread of gold, woven elegantly together with blue, purple, fine linen and scarlet by skilful and delicate craftsmanship, a mixture of all of them, made the radiance of the fabric glitter as in the rays of a rainbow. What I have in view in beginning this way will certainly become clear to us from what is about to be said. Once again the Song of Songs lies before us, to guide us into all knowledge of God and all philosophy. This is the true tabernacle of witness. Its outer coverings, its curtains of hide and the wrapping of its hanging, are certain words and phrases of love, which express the relation to the one longed for, and a sketch of beauty, and mention of bodily members, both those visible in the face and those hidden under the covering of clothing. But within there is truly a lampstand of many lights, and an ark full of mysteries, and the altar of fragrant incense, and the cleansing from sin, that all-golden altar of incense of godliness; and the beauty of the veils, gracefully woven from the bright colours of the virtues; and the unwavering pillars of the reasoning powers, and the immovable bases of the doctrines; and the beauty of the capitals, which signifies the grace surrounding the governing part of the soul; and the basins for souls; and everything that looks toward the heavenly and incorporeal way of life, which the law commands in riddles—all these are in the thoughts hidden

beneath the letter, if only we make ourselves fit, by care for our way of life, to enter the Holy of Holies, having washed off every stain of shameful thought in the basin of the Word. Otherwise, dying against the command of the law by touching some dead thought or unclean notion, we may be shut out without seeing the wonders inside the tabernacle. For the law of the Spirit does not admit such people to enter unless, according to Moses' command, the one who has touched some dead and abominable thought washes the garment of his conscience. The sequence of what has already been examined now leads our discussion to the contemplation of what the bride said to the maidens. It is this: "I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon." The teacher rightly begins her instruction of the souls she is teaching in good things from the proper starting point. They are eager, as their promises show, to value the grace flowing from her spiritual breasts above every human word, which they figuratively call wine. This is what they said: "We will love your breasts more than wine, because Uprightness has loved you." But she adds, for the benefit of her pupils, the wonder that concerns her, so that we may learn better the boundless love for humanity of the bridegroom, who through his love bestows beauty on the one he loved. "Do not marvel," she says, "that Uprightness has loved me, but rather that, when I was black from sin and akin to darkness through my deeds, he made me beautiful by his love, exchanging his own beauty for my ugliness. For he transferred to himself the filth of my sins and gave me a share in his own purity, making me a partner in his own beauty. He first made me lovely instead of hideous, and then loved me." After this she urges the maidens to become beautiful themselves, showing them her own beauty as an example, just as the great Paul says, "Become as I am, for I also have become as you are," and, "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." For this reason she does not let the souls who are her pupils look at their past life and despair of becoming beautiful. Rather, by looking at her they are to learn from her example that the present becomes a covering for the past, if it is blameless. For she says, "Even if beauty now shines on me, the beauty with which I was formed through being loved by Uprightness, still I know that I was not bright in the beginning, but black. My former life produced this appearance in me, dark and gloomy. Yet though I was that, I am this. For the likeness of ugliness has been transformed into the form of beauty. So you too, daughters of Jerusalem, look up to your mother, the Jerusalem above. Even if you were tents of Kedar, because

the ruler of the power of the air dwelt in you, [?] … darkness … [?]. In the same way, when the soul is transferred from error to truth, the dark form of its life is changed along with it into luminous grace." What the bride of Christ says to the maidens, Paul also says to Timothy—Paul, who afterwards became bright instead of black. He says that he too was counted worthy to become beautiful, he who was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, an insolent man, and black; for Christ came into the world to make the black bright, calling not the righteous to himself but sinners to repentance. These he made to shine like luminaries through the washing of regeneration, washing their dark appearance away with water. David's eye sees this very thing in the city above, and regards the sight with wonder: how in the city of God, of which glorious things have been spoken, Babylon is settled, and Rahab the harlot is remembered, and foreigners and Tyre and the people of the Ethiopians come to be in her. So no one can any longer reproach this city for having no inhabitants, saying, "Shall anyone still say to Zion, 'A man was born in her'?" For there the foreigners become citizens of the city, the Babylonians become people of Jerusalem, the harlot becomes a virgin, the Ethiopians become bright, and Tyre becomes the city above. In the same way, here too the bride encourages the daughters of Jerusalem, commending the bridegroom's [?]: that even if he takes a soul that is black, he makes it beautiful by fellowship with himself; and even if someone is a tent of Kedar, he becomes a dwelling of light for the true Solomon, that is, for the King of peace who has come to dwell in him. This is why she says, "I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem," so that by looking at me you too may become curtains of Solomon, even if you were tents of Kedar. Then she adds what follows to what has been said, and by it she necessarily safeguards the minds of her pupils, so that they do not attribute the cause of the dark appearance to the Creator, but understand that each person's own choice lays the foundations of such an appearance. "Do not look at me," she says, "because I have been darkened." I was not like this at the beginning. For it would not be fitting

that one fashioned by the luminous hands of God should be coloured with a dark and black appearance. "I was not like this," she says, "but I became so. I am not darkened by nature; this ugliness was brought upon me from outside, when the sun changed my form from bright to black." "For the sun," she says, "has looked upon me." What, then, do we learn from this? The Lord tells the crowds in a parable that the one who sows the word does not sow only the good heart. Even if a heart is stony, or overgrown with thorns, or beside the road and trampled, out of love for humanity he casts the seeds of the word on all of them. And in explaining the characteristics of each, he says that this is what happens with the stony soul: what is sown does not take root in depth. At once, by a shallow sprouting, it promises an ear of grain, but when the sun heats the ground too fiercely, it withers because there is no moisture beneath the roots. In his explanation he calls the sun temptation. So this is the teaching we learn from our teacher: human nature came into being as an image of the true light, far from any dark features, shining with likeness to the archetypal beauty. But temptation, bringing its fiery heat upon it through deceit, struck down the first shoot while it was still tender and without roots. Before it could acquire any settled state of goodness and give its roots water to the depth through the cultivation of the reasoning powers, temptation at once dried up its green and flourishing appearance through disobedience, and by the burning made it black. Let none of my hearers be surprised that the hostile assault of temptation is called the sun, since he is taught this in many places by divinely inspired Scripture. In the second Song of Ascents, for example, this blessing is pronounced on the one who has the help of him who made heaven and earth: that he will not be burned by the sun by day. And the prophet Isaiah, prophesying the condition of the Church, describes its way of life as a kind of procession, brightening the account with his words. He speaks of daughters carried on shoulders, and children borne in litters, and warding off the glare with sunshades. In these riddles he depicts the life of virtue: by the age of infancy he indicates what is newborn and innocent; by the sunshades, the relief from the heat that comes to souls through self-control and purity. From this we learn that the soul being made ready as a bride for God must be carried on shoulders, not trampled by the flesh but seated on top of the bulk of the body. When we hear of a litter, we understand the radiant grace of baptism, through which we become children, no longer planting our footsteps on the earth but borne upon it toward the heavenly life. And our life becomes shaded and dewy, as the heat is

quenched by the sunshades of virtue. This, then, is the sun that does harm by looking askance, whenever its blaze is not walled off by the cloud of the Spirit, which the Lord spread out for them as a shelter. For this is the sun that scorches the bright surface of the body with the assault of temptations and blackens its appearance into ugliness. Next she tells where the change of our fair complexion into black had its beginning. "My mother's sons," she says, "fought against me; they made me keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep." Let the hearer grant me this: not to scrutinize the construction of the wording too closely, but to look to the thread of the thought. If something does not seem precisely connected, let him attribute it to the weakness of the phrasing of those who rendered the Hebrew tongue into Greek. For those who have taken the trouble to be trained in the Hebrew language find nothing of the kind that seems disconnected. But the structure of our language, not matching the structure of Hebrew expression, produces a certain confusion for those who follow the meaning of the words too superficially. As far as we have grasped it, the sense of the words just quoted is this: in the beginning man came into being lacking none of the divine goods. His only task was to keep the good things, not to acquire them. But the plotting of enemies stripped him of what he possessed, because he did not keep the good inheritance given to his nature by God. This, then, is the sense of the words. The way this thought is conveyed through the enigmatic words takes the following

[?] form: "My mother's sons," she says, "fought against me; they made me keeper in the vineyard; my own vineyard I did not keep." In a few words the text teaches much doctrine. First, as Paul also declared, all things are from God, and there is one God and Father, from whom are all things, and nothing that exists has its being otherwise than through him and from him. "For all things," it says, "came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being." Now since everything God made is very good (for he made all things in wisdom), he gave rational nature the grace of free will and added the power to discover what it desires, so that what depends on us might have its place, and the good might not be compelled and involuntary but the achievement of free choice. But since this free movement leads us with sovereign authority toward whatever seems good to us, someone was found among the beings who misused this freedom and, in the words of the Apostle, became an inventor of evil things. Because he too is from God, he is our brother. But because he willingly fell away from participation in the good, devised the entrance of evils, and became the father of lies, he set himself in the ranks of the enemy against all those whose choice aims at what is better. Through him, then, the occasion for the flight from good things was also given to the rest

[?] that arises within. This is what happened to human nature as well: she who was once black but is now beautiful lays the blame for her gloomy appearance on these sons of her mother. By what she says she teaches us that there is one cause of all existing things, a kind of father to them all, namely the cause of whatever exists. For this reason everything we can conceive among existing things is brother and sister to everything else; but the difference of free choice has split nature into friend and foe. Those who have stood apart from their relation to the good, and by turning away from the better have given evil its existence (for evil has no other existence than separation from the better), put all their effort and ingenuity into drawing others too into partnership in evil. That is why she says, "The sons of my mother" (the plural shows how many-sided wickedness is) "have made war in me." They do not fight from outside by invasion; they make the soul itself the battlefield of the war within it. For in each of us there is war, as the divine Apostle explains when he says: "But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members." So, since this civil war was stirred up within me by my brothers, the enemies of my salvation, I became black, defeated by the enemy, and "my own vineyard I did not keep." We should take the vineyard to be the same as paradise. For there too man was appointed to keep paradise; but neglect of that keeping casts man out of paradise, removes him from the east, and makes him a dweller in the west. That is why the East appears to the west. For it says, "Sing to the Lord who rides upon the west," so that, as the light shines in the darkness, the darkness may be changed into the ray of light, and the black one may become beautiful again. The apparent mismatch between the wording and the meaning we have found can be resolved in this way. "They made me," she says, "a keeper in the vineyards." This is equivalent to "They have made Jerusalem a fruit-watcher's hut." For it was not they who appointed her keeper of the divine vineyard, as one might suppose at first sight. The one who appointed her is God; they only made war within her and made her "like a booth in a vineyard and like a watchman's hut in a cucumber field." For once she had been deprived through disobedience of the fruit she was guarding, she was left a useless sight, since what had been guarded in her was no longer there. And since God placed man to work and keep paradise, the bride says this: "Though God had placed my soul in life" (for the delight of paradise was life, and God placed man in it to work and keep it), "the enemies removed it from the delight of paradise to labour over their own vineyard, whose cluster yields bitterness and whose grape yields gall." Such a vineyard was Sodom;

such a vine-branch was Gomorrah, burned up together with Sodom, through which the incurable wrath of dragons overflowed in the wicked winepresses of the Sodomites. Even now one can see people who tend and keep such vineyards, who carefully preserve the passions within themselves as if afraid of losing any. You see the wicked keepers of idolatry, both the kind practised through impiety and the kind practised through greed: how they stay awake guarding their evils, thinking it a loss to be deprived of lawlessness. In the other cases too one can likewise see those who have taken pleasure, or arrogance, or vanity, or anything else of that kind deep into themselves, and how they cling to it with all vigilance [?], counting it a gain never to be cleansed of the passions. This, then, is what the bride laments when she says: "I became black for this reason, that while I kept and tended the tares of the enemy and their wicked vine-branches, my own vineyard I did not keep." Oh, how deeply "My own vineyard I did not keep" moves those who listen with feeling! It is plainly a lament [?], stirring the groans of the prophets to compassion: "How has the faithful city, Zion, full of justice, become a harlot?" "How has the daughter of Zion been left like a booth in a vineyard?" "How the city once full of people sits alone! She who ruled over provinces has become a tributary." "How the gold has grown dim, how the good silver has been changed!" How has she become black, who once shone together with the true light? "All these things have happened to me," she says, "because my own vineyard I did not keep." The vineyard is immortality; the vineyard is freedom from passion, likeness to the Divine, and estrangement from evil. The fruit of this vineyard is [?], this bright and ripe cluster [?], gleaming [?] in its form and sweetening the senses of the soul in purity. The tendril of the vineyard is the soul's entwining with and growing into eternal life. The growing branches are the [?] of the virtues, climbing like trees to the height of the angels. The flourishing leaves, gracefully stirred on the branches by the gentle breeze, are the many-sided adornment of the divine virtues that flourish together with the Spirit. "I possessed all these things," she says, "and was made radiant by enjoying them, but because I did not keep the vineyard I was blackened with grief. For when I fell from purity I put on [?] the dark form, since such in appearance is the garment of skin. But now that I have become beautiful and full of light again through the uprightness that loved me, I am wary of [?], lest I lose my beauty again, [?] the way to keep it safe." For this reason she leaves off speaking to the maidens and calls on the bridegroom again in prayer, making her loving relation to the one she longs for into his name. For what does she say? "Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture your flock, where you

make it rest at noon, lest I become like one veiled among the flocks of your companions." Where do you pasture, O good shepherd, you who carry the whole flock on your shoulders? For the whole of human nature is one sheep, and you took it up on your shoulders. Show me the place of green pasture, make known to me the water of rest, lead me out to the nourishing grass, call me by name, so that I, your sheep, may hear your voice; and through your voice give me eternal life. "Tell me, you whom my soul has loved." That is what I call you, since your name is above every name, inexpressible and beyond the grasp of every rational nature. So the name that makes your goodness known is my soul's relation to you. For how could I not love you, who loved me so much, and that while I was black, that you laid down your life for the sheep you pasture? No greater love can be conceived than this, that you gave your life in exchange for my salvation. "Show me, then," she says, "where you pasture, so that when I find the saving pasture I may be filled with the heavenly food, without eating which no one can enter into life; and running to you, the spring, I may draw from the divine drink that you pour out for the thirsty, the water you made flow from your side when the iron opened that vein. Whoever tastes of it becomes a spring of water welling up to eternal life. For if you pasture me on these things, you will surely make me rest at noon, when I have lain down in peace and rest in the light without shadow." For noon is without shadow on every side, when the sun shines from overhead; and in it you make those you have shepherded lie down, when you receive your children with you into your bed. But no one is found worthy of the noonday rest who has not become a son of light and a son of the day. Whoever separates himself equally from the darkness of evening and the darkness of dawn, that is, from where evil begins and where it ends, is made to rest at noon by the sun of righteousness. "Make known to me, then," she says, "how I must lie down to rest, and what the way to the noonday rest is, lest I slip from your good guidance [?] and ignorance of the truth herd me together with flocks that are not yours." She said this in anxiety over the beauty that had come to her from God, asking to learn how her loveliness might stay with her forever. But she is not yet [?] found worthy of the bridegroom's voice, because God had foreseen something better for her: that delay in enjoyment might kindle her to a greater desire, so that her joy might grow along with her longing. Instead, the friends of the bridegroom speak with her, and by their counsel show her how to keep safe the goods she has. For the text runs as follows: "If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out in the heels of the flocks

and pasture the kids by the shepherds' tents." The meaning of these words is quite clear from the sequence of what we have examined, but the syntax seems somewhat obscure. What, then, is the meaning? Our surest safeguard is not to be ignorant of ourselves, and not to look at something else among the things around us and suppose that we are looking at ourselves. Yet this is exactly what happens to those who have never examined themselves: when they see strength in themselves, or beauty, or reputation, or power, or an abundance of wealth, or vanity, or pomp, or bodily size, or good looks, or anything else of the kind, they think that this is what they are. That is why they are unreliable guardians of themselves: through their attachment to what belongs to another, they leave what is their own unguarded. For how could anyone guard what he does not know? So the surest protection of the goods within us is not to be ignorant of ourselves: for each of us to know himself as he really is and to distinguish himself precisely from what surrounds him, so that he does not unknowingly guard what belongs to another in place of himself. For whoever looks to life in this world and judges the honours of this place worth guarding does not know how to distinguish what is his own from what belongs to another. Nothing that passes away is ours. How could anyone hold on to what is transient and flowing? Since, then, the intelligible and immaterial nature is abiding and always the same, while matter passes away in a kind of flux and motion, constantly changing, it follows necessarily that whoever separates himself from what stands firm is swept along with what is unstable; and whoever [?] what passes away and abandons what stands firm misses both, having [?] the one and being unable to hold on to the other. That is why the counsel of the bridegroom's friends speaks the words quoted: "If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out in the heels of the flocks and pasture the kids by the tents of the flocks." What does this mean? That whoever is ignorant of himself falls out of the flock of sheep and comes to graze with the kids, whose place has been pushed off to the left. For so the good shepherd sets the sheep on his right, but separates the kids from the better lot and sets them on his left. This, then, is what we are taught by the counsel of the bridegroom's friends: that we must look to the very nature of things, and not try to hit the truth by following tracks that lead us astray. But the account of these things must be set out more clearly. Many people do not judge for themselves how things are by nature; instead they look to the custom of those who went before them and so fail to judge [?] soundly, putting forward as the criterion of the good not some sensible reasoning but irrational custom. Hence they push themselves into offices and positions of power, and set great store by worldly distinction and material pomp, though it is unclear how each of these things will end after this life. For custom is no safe guarantor of what is to come, since its end is often found to be [?], not a flock of sheep. You surely understand

the point from the words of the Gospel. But whoever looks to what is proper to human nature, that is, reason, will despise irrational custom and will choose nothing as good that does not bring profit to the soul. So we must not look at the tracks of the cattle, which those who travelled through life before us have stamped with their heels upon this earthly life. For which choice is better is hidden from what we can see, until we are outside this life and there learn whom we have followed. So whoever does not distinguish the good from the worse by looking at things themselves, but follows the tracks of those who went before, and makes the past custom of life the teacher of his own, often turns out, without realising it, at the time of the just judgment, to be a kid instead of a sheep. So we can hear the friends saying this: "You, O soul, who from black have become beautiful, if you care that the grace of your beauty should stay with you forever, do not wander after the tracks of those who have travelled through life before you. For it is not clear that the path you see is not a track of kids. You follow behind them, but those who wore the path with their footprints cannot be seen; so when you have passed through life and slipped down into the fold of death, you may be added to the herd of the kids whom you unknowingly followed along the tracks of life. For if you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out in the heels of the flocks and pasture the kids by the tents of the flocks." This can be understood more clearly from another copy of the text, so that the syntax of the words does not seem incoherent. For it reads: "If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, you have gone out from the heels of the flock and you pasture kids instead of the tents of flocks." Thus the meaning shown in these words agrees exactly with the interpretation of the text given above. "So, to avoid suffering these things," says the word, "attend to yourself." For this is the safe safeguard of good things: know how far your Maker has honoured you above the rest of creation. The heaven did not become the image of God, nor the moon, nor the sun, nor the beauty of the stars, nor anything else that can be seen in creation. You alone have become the likeness of the nature that surpasses all understanding, the resemblance of incorruptible beauty, the imprint of the true Godhead, the vessel of the blessed life, the impression of the true light. When you look to him, you become what he is, imitating the one who shines in you by the radiance reflected back from your purity. Nothing that exists is so great that it can be measured against your greatness. The whole heaven is spanned by God's hand, and the earth and the sea are enclosed in the hollow of his palm. Yet he who is so great and so mighty, who holds all creation in his palm, becomes wholly contained in you, dwells in you, and is not cramped as he moves through your whole nature, he who said: "I will dwell

in them and walk among them." If you see these things, you will not busy [?] your eye with anything on earth. Why do I say this? Not even the heaven will seem marvellous to you. For how can you marvel at the heavens, [?] when they pass away, while you abide forever with the Eternal [?]? You will not marvel at the breadth of the earth, nor at the seas stretched out without limit, over which you were appointed to preside, like the driver of a team of colts, keeping these elements obedient to your will and under your authority. For the earth serves you for the needs of life, and the sea, like a well-broken colt, offers you its back and receives man as its rider. If, then, you know yourself, O beautiful among women, you will look down on the whole world and, intent on the immaterial good, will always disregard the misleading tracks of this life. So always attend to yourself, and you will never stray among the herd of the kids. You will not be shown to be a kid instead of a sheep at the time of judgment, nor be separated from the seat on the right; but you will hear the sweet voice that says to the woolly and gentle sheep: "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." May we too be found worthy of this, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.

"To my mare among Pharaoh's chariots I have likened you, my close one. How lovely your cheeks have become, like turtledoves, your neck like necklaces. We will make you likenesses of gold, with studs of silver. While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance. My kinsman is to me a sachet of myrrh; he shall lodge between my breasts. My kinsman is to me a cluster of Cyprus, in the vineyards of Engedi." All that we examined [?] before the present reading, in the opening of the Song of Songs, is like the glow that comes at dawn after the night. That glow is not yet pure light but a prelude to light; and what was said there was such as to announce to us the rising of the true light, without yet containing the sun's disk itself shining out far and wide. For in those passages it is the bride who speaks, and the friends, and the maidens; but now the voice of the bridegroom himself rises like the disk of the sun, hiding with the brightness of its rays all the brilliance of the stars that had appeared and of the dawn that had faintly glimmered. All those passages had the power of purifications and sprinklings, by which the soul is cleansed and prepared to receive divine things; but the present word is a participation in the Godhead itself, as God the Word, by his own voice, gives the hearer a share in his undefiled power. And

just as at Sinai Israel was prepared beforehand by purifications for two days, and on the third, at dawn, was found worthy of the appearance of God, no longer busy washing garments but openly receiving God himself, for whose sake it had washed away the filth of the soul by the earlier purifications, so now too the contemplation of the opening of the Song in the preceding discourses, corresponding to the two preceding days, has done this much good: it has washed and rinsed our understanding of what is said clean of the filth of the flesh. But today, which is the third day, after the first and second purification, God the Word himself will appear. He will not make his presence plain and evident by darkness and storm and the sound of a trumpet and fire smouldering fearfully over the whole mountain from its base to its summit; he will come sweet and approachable, having changed from that fearful form to the gladness of a bridegroom. For the bride asked to learn the places of rest where the good shepherd stays, so as not to suffer anything unwanted through ignorance. Then the friends set out for her the safe criterion of truth: that the soul should look to itself and know itself. For they declared that ignorance of oneself is the beginning and consequence [?] of not knowing anything else one ought to know. How could anyone learn anything else while ignorant of himself? After this, since the governing part of her soul has now been sufficiently purified, the Word rises upon her who longs for him, urging her toward perfection by approving what she already has. For praise of good deeds makes those who have done them more eager for what is better.

What, then, is the word spoken by the true Word to the virgin? "To my mare," he says, "among Pharaoh's chariots I have likened you, my close one." But since the meaning of these words cannot be seen at first sight, it is right to examine the passage carefully, as far as we can. From the history we learned of another force that was arrayed against Pharaoh's cavalry: a cloud, a rod, a violent wind, the sea divided in two, the deep turned to dust, walls made of waves, and a dry abyss, made into dry land in the midst of the springs of water. Through all these things salvation came to the Israelites, while Pharaoh, with his whole army, his horses and his chariots, was covered by the waves. Since, then, no cavalry force was brought against the Egyptian army, it would be hard to learn to what mare, appearing against the Egyptian chariots, the bride is now compared by the Word. For he says, "To my mare, which won the victory among Pharaoh's chariots, I have likened you, my close one." From this it is clear that, just as no one can be defeated in a sea battle unless a naval force destroys the enemy's strength in their ships, so no one could be defeated in a cavalry battle unless some cavalry force were arrayed against him from the other side. If, then, the strongest part of the Egyptian army, [?]

Patrol. Gr. XLIV.

[?] …was the horse. The power brought against them invisibly, through which the victory over the Egyptians was won, the text named a “horse.” For they too sensed Someone fighting against them, and they shouted to one another, “The Lord is fighting against the Egyptians; let us flee from the face of the Lord.” Clearly the true Commander-in-chief armed his own force to match the equipment of the enemy. So there was an invisible power, working the destruction of the Egyptians through the wonders at the sea, which the text named a horse. We take this to be the angelic host, of which the prophet says, “You will mount your horses, and your riding is salvation.” David too spoke of God’s chariot, saying, “The chariot of God is ten-thousandfold,” to which the thousands of those who prosper are yoked. Further, the power that took the prophet Elijah up from earth to the region of the upper air [?] is called by Scripture by the name of horses, and the narrative calls the prophet himself “the chariot of Israel and its horseman.” And those who go about the whole inhabited world, through whom it is settled and kept at rest, the prophet Zechariah called horses, speaking with the rider who stands between the two mountains. So the Owner of all things has a kind of cavalry: one horse carries the prophet up, another settles the world, another is yoked to the chariot, another takes its own rider for the salvation of humankind, and another destroys the power of Egypt. Since, then, the divine Scriptures show many differences among these horses through what they do, it is to the horse that destroys the Egyptian power that the soul is likened which has drawn near to God along the course of virtue. For the Word says to her, “To my mare among Pharaoh’s chariots I have likened you, my close one.” The text has packed many great praises into this, and the likening to this mare is a kind of catalogue of achievements.
