For everything recorded of Israel during its sojourn among the Egyptians—the slavery, the straw, the clay, the brick-making, all the toil on the land, the harsh overseers of such work who demanded of them each day their tribute of clay, on whose account the water turns to blood, and the light is darkened, and frogs creep into the houses, and the soot of the furnace makes boils break out on bodies, and all the rest one by one—the locust, the gnats, the thunder, the hail, the sufferings of the firstborn—all these, and whatever the narrative relates on the better side, through which salvation comes to the Israelites, are matter for praising the soul joined to God. For she would not have been likened to that power which destroyed the evils of the Egyptians, through which Israel is set free from wicked tyranny, unless she too had accomplished all these things: both what brings Egypt down and what prepares the journey toward God of those who are moving to the land of promise

out of the Egyptian mud. Since, then, as the divine Apostle says, everything contained in the divinely inspired Scripture was written for our instruction, the Word advises us nothing else through what is said to the bride than this: that we too must receive the Word as rider upon ourselves, overcome the Egyptian horse with its chariots and riders, drown all its wicked dominion in the water, and so be made like that power, as though we were a horse, having let the hostile army loose into the water. To grasp the meaning more clearly, it is this: no one can be made like the mare through which the chariots of the Egyptians were sunk in the deep unless, being freed through the mystical water from slavery to the adversary, he leaves behind in the water every Egyptian thought and every foreign vice and sin, and comes up pure, bringing nothing of the Egyptian conscience with him into his subsequent life. For one who has been thoroughly cleansed of all the Egyptian plagues—blood, frogs, boils, darkness, locusts and gnats, hail, the rain of fire, and the rest that the narrative records—is worthy to be likened to that power on which the Word rides. And surely we are not ignorant of what the plagues signify: how blood becomes a plague for the Egyptians, and the stench of the frogs, and the change of light into darkness, and all the rest in turn. For who does not know by what sort of life a person becomes blood, changing from what was once drinkable into corruption? And what he does to breed the stink of frogs in his own house? And how he turns a life of light into works dear to the night and full of gloom, through which the furnace of Gehenna makes the evil boils of condemnation break out? In the same way it would be easy to turn each of the evils in Egypt to the instruction and correction of the hearer, but it would be superfluous to lengthen the discourse with what is agreed by all. If, then, we rise above these things and things like them, and draw near to God, we too shall certainly hear, “To my mare among Pharaoh’s chariots I have likened you, my close one.” But perhaps the likening to a horse grieves those who are chaste and have trained themselves in a pure life, since many of the prophets forbid us to become like horses. Jeremiah marked adulterous frenzy by the name of horses when he said, “They became horses mad for females; each neighed after his neighbor’s wife.” And the great David makes it a fearful thing to become like a horse or a mule, whose jaws he commands to be held in with muzzle and bridle. That is why the following words soothe such a thought, as if saying: “Your jaws are not such that, though you are a horse, they need muzzle and bridle to the point of choking; rather your jaw is adorned with the purity of turtledoves.”

For it says, “How lovely your cheeks have become, like turtledoves!” Those who have observed such things testify that this bird, if parted from its mate, remains unpaired from then on, so that chastity is achieved in it by nature. That is why the Word took this bird into the riddle of its praises: so that, instead of a bridle, the likeness of the turtledove might be on the jaw of the divine mare, signifying that a pure life befits such a mare. Hence the Word says to her in admiration, “How lovely your cheeks have become, like turtledoves!” To this it adds another praise by way of a likeness, saying, “Your neck is like little necklaces.” Having once entered upon the figurative meaning, it devises the bride’s praise from what is observed in horses. For it praises the neck curved in the shape of a circle, which we see in spirited colts. The mention of necklaces indicates the circle, and this shape, displayed in the neck, makes the colt handsomer than it would otherwise be. The word hormos is used in its proper sense of coastal places where the shore is hollowed inward in the shape of a crescent, receives the sea into its bay, and gives rest to those sailing in from the open sea. By a metaphor based on the shape, the ornament worn around the neck is also called hormos. And when we use the diminutive hormiskos instead of hormos, by such a word we indicate a likeness of the shape on a small scale. The likeness of the neck to necklaces, then, shows many things that contribute to the bride’s praise. First, a colt that bends its neck into the shape of a circle looks at its own footing, and so runs its course without stumbling and safely, neither tripping on a stone nor stepping into empty space over a pit. And this is no small praise for a soul: to look to itself and to press on the divine course in all safety, leaping over and stepping across every obstacle on the course that arises from temptations. Next, the original sense of the word hormos itself, from which, because of the likeness in shape, the ornament for the neck has been named hormiskos, contains an abundance of great praises when the neck is likened to harbors. What are the praises the text shows us by these things? A harbor is something sweet and saving to those who sail into it, and so is coming upon a calm anchorage after hardships at sea. There, forgetting the evils of the sea, they give themselves wholly to rest, consoling their long toils with quiet; they no longer have any fear of shipwreck, nor suspicion of hidden reefs, nor danger from pirates, nor turbulence of winds, nor a sea swelling up from the depths under the winds. Instead the storm-tossed are beyond all such dangers, since the sea lies calm in the harbor. If, then, someone so establishes his own soul that it is itself calm, in a quiet without waves, not stirred at all by the winds

of wickedness, neither swelling with pride, nor foaming with the waves of anger, nor tossed about by some other passion and carried around by every wind that raises the varied waves of the passions—if, then, the soul is itself in such a state, and also calms within itself those storm-tossed on the sea of life in the swells of all kinds of evils, spreading out for them a life of virtue that is utterly smooth and waveless, so that those who come into her are beyond the evils of shipwreck, then she is rightly likened to the necklaces the Word praises, the plural signifying perfection in every kind of virtue. For if she had been compared to only one necklace, the praise would surely have been incomplete, since it would not bear the same witness to the other virtues; as it is, the likening to many necklaces embraces in the text the witness to all the virtues. And this is a piece of advice offered by the Word to the whole Church: that we must not look to one particular good and be careless about the rest of right conduct. Rather, if chastity has become a necklace for you, making your neck shine with a pure life as with pearls, let there be another necklace for you too, enclosing within itself the precious stones of the commandments and adding beauty to your throat; let there be yet another ornament for your neck, a devout and sound faith, encircling the neck of the soul. This is the golden chain made from the pure gold of the knowledge of God, gleaming around the neck, of which the proverb says, “You will receive a crown of graces upon your head, and a golden chain around your neck.” Such, then, is the advice given through the necklaces. Now it is time to add to our study the next words, which the friends of the bridegroom have spoken to the virgin. The text is this: “We will make you likenesses of gold with studs of silver, until the king is at his reclining.” To one who looks at the sequence of the interpretation already given, the meaning of these words seems somehow connected and consistent with it; but the wording, sinking deep into figurative meanings, makes what is shown through the riddles hard to understand. Since the beauty of the soul has been likened to the mare that destroyed the chariots of the Egyptians, that is, to the angelic host, and the noble rider says of that mare that its bridle is purity—which he indicated by likening the cheeks to turtledoves—and that the ornament for its neck is the various necklaces that shine with the virtues, the friends too want to add something to the mare’s beauty, adorning its trappings with likenesses of gold, into which they set the purity of silver as studs, so that the beauty of the ornament may shine the more, the gleam of the silver blending with the brilliance of the gold. But we must leave aside the figurative images and not let the discourse stray from a meaning that benefits us. The soul cleansed through the virtues has been likened to that mare.

But it has not yet come under the Word’s control, nor has it carried upon itself the One who rides such horses for salvation. For the horse must first be adorned in every way, and only then receive the King as its rider. Whether he who, according to the Prophet, mounts us as his horses and rides for our salvation fits the horse to himself from above, or whether he comes to be within us, dwelling and walking about in us and penetrating to the depths of our soul, makes no difference to the meaning. For in whomever one of the two happens, the other is accomplished along with it. Whoever has God upon himself certainly has him within himself as well; and whoever has received him within himself has gone beneath, and carries, the One who has come to be in him. So the King is about to rest upon this horse. In the case of the divine power, as has been said, sitting and reclining are the same thing; for whichever of the two happens in us, the grace is equal. Since, then, the King’s attendants make the horse fit to receive him by means of the ornaments—and with God, being in someone and being upon someone are the same—these preparers and servants abandon the consistency of the figurative meaning and make the horse into a couch. “We must,” they say, “make likenesses of gold with studs of silver to beautify the horse’s form, so that the King may be not on a seat,” it says, “but reclining.”

Such, then, is the sequence of the text, as the Word has shown. But it is worth not passing over without study the question why it is not gold itself that is used for adornment, but likenesses of gold, and not silver itself, but studs of that material hammered into the likeness of gold. What we have understood about these things is this. All teaching about the ineffable nature, however much it may seem to present a lofty conception worthy of God, is a likeness of gold, not gold itself. For it is impossible to represent accurately the good that is beyond thought. Even if someone is a Paul, initiated into hidden things in paradise, even if he hears unutterable words, thoughts about God remain inexpressible; for he says that the words of these thoughts are unspeakable. Those, then, who instill in us good reflections for understanding the mysteries cannot say what that nature is in itself, but they speak of “the radiance of glory,” and “the exact imprint of his being,” “the form of God,” “the Word in the beginning,” “the Word who is God.” All these seem gold to us who have not beheld that treasure; but to those able to look up toward the truth they are a likeness of gold and not gold, showing through the fine studs of silver. Silver is the meaning conveyed in words, as Scripture says: “The tongue of the righteous is refined silver.” What is shown through these things, then, is this: the divine nature lies beyond every comprehending thought, and the notion of it that arises in us

is a likeness of what is sought. For it does not show that form itself, which no one has seen or can see; but in a mirror and in a riddle it sketches some image of what is sought, which arises in souls from a kind of conjecture. Every word that signifies such thoughts has the force of a point without parts, unable to express what the mind intends; so that every thought falls short of understanding God, and every explanatory word seems a tiny point, unable to stretch out to the breadth of the thought. It says, then, that the soul, led by the hand through such thoughts toward the understanding of what cannot be grasped, must by faith alone make the nature that surpasses all understanding dwell within itself. And this is what the friends say: “O soul, so well likened to the horse, let us make you certain images and likenesses of the truth.” For such is the power of the silver of these words that the words seem to be like sparks of kindling, unable to express precisely the thought contained in them. “But when you have received them, you will become, through faith, both the mount and the dwelling-place of the One who is about to recline in you by dwelling in you; for you will become both throne and house of the same One.” Perhaps one might say that Paul’s soul, and any other like it, was counted worthy of such words. For once he had become a chosen vessel for the Master, he had the Lord both upon himself and within himself: he became a horse in carrying his name before nations and kings; and in no longer living himself, but showing Christ living in him and giving proof of Christ speaking in him, he became a house that contains the nature that cannot be contained. When the friends of the bridegroom have bestowed these gifts on the pure and virgin soul (and these would be the ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation), the bride becomes somehow more perfect by the addition of the gifts. And drawing nearer to the one she longs for, before his beauty appears to her eyes, she touches what she seeks through the sense of smell, as though recognizing by her power of smell the distinctive scent of someone’s skin. She says that she has recognized his scent by the fragrance of the ointment whose name is nard, using these words to the friends: “My nard gave forth his scent.” “Just as you,” she says, “bestow on us not the pure gold of the Godhead itself, but likenesses of the gold, through thoughts we can take in—not unveiling the truth about him in a far-shining word, but offering certain images of what is sought through the brevity of the studs of the silver of speech—so I too, through the sweet breath of my ointment, have received his very fragrance with my sense

of smell.” What is said seems to me to have this kind of meaning. Ointment of this sort is produced by a skillful and measured mixture of many different spices, each fragrant with its own particular quality, and one fragrant herb among those mixed in, whose name is nard, gives its name to the whole compound; and the pure sense receives as the very fragrance of the bridegroom the scent gathered together into one fragrance from all the aromatic qualities. By these words, we think, the Word teaches us this: what that which is above the whole structure and ordering of beings is in its essence is unapproachable, untouchable, and incomprehensible; but the fragrance compounded in us through the purity of the virtues takes its place for us, imitating by its own purity what is undefiled by nature, by its goodness the Good, by its incorruptibility the Incorruptible, by its unchangeableness the Unchangeable, and by all the virtues achieved in us the true Virtue, of which the prophet Habakkuk says that it covered all the heavens. So when she tells the friends of the bridegroom, “My nard gives me his scent,” she seems to me to be philosophizing and saying something like this: if someone gathers every fragrant flower or spice from the varied meadows of virtue, makes his whole life fragrant through the sweet scent of each of his practices, and becomes perfect in all things, he still cannot by nature gaze steadily at God the Word himself, any more than at the disk of the sun; but he sees the sun within himself as in a mirror. For the rays of that true and divine Virtue, shining in a purified life through the freedom from passion that flows from them, make the invisible visible to us and the unapproachable graspable, painting the sun in our mirror. As far as the underlying meaning goes, it is the same whether we speak of the sun’s rays, or the outflowings of virtue, or the fragrance of spices. Whichever of these we take for the purpose of the discourse, the thought that arises from them all is one: that through the virtues the knowledge of the Good that surpasses all understanding arises in us, just as one may infer the archetypal beauty from an image. So too Paul, the bride, who imitated the bridegroom through the virtues and painted in himself through his life the unapproachable beauty, compounding this nard from the fruits of the Spirit—love, joy, peace, and the like—said that he was the fragrance of Christ. He smelled within himself that unapproachable and surpassing grace, and offered himself to others like incense to partake of freely; and according to the disposition of each, he became to them either a life-giving or a death-bringing fragrance. In the same way, if the same ointment is set before a beetle and a dove, it does not have the same effect on both: the dove grows stronger through the fragrance,

…of the perfume, while the beetle perishes. In the same way the great Paul was that divine incense. If anyone was a dove, like Titus, or Silvanus, or Timothy, he shared with him the fragrance of the perfume and advanced in every good thing by following his example. But if anyone was a Demas, or an Alexander, or a Hermogenes, such people could not bear the incense of self-control, and like beetles they were driven away by the fragrance. That is why the one who breathed out such perfumes said, “We are the aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the one a scent from death to death, to the other a scent from life to life.” Whether the nard of the Gospel has any kinship with the bride's perfume, anyone who wishes may work out from what is written what that nard was: the pure nard, the very costly nard, which was poured over the Lord's head and filled the whole house with its fragrance. For perhaps that perfume is no stranger to this perfume, which gives the bride the scent of the bridegroom, and which in the Gospel, poured over the Lord, fills with fragrance the house where the banquet was held. It seems to me that there too the woman, by a kind of prophetic spirit, foretold through the perfume the mystery of his death, as the Lord testifies about what she had done when he says, “She has anointed me beforehand for burial.” And he suggests that the house filled with fragrance should be understood as the whole world and the entire inhabited earth, when he says, “Wherever this gospel is preached in the whole world, the fragrance of the deed will be spread along with it [?] … in the proclamation of the Gospel, and a memorial

of her,” he says, “the Gospel will be.” So in the Song of Songs the nard gives the bride the scent of the bridegroom, while in the Gospel the nard that once filled the house becomes the fragrance of Christ for the whole body of the Church throughout the inhabited earth and the whole world. Perhaps, then, some shared meaning is found in both, as if one the…

[?] But enough of this. The next saying seems to fit the plot of the wedding drama, as spoken by the one made ready in the bridal chamber. Yet it reveals a greater and more perfect philosophy, which only those already perfected can achieve. What, then, does it say? “My kinsman is to me a sachet of myrrh; he shall lodge between my breasts.” They say that women who love adornment take care not only to devise outward ornaments for themselves [?] for the sake of those they live with, but also make it their practice to seem sweeter to their husbands through some fragrance on their bodies. For this purpose they hide a suitable perfume within the folds of their clothing, and as it gives off its own scent, the body is tinged with the fragrance of the perfume. Since

this is their custom, see what this high-minded maiden dares to say. “My sachet,” she says, “which I hang from my neck onto my breast, and by which I give my body its fragrance, is not some other fragrant spice. The Lord himself has become myrrh and lies in the sachet of my conscience, lodging in my very heart.” For those who have studied such matters say that the heart is situated in the middle between the breasts. There, the bride says, she keeps the sachet, in the place where the good is stored up as treasure. They also say that the heart is a kind of source of the heat within us. From it heat is distributed through the arteries to the whole body, and by it the members of the body become warm and full of life, kept warm by the fire of the heart. So the soul that has received the fragrance of Christ in her ruling faculty, and has made her heart the sachet for such incense, makes every particular pursuit of her life glow, like the members of a body, with the spirit that spreads from the heart; and no lawlessness chills her love for God in any member of the body. But let us move on to the next saying. Let us hear what the flourishing vine says about her fruit, the vine that is spread out, as the Prophet says, along all the sides of God's house, and that twines the tendrils of love around the divine and pure life. “My kinsman is to me a cluster of henna blossom in the vineyards of Engedi,” she says. Who is so blessed, or rather, who so surpasses all blessedness, that when he looks at his own fruit he sees in the very cluster of his own soul the master of the vineyard? See how far she has grown! She recognized the bridegroom's fragrance in her own nard, she made myrrh fragrant for him, and she held the spice in the sachet of her heart so that the good might stay with her always without fading away. Now she becomes the mother of the divine cluster, which before the passion is in blossom (that is what “henna blossom” means) and in the passion pours out wine. For the wine that gladdens the heart becomes, and is called, the blood of the grape after the saving dispensation of the passion. The cluster offers a twofold enjoyment: one from the blossom, when it delights the senses with its fragrance, and the other from the fruit once it is ripe, when one may either feast on eating it or be cheered by its wine at banquets. Here the bride asks that the blossoming cluster bear fruit, calling the vine blossom “henna.” For the child Jesus who was born to us advances in different ways in those who receive him, in wisdom and stature and grace. He is not the same in everyone, but appears according to the measure of the one in whom he comes to be, as far as the one who receives him is able: as an infant, or as advancing, or as grown to perfection. In this he is like the cluster of grapes, which is not always seen on the vine in the same form, but changes

its form with time, blooming, blossoming, maturing, ripening. So the vine makes a promise through its own fruit, which is not yet ripe for wine but awaits the fullness of time. Even so, it does not fail to give delight. Instead of taste it gladdens the sense of smell with the expectation of good things, sweetening the senses of the soul with the scents of hope. For when the hoped-for grace is sure and beyond doubt, that certainty becomes enjoyment for those who wait patiently for what is expected. So the cluster of henna blossom is a cluster that promises wine but has not yet become wine; through its blossom (and hope is the blossom) it guarantees the grace to come. The addition of “Engedi” signifies the rich soil in which the vine is rooted and produces well-nourished, sweet fruit. Those who have written about the geography of the region say that the territory of Engedi is well suited to raising grapes. Now the one whose will is in harmony with the law of the Lord, and who meditates on it all night and all day, becomes an evergreen tree, enriched by streams of water, and yields its fruit in due season. For this reason the bridegroom's vine too, rooted in Engedi, the rich place, that is, in a deep mind watered by divine teachings and growing through them, has borne this fair-blossoming, flowering cluster, in which she sees her own farmer and gardener. How blessed is such a crop, whose fruit is made like the form of the bridegroom! For he is the true light, and true life, and true righteousness, as Wisdom says, and everything of this kind. So when someone becomes through his works what the bridegroom is, then in looking at the cluster of his own conscience he sees the bridegroom himself in it. The soul perceives the light of truth in the luminous and pure life, and says, “My cluster is in blossom through its flower; he himself is the true cluster.” He showed himself on the wooden pole, and his blood becomes drink and salvation for those who are saved and who rejoice, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.

“Behold, you are beautiful, my close one; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves'. Behold, you are beautiful, my kinsman, and lovely indeed. Our couch is shaded; our beams are cedars, our panels are cypresses. A flower of the plain, a lily of the valleys. As a lily among thorns, so is my close one among the daughters. As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my kinsman among the sons. In his shade I longed to be, and I sat down, and his fruit was sweet in my throat. Bring me into the house of wine; set love upon me. Strengthen me with perfumes, heap me with apples, for I am wounded by love. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. I have charged you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field, that you not rouse or awaken love until it pleases.”

They say that when people refine gold, and the beauty of its brilliance has been dimmed by some baser material that happened to get mixed in, they cure the discoloration by smelting it in the fire. They do this many times, and after each smelting they check how much brighter the gold [?] has become in each successive stage compared with the one before. They do not stop purifying the material with fire until the very look of the gold testifies that it is pure and unalloyed. Why we have mentioned this as we take up the contemplation of the passage just read will become clear to us from the meaning of the text itself. At the beginning human nature was a kind of gold, shining in its likeness to the pure good. But afterwards it became discolored and black through the admixture of evil, as we heard from the bride at the beginning of the Song: neglect of the vineyard made her black. God, who crafts all things in wisdom, heals her ugliness, not by contriving some new beauty for her that did not exist before, but by leading her back to her original grace. He melts down the one who was blackened by evil and recasts her into purity. Expert assayers of gold, after the first smelting, check how far the material has advanced in beauty by burning off its dross in the fire. After a second smelting, if it has not been sufficiently purified beyond the first, they reckon up the beauty that has been added, and by doing the same many times they always recognize the increases in beauty through their skilled testing. In the same way, the one who heals the blackened gold has now brightened the soul, as in a crucible, through the remedies he applied to her. In the earlier passages he bore witness to her appearance as having the comeliness of a horse; but now he welcomes the beauty that has appeared in her as the beauty of a maiden. For he says, “Behold, you are beautiful, my close one; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes

Through these words the Word teaches that the recovery of beauty consists in coming close to the source of the good and approaching again the true beauty from which she had departed. For he says, “Behold, you are beautiful, my close one.” “This is why you were not beautiful before: you were estranged from the archetypal beauty and, through your wicked closeness to evil, you were changed into something hideous.” What is being said is this. Human nature has become receptive of whatever it chooses, and it is changed into whatever the inclination of its free choice leads it toward. When it admits the passion of anger, it becomes wrathful; when desire prevails, it dissolves into pleasure. When it inclines toward cowardice and fear and the other particular passions, it takes on the form of each of them. So too, on the other hand, when it admits patience, purity, peaceableness, freedom from anger and from grief, courage, and fearlessness, it bears the stamp of each of these

as the soul rests calm and untroubled. Now since virtue stands directly opposed to vice, it follows that both cannot be present in one person at the same time. Whoever abandons self-control is certainly living a dissolute life, and whoever loathes an impure life has achieved purity by turning away from evil. So it is with everything else: the humble person has parted from pride, and the one who has puffed himself up with conceit has thrust humility away. But why spend time going through each one? In the case of things that are opposed by nature, the absence of one means the presence and existence of the other. Since our free choice is such that it has the power to be conformed to whatever it wishes, the Word rightly says to the one who has been made beautiful: “By departing from fellowship with evil you have drawn close to me; and by approaching the unapproachable beauty you yourself have become beautiful, formed like a mirror to my likeness.” For human nature is truly like a mirror, changing according to the images its choices reflect. If it looks at gold, it appears as gold, and by reflection displays the very gleam of the metal. If something hideous appears in it, it takes on that ugliness too by resemblance, mimicking on its own surface a frog, or a toad, or a centipede, or some other unpleasant sight, whichever of these is found facing it. So the soul purified by the Word has put evil behind her, received within herself the disk of the sun, and shines together with the light that is seen in her. That is why the Word says to her, “You have now become beautiful by drawing close to my light, attracting a share in beauty by your nearness.” “Behold, you are beautiful,” he says, “my close one.” Then he pauses, and as if seeing her grown in some further increase and intensity of beauty, he repeats the same words: “Behold, you are beautiful.” But in the first place he called her his close one; here he names her by the appearance of her eyes: “For your eyes,” he says, “are doves'.” Earlier, when she was likened to a horse, the praise lay in her cheek and neck. But now that her own beauty has appeared, it is the grace of her eyes that is praised. And the praise of her eyes is that they are doves' eyes. This seems to me to convey the following sense. In the clear pupils of the eyes the faces of those who look into them can be seen. For those learned in natural science say that the eye produces sight by receiving the impressions of the images that flow off from visible things. That is why the form of the dove reflected in her pupils becomes praise of the beauty of her eyes. For whatever one gazes at, one receives its likeness within oneself. So the one who no longer looks to flesh and blood but looks toward the spiritual life, as the Apostle says, living by the Spirit, walking by the Spirit, putting to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit, and becoming wholly spiritual, neither soulish nor fleshly: for this reason

the soul that has given up its attachment to the body is praised for having the form of the dove in her eyes. That is, the character of the spiritual life shines out in the soul's power of insight. Now that her eye has become pure and able to receive the character of the dove, she is able to behold the bridegroom's beauty too. For now [?] the maiden gazes on the bridegroom's form, once she has the dove in her eyes. For no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit. And she says, “Behold, you are beautiful, my kinsman, and lovely indeed. Since nothing else seems beautiful to me, and I have turned away from everything that was formerly counted beautiful, my judgment of beauty is no longer led astray into thinking anything beautiful besides you: not human praise, not glory, not fame, not worldly power. To those who see only with the senses, these things are tinged with the appearance of beauty, but they are not what they are thought to be. For how could anything be beautiful that has no real existence at all? What is honored in this world has its being only in the opinion of those who think it exists. But you are truly beautiful, and not merely beautiful: you are always such in the very essence of beauty, always being what you are. You do not bloom for a season and then shed your bloom again at another season, but your loveliness stretches out together with the eternity of your life. Your name is love for humankind.” For Christ arose for us from Judah, and the Jewish people is a brother to the people that comes to you from the Gentiles. So, because your Godhead was revealed in the flesh, you were rightly named the kinsman of her who longs for you. Then she adds, “Our couch is shaded.” That is, human nature has recognized you, or will recognize you, as shaded through the saving dispensation. “For you came,” she says, “the beautiful one, the kinsman, the lovely one, to our couch, shaded. If you had not shaded yourself, veiling the undiluted ray of your Godhead with the form of a servant, who could have endured your appearing? For no one shall see the face of God and live. So you came, the lovely one, but having become such as we could receive. You came having shaded the rays of your Godhead with the garment of the body. For how could a mortal and perishable nature have been joined in union with the pure and unapproachable one, unless the shadow of the body had mediated the light to us who live in darkness?” The bride calls it a couch, using a figure of speech to express the blending of human nature with the Divine. So too the great Apostle betroths us as a virgin to Christ, and dresses the soul as a bride, and says that the joining of two into the union of one body is the great mystery of the union of Christ with the Church. For after saying, “The two shall become one flesh,” he added, “This mystery is great, but I am speaking of Christ and the Church.” Because of this mystery, then, the

virgin soul called her fellowship with the Divine a couch. This could not have come about in any other way than by the Lord appearing to us shaded through the body. He is not only bridegroom but also builder: within us he both crafts the house and becomes [?] the whole of the craft. He puts a roof on the house and adorns the work with incorruptible material. Cedar and cypress are of this kind: the strength inherent in their wood is proof against every cause of rot. It does not yield to time, it does not breed moths, it is not spoiled by mold. Of these, the cedars, because they are long, span the breadth of the house in the roof, while the cypresses, through what is called paneling, beautify the inside of the house. The text reads: “The beams of our houses are cedars, our panels are cypress.” Surely the riddles signified by these woods are plain to those who follow the thread of the meaning. In the Gospel the Lord calls the various assaults of temptation “rain.” He says of the one who wisely built his house on the rock that “the rain came down, and the winds blew, and the rivers came,” and the building remained unharmed by them. Because of this evil downpour we need such beams. These would be the virtues, which do not let the floods of temptation in, because they are firm and unyielding and keep themselves from being softened toward evil in times of temptation. We may learn what this means by examining the present text together with the saying in Ecclesiastes. There it says, “Through sloth the beams will sag, and through idleness of hands the house will leak.” Suppose the timbers spanning the roof are weak and slack because they are too thin, and the master of the house is lazy about caring for the roof. He gets no benefit from his roof, because the rain drips in. The roof necessarily sags, giving way under the weight of the water, and the weak timbers cannot hold out but buckle under the pressure of the weight. So the water that has collected in the hollow passes through to the inside, and these drops, as the proverb says, drive a man out of his own house on a rainy day. In this way, through the riddle of the parable, he commands us to be unyielding against the floods of temptation through the firmness of the virtues, so that we do not become softened by the onset of the passions and sag into hollows, and so let such waters flow in from outside into the heart, into our storerooms, where they would spoil what we have stored up. These are the cedars of Lebanon which the Lord planted, in which the sparrows will nest, and which the heron's nest leads. These cedars, then, the virtues, make the house of the bridal chamber secure. In them souls will nest, becoming sparrows and flying above the snares, led by the heron's nest, which [?]…

[?] is the name the text gives it. They say that this bird has an aversion to mating, and that the birds pair with one another only under a kind of natural compulsion, crouching down, chafing against it and showing their distaste. For this reason I think the text uses this name to point, in a riddle, to purity. These, then, are the beams the bride sees on the ceilings of the pure bridal chamber. She also sees the cypress ornament, which makes the visible beauty shine through its smooth and harmonious construction. For she said that the coffers of the ceiling are cypress; and coffers are said to be a well-proportioned, carved fitting-together of boards that decorates the beauty of the ceiling with variety. What, then, do we learn from this? Cypress is naturally fragrant; it also does not admit rot, and it lends itself to every kind of fine carpentry, since it planes smooth and fits well, and is suited to decoration by carving. This, then, I think, is what these words teach us: not only to achieve the virtues as a settled state in the hidden places of the soul, but also not to be careless about seemliness in what is seen. For we must take thought for what is good in the sight of the Lord and of men; we must be made manifest to God, but persuade men; we must have a good testimony from those outside, shine with works of light before men, and walk decently toward outsiders. These are the coffers, made through the fragrance of Christ, of which the cypress is a figure, and crafted in the seemliness of our life, just as the wise master builder Paul knew how to put such things together well and harmoniously when he said, “Let all things be done among you decently and in order.” When these things have been achieved in this way, the beauty within us increases, as the broad plain of our nature puts forth its fragrant and pure flower. The flower's name is lily, whose natural brilliance hints at the radiance of chastity. For the bride describes these things about herself, saying: “After the bridegroom came to our bed, overshadowed by the body—he who built for himself his house, which is me—roofing its covering with the cedars of the virtues and adorning its ceiling with the fragrance of the cypresses, I have become a flower from the plain of nature, surpassing the other flowers in fine color and fragrance. For I have sprung up as a lily from the valleys.” The text runs thus: “I am a flower of the plain, a lily of the valleys.” And truly so is the soul that has been cultivated in the breadth of nature by the means we have already considered. For when we heard “plain,” we understood the breadth of human nature, because it is able to receive many, indeed countless, thoughts, words and teachings. So the soul that has been worked in the manner described by the one who cultivates our nature springs up from the plain of our nature as a fragrant, brilliant and pure flower. And this plain, even if it is called a valley when compared with the heavenly way of life, is no less a plain, and nothing prevents the soul

that has been well cultivated in it from becoming a flower. For the shoot rises from the hollow to the height, as one can see happening with the lily. The stalk of the lily runs up a long way straight from the root, like a reed, and only then puts forth its flower from the top, holding it a good distance away from the earth—so that, I think, its beauty may remain pure on high, unsoiled by contact with the earth. For this reason the just eye, looking on her who has become this, or who has longed to become it—for we have understood both from what was said: either that she boasts of having already become what she longed for, or that she begs the husbandman that she may become a flower, rising through his wisdom from the valleys of human life to the beauty of a lily—whether, then, she wishes to become this or has already become what she wished, the just eye of the bridegroom, seeing the good desire of her who looks toward him, rightly granted that she should become a lily, not choked by the thorns of life. These thorns he named daughters, hinting, I think, without saying so, at the powers hostile to human life, whose father is called the inventor of evil. “As a lily among thorns,” he says, “so is my sister among the daughters.” See how great the progress is in the soul's ascent to the height! The first ascent was to be likened to the horse that destroyed the power of Egypt. The second ascent was to become his close one and to have the eyes of a dove. The third ascent, then, is to be called no longer his close one but the sister of the Master. “Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven,” he says, “is my brother and sister and mother.” Since she has become a flower, therefore, not harmed by the thorny temptations in becoming a lily, and since, forgetting her people and her father's house, she has looked toward the true Father, she is for this reason called the Lord's sister, adopted into this kinship by the Spirit of adoption. And now, set free from fellowship with the daughters of the falsely named father, she again rises higher than herself and sees the mystery through the eyes of the dove—I mean by the spirit of prophecy. What she says is this: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my kinsman among the sons.” What, then, is it that she has seen? Holy Scripture regularly calls the material life of human beings a forest, overgrown with the various kinds of passions, in which destructive beasts lurk and hide. Their nature remains inactive in the light and the sun, and has its strength through darkness. For after the sun has set, the prophet says, when night comes on, the beasts come out of their dens in it. Since, then, the solitary boar that feeds in the forest ravaged the good vine of human nature, as the prophet says, “The boar out of the forest ravaged it, and the wild solitary beast

fed upon it,” for this reason the apple tree springs up in the forest. In being a tree, it is of one substance with human matter—for he was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin; but in bearing such fruit as sweetens the senses of the soul, it differs from the forest even more than the lily differs from the thorns. For the lily's delight extends only to its appearance and its fragrance, while the charm of the apple is aptly shared among three senses: it gladdens the eye with the bloom of its appearance, pleases the sense of smell with its fragrance, and, becoming food, sweetens the organs of taste. Rightly, then, the bride saw how she differs from the Master: he becomes for us the delight of the eyes, being light; perfume to the sense of smell; and life to those who eat. For “whoever eats me will live,” as the Gospel says somewhere. But human nature, when perfected through virtue, becomes a flower, which does not feed the husbandman but adorns itself. For he is not in need of our goods; it is we who need his, as the prophet says, “You have no need of my goods.” For this reason the purified soul sees the bridegroom become an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so that by grafting into himself all the wild branches of the forest he may make them teem with the same fruit. Just as we understood the daughters, since they were likened to thorns, to be the children of the falsely named father—who, growing up beside the flower, in time themselves pass over to the grace of the lily—so here too, when we hear of those likened to the trees of the forest, we have understood that what is meant is not the bridegroom's friends but his opponents. Though they are sons of darkness and children of wrath, he transforms them by sharing his fruit into sons of light and sons of the day. That is why the soul whose senses have been trained says, “His fruit is sweet in my throat”; and the fruit is surely his teaching. “How sweet to my throat are your words,” says the prophet, “sweeter than honey to my mouth.” “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my kinsman among the sons. In his shade I longed to sit, and I sat down, and his fruit was sweet in my throat.” For the senses of the soul are truly sweetened by the Word when the shade of the apple tree walls us off from the scorching heat of temptations, so that we are not burned up by that sun as it blazes on a bare head. And there is no other way to be refreshed under the shade of the tree of life unless desire leads the soul up to it. Do you see why the faculty of desire has been set within you? It is to make you long for the apple, whose enjoyment takes many forms for those who draw near. The eye rests on the bloom of its beauty, the nostril breathes in its fragrance, the body is nourished, the mouth is sweetened, the burning heat is turned away, and the shade becomes a throne on which the soul sits that has refused the seat of the pestilent.

Then she says: “Bring me into the house of wine; set love over me; strengthen me with perfumes; cover me with apples; for I am wounded with love.” See how the soul, aptly likened to the horse, runs the divine course; how with rapid, outstretched leaps she strains toward what lies ahead and does not turn back to what is behind. How much she has already received in what came before! And still she thirsts. So intense is her thirst that she is not satisfied with the bowl of wisdom, nor does she think it enough to cure her thirst that the whole bowl be poured into her mouth. She asks to be brought into the very house of wine, to put her mouth to the very winepresses overflowing with sweet wine, and to see the cluster crushed in the presses, and the vine that nourishes such a cluster, and the husbandman of the true vine, who makes the cluster so plump and sweet. It would be superfluous to explain each of these, since the figurative meaning in each is plain. But she certainly wants also to behold that mystery: how the bridegroom's garments are reddened by the treading of the winepress, of which the prophet says, “Why are your garments red, and your clothing as if from a trodden winepress?” For these and similar reasons she longs to come inside the house in which the mystery of the wine is found. Then, once inside, she leaps again toward something greater. For she asks to be made subject to love. And God is love, according to the words of John; and David declared that for the soul to be subject to him is salvation. “Since, then, I have come into the house of wine,” she says, “subject me to love,” or “set love over me.” However you take the inverted phrasing, the meaning is the same either way: to be set under love and to have love set over her. Or perhaps through this phrase we are taught a doctrine of a more refined kind: what sort of love it is fitting to offer to God, and how to be disposed toward others. For if all things must be done decently and in order, much more is order fitting in such matters. Cain would not have been condemned for dividing wrongly if, after offering rightly, he had also kept what was proper in its order between what was left for his own use and what was dedicated to God. For though he ought to have offered God the first share of the sacrifice from the firstfruits, he gorged himself on the choicer portions and regaled God with the leftovers. One must know, then, the order of love which he teaches through the law: how God is to be loved, how one's neighbor, one's wife and one's enemy, so that the fulfilment of love may not become disordered and confused. For one must love God with all one's heart and soul and strength and understanding; one's neighbor as oneself; and one's wife, if one is of purer soul, as Christ loves the Church, but if one is more subject to passion, as one's own body;

for this is what Paul, who set such matters in order, commands. And the enemy one loves by not returning evil for evil but repaying injustice with kindness. But now one can see that among most people love is confused and disordered, working astray through an incongruous lack of harmony. Money, honors and women, if they happen to be warmly attached to them, they love with all their soul and strength, so much so that they would be willing even to give up their life for them; but God they love only for appearance's sake, and to their neighbor they would scarcely show the love assigned to enemies. And their attitude toward those who hate them is to retaliate with a greater evil against those who first did them harm. “Set love over me, then,” she says, “so that I may render to God as much as is owed, and not miss the fitting measure in the case of each of the others.” Or perhaps this too may be understood from her words: “Since, though I was loved in the beginning, I was counted among the enemies through my disobedience, but now I have returned to the same grace, joined to the bridegroom through love, confirm for me,” she says, “the settled and unchanging state of this grace, you friends of the bridegroom, preserving firm for me, with care and attention, my inclination toward what is better.” Having said this, she passes again to something higher, for she asks to be strengthened with perfumes for steadfastness in good things. “Strengthen me with perfumes,” she says. What strange and novel props! How do perfumes become pillars of a house? How is the firmness of the roof's structure supported by fragrance? Surely it is clear that the business of virtue, achieved in us in many forms, is also named according to the differences of its operations. For virtue is not only seeing the good and coming to share in what is better, but also being kept unwavering in what is noble. Whoever wishes to be strengthened with perfumes, therefore, asks to acquire steadfastness in the virtues. For virtue is the perfume, because it is separated from every foul smell of sin. One might also marvel at what follows from these words: with what she desires the house to be covered. Not with brambles and thorns and grass and straw (or rather, as the Apostle says, not with wood and hay and straw), with which material houses are built; instead, apples become the covering of the house's roof. For she says, “Cover me with apples,” so that this fruit may become all in all to her: beauty, perfume, sweetness, food, refreshment through its shade, the throne that gives rest, the pillar that makes firm, the roof that shelters. As beauty it is looked upon with desire; as perfume it delights the sense of smell; as food it fattens the body and sweetens the taste; as shade it cools the burning heat; as a throne it gives rest from weariness; as the roof of the house it becomes shelter for the one who lives there; as a pillar it provides steadfastness;

as a visible apple it beautifies the ceiling. For what more beautiful sight could one imagine than apples arranged together, when the fruit, neatly set out in close order on some level surface and joined together to the eye, forms a varied pattern, the red of the fruit mingling with the whitish? If, then, it were possible to see such an arrangement of apples on a flat surface suspended overhead, what sight could be more elegant? In the desire for intelligible goods this is not impossible. For the form of that fruit is not heavy, nor weighed down and dragged toward the earth; by its nature it inclines toward the height. For virtue grows upward and looks above. That is why the bride desires the ceiling of her house to be adorned with the beauty of such apples. For I do not think the text's chief concern is that some visible spectacle should be seen through the arrangement of apples on the roof covering. What guidance toward virtue could come from that, unless some thought of benefit to us were contemplated in what is said? What, then, do we take it to mean? He who, out of his love for humanity, sprang up in the forest of our nature became an apple by sharing in flesh and blood. For in this fruit one can see, through its color, a likeness to each of these: by its whiteness it imitates the property of flesh, and the red tint that colors it testifies by its appearance to its kinship with the nature of blood. When, then, the soul that delights in divine things desires to look up at this roof, this is what we are taught by the riddle. By looking up and attending to the apples, we are led to a heavenly way of life through the teachings of the Gospel. These teachings he who comes from above and is above all showed us through his manifestation in the flesh, displaying in himself the patterns of every good way of life, as the Lord says, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart.” The Apostle says the same when guiding us in humility—for it is possible to confirm the whole truth of the argument with a single example. To those who look to the things above he says, “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself [?].” For this reason the bride says, “Cover me with apples,” so that, always looking up, I may see the patterns of good things displayed in the bridegroom. There is gentleness; there is freedom from anger; there is the bearing of no grudge against enemies, kindness toward those who wrong us, and repaying evil with good; there is self-control, purity,

patience, and freedom from any taint of vainglory and the deceit of this life. Having said this, she praises the archer for his good aim, since he directed his arrow at her so well. “For I am wounded with love,” she says. By this word she shows the arrow lodged deep in her heart. The archer of the arrow is love. And we have learned from Holy Scripture that God is love, who sends forth his chosen arrow, his only-begotten Son, upon those who are being saved, having smeared the threefold edge of its point with the Spirit of life. The point is faith, so that whomever it enters, it may bring in the archer along with the arrow, as the Lord says, “I and the Father are one,” and “We will come and make our home with him.” The soul, then, exalted through the divine ascents, sees within herself the sweet arrow of love by which she was wounded, and she makes the wound her boast, saying, “I am wounded with love.” O beautiful wound and sweet blow, through which life penetrates to the inner parts, opening for itself the cleft made by the arrow as a kind of door and entrance! For the moment she received the arrow of love, the archery was at once transformed into bridal joy. It is plain how the hands handle a bow, dividing their work as the task requires. The left hand grips the bow, while the right draws the string toward itself, pulling back the arrow by its notch, while the arrow is aimed at the target by the left hand thrust forward. She, then, who a little earlier was the arrow's target now sees herself in the archer's hands in place of the arrow, the right hand holding the arrow in one way and the left in another. But since, through the nuptial figure, the meanings of what is contemplated are carried forward in sequence, the text did not have the arrow's point held by the left hand and the other end gripped by the right, so that the soul would become an arrow in the hand of the mighty one, aimed at the target above. Instead it had the left hand placed under the head in place of the point, and the right hand take hold of the rest. It did so, I think, so that the text might at the same time philosophize about the divine ascent in double riddles, showing that the same one is both our bridegroom and our archer, using the purified soul both as bride and as arrow: as an arrow, he aims her at the good target; as a bride, he takes her up to share in incorruptible eternity, granting length of days and years of life by his right hand, and by his left the riches of eternal goods and the glory of God, which those who seek the glory of the world do not share. That is why she says, “His left hand is under my head”—the hand by which the arrow is aimed at the target—“and his right hand,” taking hold of me and drawing me to itself, makes me light for the upward course, sending me there yet not parting me from the archer, so that I am at once carried by
…to cease. And the properties of these hands, says [?], are that length of life and years of living are in the right hand of wisdom [?], and in her left hand, wealth

Then she turns her speech to the daughters of the Jerusalem above. Her speech is an exhortation delivered with an oath, to increase and enlarge [?] until he makes his will effective, he who wills that all be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. The speech she has made is this: “I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field, if you rouse and awaken love, until it pleases.” An oath is a word that confirms the truth by itself. Its force is twofold [?]: either one confirms the truth to the hearer by it, or by adjuring others one lays on them the necessity of telling no lie. For example: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not set it aside.” Here the trustworthiness of the promise is made firm by the oath. But when Abraham, concerned to find a noble match for his only-begotten son, commands his own servant not to join to Isaac in marriage any woman of the race of Canaan, a people condemned to slavery, so that mixture with a servile race might not spoil the nobility of his line, but to arrange the boy's marriage from his ancestral land and kindred, he lays on him, by putting him under oath, the necessity of not being careless about the command, if he sends him to do on his behalf [?] what he had decided concerning his son. So the servant is put under oath by Abraham to arrange a fitting marriage for Isaac. Since, then, the operation of an oath is twofold, here she [?], having run up to such a height as we beheld in what we examined earlier, and guiding the souls who are her disciples in their progress toward perfection, does not use the oath to give her hearers certainty about what she herself has attained. Rather, by adjuring them she leads them by the hand toward the life of virtue, so that they keep love sleepless and wakeful until his good will comes to its fulfillment. And this is that all be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. And as the adjuration there was made by the thigh of the patriarch, so here it is made by the powers and the strengths of the field, for the text says: “I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field, if you rouse and awaken love, until it pleases.” In these words, then, we must consider first what the field is; [?] whether these differ from one another, and what each of them signifies; and further, what it is to rouse love, and what it is to awaken it. For “until it pleases” has already been explained in what was said above.

That the voice of the Master signifies the world by “the field” is plain to everyone from the Gospels. And that the form of this world is passing away, and that nothing stable is to be found in a nature that is never at rest, is plain from the grand utterance of Ecclesiastes, who counted everything that appears and passes away among vanities. What, then, is the power of such a field, that is, of the world? Or what is the strength, the mention of which makes the command inviolable for the daughters of Jerusalem through the adjuration? For if we look to visible things as though there were some power in them, Ecclesiastes rules out such a supposition by calling vain everything that is displayed and pursued among them. For what is vain has no real existence, and what does not exist in substance has no strength. Or perhaps we can find some clue to the meaning in the plural form of “power.” For we have learned that holy Scripture makes the following distinction with such words: when “power” is said in the singular, the mind is directed by that word to the Divine; but when it is spoken in the plural, it presents the angelic nature to our thought. For example, in “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God,” the singular makes the Divine known. In “Bless the Lord, all you his powers,” the plural “powers” indicates the intelligible nature of the angels. And the word “strength,” taken together with “power,” intensifies the force of the meaning, for Scripture shows more firmly what it intends by repeating words of equal meaning, as in “Lord, my strength and my firmament.” Each of the two words signifies the same thing, but the combination of equivalents indicates an intensification of the meaning. So the plural sense of “powers,” and the similar mention of “strengths,” seem to lead the hearers' thought to the angelic nature. Thus the adjuration, applied to the souls who are disciples to confirm what the teaching has decided, is made not by the world that passes away but by the nature of the angels that endures forever, to whom she bids them look, so that by their example she may confirm the firmness and stability of the virtuous way of life. For since it has been promised that the life after the resurrection will be like the condition of the angels [?] (and the one who promised does not lie), it would follow that our life in the world too should be prepared for the life hoped for hereafter, so that while living in the flesh and passing our time in the field of this world, we do not live according to the flesh, nor are conformed to this age, but rehearse beforehand, through our life in the world, the life we hope for. For this reason the bride instills in the souls of her disciples the assurance given by the oath, so that their life, as it is lived out rightly in this field, may look to the powers,

imitating the purity of the angels through freedom from passion. For when love is thus roused and awakened—that is, exalted and constantly increased toward what is greater by continual addition—she said that the good will of God is fulfilled, as in heaven so also on earth, since the angelic freedom from passion is achieved in us as well. These are our reflections on “I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field, if you rouse and awaken love, until it pleases.” But if some other explanation should be found that comes nearer to the truth of what we are seeking, we will receive the gift and give thanks to the one who reveals hidden mysteries through the Holy Spirit, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

“The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle, or a fawn of the deer, upon the mountains of Bethel. Behold, he is behind our wall, peeping in through the windows, peering through the lattices. My beloved answers and says to me: Arise, come, my close one, my fair one, my dove. For behold, the winter has passed, the rain has gone, it has departed. The flowers have appeared in the land, the time of cutting has come, the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land. The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs; the vines are in blossom, they have given their fragrance. Arise, come, my close one, my fair one, my dove. In the shelter of the rock, close by the outer wall, show me your face and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely. Catch us the little foxes that ruin the vineyards, for our vines are in blossom. My beloved is mine and I am his, who pastures his flock among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows move. Turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle, or a fawn of the deer, upon the mountains of the hollows.” The words of the philosophy of the Song of Songs now set before us in the reading both lead us to a longing to contemplate the goods that lie above us and put grief into our souls, producing in a way despair of ever understanding what cannot be grasped. For how could anyone remain untouched by grief when he considers that the purified soul, raised through love by so many ascents toward participation in the good, has not yet, as the Apostle says, laid hold of what it seeks? And yet, when I looked at those ascents traversed in the preceding discourses, I counted her blessed for her climb: when she recognized the sweet apple tree and distinguished it from the fruitlessness of the thicket, and made its shade her desire, and, sweetened by its fruit, came into the chambers of gladness. And by “wine” she names

gladness, by which the heart of those who partake of it is made glad; and how, set in order in love, she is sustained with perfumes, encompassed by the apples; and how, having received the arrow of love into her heart, she in turn becomes herself an arrow in the hands of the archer, aimed at the target of truth, directed by the hands of the Mighty One. Seeing these and similar things, I supposed that she who had been raised so high through so many stages had reached the very summit of blessedness. But, it seems, all she has traversed is still only the beginning of the ascent. For after all those ascents she speaks not of some contemplation or clear grasp of the truth, but of the voice of the one she longs for—a voice recognized by its distinctive marks through hearing, not known and enjoyed through understanding. If, then, she who has been raised so high—as we learn of the great Paul, who was caught up as far as the third heaven—shows that she has not yet precisely grasped what lies before her, what must we expect to feel, or where should we reckon ourselves to be, who have not yet even come near the porches of the sanctuary of contemplation? One can see from her own words how hard to contemplate are the things we seek. “The voice of my beloved,” she says: not a form, not a face, not a feature revealing the nature of the one sought, but a voice, which produces only a conjecture, rather than certainty, about who the speaker is. That what she says resembles guesswork rather than any unambiguous assurance of comprehension is clear from the fact that her speech does not attach itself to any one idea or look to a single form, but is carried in many directions by her visions, thinking she sees now one thing, now another, and never keeping to the same character of what she has grasped. This is clear from what is said. For “Behold,” she says, “he comes”—neither standing nor staying, so as to become known through his lingering to the one gazing at him, but snatching himself from her sight before she can arrive at perfect knowledge. For “leaping,” she says, “upon the mountains, and bounding over the hills.” And now he is recognized as a gazelle, and again likened to a fawn. “For my beloved,” she says, “is like a gazelle, or a fawn of the deer, upon the mountain of Bethel.” Thus what is grasped bears a different character at different times. These are the things which, on a first reading, bring me to grief, producing despair of any exact understanding of the things above. Nevertheless, placing our hope in God, who gives the word with great power to those who proclaim the good news, we must try to fit our contemplation in an orderly sequence to what we have already understood. “The voice of my beloved,” she says, and at once she adds, “Behold, he comes.” What, then, have we perceived in these words? Perhaps what is said looks ahead to the dispensation of God the Word that was made manifest to us through the Gospel—announced beforehand through the

prophets, but made manifest through the Son's appearing in the flesh. For the divine voice is borne out by deeds, and the fulfillment is joined to the word of promise, as the Prophet says: “As we have heard, so have we also seen.” “The voice of my beloved,” she says: this is what we heard. “Behold, he comes”: this we received with our eyes. “In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old to our fathers in the prophets”: this is the hearing of the voice. “In these last days he has spoken to us in a Son”: that is what is meant by “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills,” fittingly and aptly likened to the gazelle in one particular sense, and again to the fawn of the deer in another. The gazelle signifies the keen sight of the one who surveys all things. For they say that this animal, which sees extraordinarily well, takes its name (dorkas) from that activity. Now “to see” (derkesthai) is the same as “to behold” (theasasthai). Therefore the one who oversees and surveys all things is called God (Theos) of all from his beholding all things. Since, then, God was made manifest in the flesh, appearing in this life to destroy the opposing powers, he is for this reason likened to a gazelle, as the one who looked down from heaven upon the earth, and to a fawn, as crossing the mountains and hills with his leaps—that is, trampling down and destroying the wicked heights of demonic evil. For by “mountains” it means those that are shaken by his might, as David says, “those that are carried into the heart of the seas” and sink into the abyss, the place akin to them. Of these the Lord said to his disciples, “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain” (pointing by this word to that wicked lunatic demon), “Be lifted up and cast into the sea.” Since, then, it is characteristic of the nature of deer to destroy wild creatures and to put the whole race of snakes to flight by their breath and by a property of their skin, for this reason the one who oversees all things is likened to a gazelle, and to a fawn of the deer as the one who tramples and destroys the hostile power, which the figurative sense has called mountains and hills. So the voice of the bridegroom came through the prophets, in whom God spoke; and after the voice came the Word, leaping upon the opposing mountains and bounding down upon the hills, making the whole apostate power alike a footstool beneath his tread, both the lesser and the leading. For this is what the distinction between hills and mountains hints at: that what is eminent among the adversaries is brought down just as what is lower, trodden underfoot by his power and authority. For the lion and the dragon, which are the greater, are trampled alike with the snake and the scorpion, which seem lesser. I mean something like this: among the crowds that followed him there were mountains—demons—whether

in the synagogues, or in the country of the Gerasenes, or in many other places, rising up and towering over human nature. Among these there were hills and mountains, some superior and some subordinate. But the fawn of the deer, the destroyer of snakes—who also fits his disciples for the nature of deer when he says, “I have given you authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions”—sets his foot on all of them alike, putting them to flight and leaping from these to others, so that through this the greatness of those who are exalted in virtue might come into view, no longer overshadowed by the mounds of evil. For the mountains of Bethel seem, from the meaning of the name, to indicate the lofty and heavenly life, since those skilled in the Hebrew language say that this word means “house of God.” That is why she says, “upon the mountains of Bethel.” The purified and clear-sighted eye of the soul saw these things, leaping along with those divine leaps made against the hostile mounds; and it speaks of a time that would come later as though it were already present, because of the trustworthiness and certainty of the grace hoped for, seeing the hope as an accomplished fact. For she says that he who leaps over the mountains with nimble speed and bounds from hill to hill shows himself standing still, having come behind the wall and conversing through the lattices of the windows. The text reads thus: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, peeping in through the windows, peering through the lattices.” What the passage sketches in bodily terms is this: the lover converses through the windows with the bride, who stays at home inside; and though the wall stands between them and separates them, their conversation is unhindered, his head peeping in through the windows and his eye peering through the lattices in the windows toward what is inside. But the anagogical contemplation keeps to the sense examined earlier. For the Word brings human nature into intimacy with God step by step and in due order, first illuminating it through the prophets and the commandments of the law. For this is how we understand it: the windows are the prophets, who let in the light, and the lattices are the network of the law's commandments, through both of which the radiance of the

For, she says, my beloved [answers] and says to me: “Arise, come, my close one, my fair one, my dove. For behold, the winter has passed, the rain has gone, it has departed. The flowers have appeared in the land, the time of cutting has come. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land. The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs. Our vines are in blossom, they have given their fragrance.” How elegantly the Maker of spring sketches for us the charm of spring—he to whom David says, “Summer and spring, you fashioned them.” He dispels the gloom of winter, saying that the wintry sullenness and the dreariness of the rains have passed. He shows meadows teeming and [?] with flowers. He says that the flowers are in their prime and ready for cutting, so that the flower-gatherers will surely pick them to weave a garland or prepare perfumes. The text sweetens the season too, filling the groves all around with the songs of birds, as the sweet voice of the turtledoves reaches the ear. And by the fig tree and the vine he means that the delight to come from them is heralded by what can already be seen: the one bringing forth its unripe figs, the other blossoming with flowers, so that the sense of smell revels in their fragrance. Thus the text luxuriates in its depiction of the springtime, casting off gloom and lingering over sweeter descriptions. But we must not, I think, let our thought linger over the depiction of these charming things; rather, we must be guided by them to the mysteries revealed through these oracles, so that the treasure of meaning hidden in the words may be uncovered. What, then, do we say? Humanity was once frozen in the frost of idolatry, the mobile nature of human beings having been changed into the nature of the immobile objects of their worship. For, it says, “May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.” And this was only to be expected from what happened. For just as those who look upon the true Godhead receive into themselves the properties of the divine nature, so the one devoted to the vanity of idols was transformed into what he looked upon, becoming stone instead of man. Since, then, human nature, turned to stone by the worship of idols, could not move toward the better, frozen as it was in the frost of idolatry, for this reason the Sun of righteousness rises upon this harsh winter and brings about spring, while the south wind, which dissolves such freezing, warms everything beneath it together with the rising of the rays; so that man, turned to stone by the cold, might be warmed through by the Spirit and heated by the ray of the Word, and become once more water springing up to eternal life. For, it says, “His wind will blow, and waters will flow,” as the rock is turned into pools of water and the sheer cliff into springs of water. This the Baptist proclaimed more plainly to the Jews when he said that the stones

…that these are raised up to become children of the Patriarch, made like him through virtue. These things, then, the Church hears from the Word. She receives the radiance of truth through the windows of the prophets and the lattices of the law, while the wall of typological teaching still stands. I mean the law, which casts the shadow of the good things to come but does not show the very image of the realities. Behind it stands the truth, closely joined to the type. First the truth lets the Word shine on the Church through the prophets. Afterward, through the manifestation of the Gospel, it consumes the whole shadowy appearance of the type. By this the dividing wall is pulled down, and the air within the house is joined to the light of heaven, so that there is no longer any need to be lit through the windows, since the true Light itself illumines everything within through the rays of the Gospel. That is why the Word, who raises up those who have fallen, cries out to the Church through the windows, saying, "Arise": that is, from your fall. You who slipped into the shame of sin, who were tripped up by the serpent and fell to the ground and came to lie in the fall of disobedience: arise. But it is not enough for you, he says, to be raised from the fall; you must also come forward by advancing in good things and completing the course of virtue. We have learned this also in the case of the paralytic. For the Word did not merely raise that burden from his bed; he also commanded him to walk. By this, it seems to me, the passage signifies progress and growth toward what is better, through movement from one place to another. "Arise, then," he says, "and come forth." O the power of the command! Truly the voice of God is a voice of power, as the psalm says: "Behold, he will give his voice, a voice of power." And: "He spoke, and they came into being; he commanded, and they were created." See, now too he has said to her who lay fallen, "Arise," and "Come forward," and at once the command becomes deed. For in the same moment that she receives the power of the Word, she stands up, comes forward, and draws near to the light.
