This is attested by the very one who called her, for the Word speaks thus: "Arise, come, my close one, my fair one, my dove." What is the order of this passage? How is one thing joined to the next? How is the sequence of thoughts kept in order, as in a chain? She hears the command, is strengthened by the word, rises, comes forward, draws near, becomes beautiful, and is called a dove. For how can one see a beautiful face in a mirror unless the mirror has received the reflection of some beautiful form? So too the mirror of human nature did not become beautiful before, but only when it drew near to the beautiful and was formed into the image of the divine beauty. For just as she bore the form of the serpent while she lay on the ground and gazed at him, so in the same way, when she rose, set herself face to face with the good, and turned her back on evil, she takes the shape of what she looks upon. And she looks upon the archetypal beauty, and the dove is that beauty. Therefore,

having drawn near to the light, she becomes light. And in the light the beautiful form of the dove is imaged: I mean that dove whose form made known the presence of the Holy Spirit. So the Word, having addressed her thus and named her, fair because she is near and a dove because of her beauty, goes on to what follows. He says that the gloom of winter no longer holds sway over souls, for cold cannot withstand the sunbeam. "Behold," he says, "the winter is past; the rain is gone, it has departed by itself." He gives evil many names, naming it according to the differences in its workings. For the same thing is winter, and rain, and drops, and each of these names signifies some particular kind of temptation. In winter what had flourished withers. The beauty of the trees, their natural adornment of leaves, falls from the branches and is mingled with the earth. The song of the musical birds falls silent: the nightingale flees, the swallow grows torpid, the turtledove leaves its nest. Everything imitates the gloom of death: the shoot dies and the grass perishes. And like bones stripped of flesh, the branches, bared of their leaves, become an ugly sight in place of the splendor their shoots once gave them. And what could one say of what the sea suffers in winter? How, churned up from its depths and swelling, it mimics crags and mountains, its water heaped up into upright peaks? How it rushes against the land like an enemy, hurling itself over its shores [?], and shakes the land with the repeated blows of its waves, as if with the assaults of siege engines? But consider with me the sufferings of winter, taking all these things and the like in a figurative sense. What is it in winter that loses its bloom and withers? What is it that falls from the branches and dissolves into the earth? What is the voice of the songbirds that falls silent? What is the sea that roars with its waters? And besides these, what is the rain? What are the drops of the rain? How does the rain depart by itself? For by this the riddle indicates that this kind of winter is a living thing, endowed with free choice. Perhaps, even if the passage does not explain each point, the meaning shown in each of them is plain to the hearer. At the beginning human nature flourished while it was in paradise, nourished and blooming with the water of that spring, when instead of leaves the shoot of immortality adorned its nature. But when the winter of disobedience dried up the root, the flower was shaken off and dissolved into earth. Man was stripped of the beauty of immortality, and the grass of the virtues withered, because love for God grew cold as lawlessness increased. As a result, various passions were whipped up into peaks within us by the hostile spirits, and through them the soul suffers its evil shipwrecks. But then came the one who brought spring to our souls. When the evil wind had once stirred up the sea,

he rebukes the winds and says to the sea, "Be still, be silent." Then everything was changed to calm and stillness, and our nature begins to bloom again and is adorned with its own flowers. The flowers of our life are the virtues, which now are in bloom and will yield their fruit in their own season. That is why the Word says, "The winter is past, the rain is gone, it has departed by itself; the flowers have appeared on the earth, the time of pruning has come." Do you see, he says, the meadow blooming with virtues? Do you see self-control, that bright and fragrant lily? Do you see modesty, the rose? The violet, the fragrance of Christ? Why then do you not weave garlands from them? Now is the time to gather them and adorn yourself with garlands woven from such flowers. "The time of pruning has come." The voice of the turtledove bears witness to this for you: that is, the voice of one crying in the wilderness. John is the turtledove. He is the forerunner of the bright spring. He showed people the beautiful flowers of virtue and offered them to those who wished to gather them. Through these flowers he pointed to the flower from the root of Jesse, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and he urged repentance from evil and a virtuous way of life. "For the voice of the turtledove," it says, "has been heard in our land." Perhaps by "land" he means those condemned for wickedness, whom the Gospel calls tax collectors and prostitutes. Among them John's word was heard, while the rest did not accept his preaching. As for what is said about the fig tree, that "it has put forth its green figs," let us understand it this way. The fig tree, by its heat, draws up moisture from the depths more than other trees do. Since much sap collects in its pith, nature, through the digestion of fluids that takes place in the plant, necessarily expels from the branches the useless and earthy part of the sap. It often does this, so that at the proper time it may put forth what is pure and nourishing, cleansed of its useless quality. This growth, which the fig tree puts forth in the form of fruit before the sweet and ripe fruit, is called the green fig. It too is sometimes edible for those who want it; yet it is not the fruit, but rather the prelude to the fruit. So whoever sees green figs fully expects the fruit very soon, for they are the sign of the edible figs, and it says that the fig tree has put them forth. For the Word is sketching the spiritual spring for the bride, and this season is the boundary between two seasons: the gloom of winter and the enjoyment of fruits in summer. Therefore he plainly announces the good news that evils are past, but does not yet display the fruits of virtue in their fullness. Instead he stores them up for the proper time, when summer comes. And you surely know what the summer harvest means from the Lord's own words, when he says, "The harvest is the

end of the age." For now he shows our hopes blooming through the virtues, whose fruit, as the Prophet says, appears in its own season. Human nature, like the fig tree mentioned here, has gathered much bad sap through the winter we have described. So he who works the spring of the soul in us, and tends humanity with fitting husbandry, rightly begins by casting out of our nature all that is earthy and useless, as from branches, getting rid of the waste through confession. Then he impresses on our life some mark of the blessedness we hope for, through a more refined way of living, and so announces the coming sweetness of the figs, as if through green figs. This is what is meant by "The fig tree has put forth its green figs." Understand the vine in blossom in the same way. Its wine, which gladdens the heart, will one day fill the mixing bowl of Wisdom and will be set before the fellow-guests from the lofty proclamation, for them to draw from freely for a good and sober drunkenness. I mean that drunkenness through which people are carried out of material things toward what is more divine. For now the vine is in blossom with its flower, and a fragrant breath goes out from it, sweet and pleasant, mingling with the surrounding air. And you surely know the Spirit who produces this fragrance in those who are being saved, for you have learned it from Paul. These are the signs of the beautiful spring of souls that the Word shows the bride in advance. He urges her on to the enjoyment of what lies before her, rousing her with his word and saying, "Arise, come, my close one, my fair one, my dove." How many doctrines the Word shows us briefly in these words! For it is not likely that divinely inspired teaching would linger on the same words out of superfluous idle talk. Rather, some great thought worthy of God is shown us through the repetition. What is said is this. The blessed and eternal nature, which surpasses all understanding, contains all beings in itself and is contained by no limit. For nothing is observed about it: no time, no place, no color, no shape, no form, no mass, no size, no extension, nor any other name, thing or concept that circumscribes. Rather, every good conceived about it goes on to infinity and without limit. For where evil has no place, there is no limit to the good. In a changeable nature, the power of choice is equally able to incline toward either of two opposites. So the good in us and the evil end in each other as they succeed one another, and the evil that comes after becomes the limit of the good. All the pursuits of our souls that stand opposed to one another as contraries end in one another and are bounded by one another. But the nature that is simple, pure, uniform, unchangeable and unalterable, always the same and never departing from itself, because it cannot admit

any communion with evil, remains without limit in the good. It sees no limit to itself, because it sees nothing of its opposite. So when it draws the human soul to share in itself, it always stands above the one who shares in it by the same measure of superiority. For the soul always becomes greater than itself by sharing in what surpasses it, and it never stops growing. But the good it shares in remains the same, and is always found to surpass by an equal margin the soul that shares in it ever more fully. We see, then, the bride being led by the hand by the Word up the ascents of virtue to the heights, as if climbing a stairway. First the Word sends his ray into her through the windows of the prophets and the lattices of the precepts of the law. He invites her to draw near to the light and become beautiful, formed in the light into the form of the dove. Then, when she has shared in good things as far as she could hold them, he draws her again from the beginning, as though she had not yet shared in good things at all, toward participation in the beauty that lies beyond. So her desire grows along with her in proportion to her progress toward what keeps appearing ahead. And because the goods always found beyond so far surpass what she has, she seems to be only beginning the ascent. That is why the Word again says "Arise" to her who has already been raised, and "Come" to her who has already come. For the one who truly rises will never cease to keep rising, and for the one who runs toward the Lord the wide space of the divine course will never be used up. One must always be roused and never stop drawing nearer through the race. So as often as he says "Arise" and "Come," just as often he gives the power to climb toward what is better. Understand in this way also what follows in the passage. For when he commands her to become beautiful from being beautiful, he plainly suggests the apostle's teaching, which commands us to be transformed into the same image from glory to glory. So what is found at each stage is always received as glory, yet, however great and lofty it may be, it is believed to be less than what is hoped for. Thus

[?] setting out, with no necessity leading her. For virtue has no master; it is voluntary and free from all necessity. Such was David, who prayed that only the voluntary acts he performed would be pleasing to God, and who promised to sacrifice willingly. Such is each of the saints, who brings himself to God and is not led by necessity. So you too, show the perfect state by taking up for yourself the desire to ascend toward what is better. And having become such, he says, you will come to the shelter of the rock, close to the outer wall. What is said is this, for we must turn the discussion from riddles to something clearer. The one shelter of the human soul is the lofty Gospel. Whoever enters it no longer needs the shadowy teaching given through typical and symbolic meanings, since the truth reveals the hidden riddles of the commandments. And no one who shares in the faith to any degree would dispute that the grace of the Gospel is called a rock, for one can learn from many places in Scripture that the Gospel is a rock. What is said, then, is this: If you have been trained in the law, O soul, and if you have seen with your mind the rays coming through the prophetic windows, do not stay any longer under the shadow of the wall of the law. For the wall casts a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the realities. Instead, pass over from the wall to the rock close by. For the rock adjoins the outer wall, since the law has become the outer wall of the Gospel faith, and the doctrines adjoin one another and are neighbors in meaning. For what is closer to "Do not commit adultery" than "Do not desire"? And what is closer to keeping clean of murder than not defiling the heart even with anger? Since the shelter of the rock adjoins the outer wall, there is no gap for you to cross when you move from the wall to the rock. There is circumcision in the wall and circumcision in the rock; a sheep and a sheep; blood and blood; Passover and Passover. Nearly everything is the same and joined together through the same things, except that the rock is spiritual, while the wall is made of earth, and bodily earthiness is molded into it. But the Gospel rock has none of the fleshly clay of literal meanings. Here a man receives circumcision and remains wholly sound, with no mutilation docking the frame of his nature. He keeps the Sabbath by abstaining from evil deeds, but does not accept idleness toward the good, having learned that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. He eats every kind of food without distinction, yet touches nothing unclean. For he is taught by the rock that nothing entering through the mouth is common. Instead, laying aside the bodily observances of the law in every case, the soul carries the meaning of the words over to what is spiritual and intelligible, as Paul says: "The law is spiritual." For whoever truly understands [?] the law comes under the shelter of the Gospel rock, which adjoins the bodily outer wall.

After the Word had cried these things to her through the windows, the dove answers well. She has been illumined by the radiance of these thoughts and has understood the rock, which is Christ. For she says, "Show me your face, and let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely." What is said is this: Speak with me no longer through the riddles of the prophets and the law. Show yourself to me plainly, in a way I am able to see, so that I may come within the Gospel rock and leave behind the outer wall of the law. And let your voice come into my ears in a way my hearing can take in. For if the voice that comes through the windows is so sweet, how much more lovely will the sight of your face be! The bride says this because she has understood the mystery of the Gospel rock. The Word, who came to the windows in many parts and many ways, had led her by the hand to this mystery. She has come to desire the manifestation of God through flesh: that the Word should become flesh, that God should be manifested in the flesh, and that he should set before our hearing the divine words that promise eternal blessedness to the worthy. And see how the words of Simeon agree with the bride's prayer. He says, "Now you are letting your servant go, Master, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation." For he saw, just as she longed to see. And his sweet voice is recognized by those who have received the grace of the Gospel, those who said, "You have the words of eternal life." For this reason the pure Bridegroom accepts the bride's prayer, since it is just. Being about to show himself plainly, he first urges the hunters on to catch the foxes, so that they may no longer keep the vineyard from blossoming. He says: "Catch us foxes, small ones, but destroyers of the vineyards." For the vines will blossom once there is nothing left to ravage them. "Catch us foxes, small ones, that ruin the vineyards, and our vines are in blossom." Is it possible to do justice to the grandeur of these thoughts? How great a wonder of the divine majesty the passage contains! How great a surpassing power of God the meaning of these words reveals! Consider how he of whom such great things are said: the man-slayer, the one mighty in wickedness, whose tongue is like a sharpened razor [of whom the Prophet says, "The arrows of the mighty one are sharpened"] with the coals of the desert; and "He lies in wait like a lion in his den"; the Dragon, the great one, the apostate; Hades, who widens his mouth; the world-ruler of the authority of darkness; he who has the power of death; in whose person the prophecy speaks. He who removes the boundaries of the nations, which the Most High, that is, set up according to the number of his angels [?]; who seizes the inhabited world like a nest and takes them up like abandoned eggs; the…

saying that he would set his throne above the clouds and become like the Most High. Then there is everything the word of God relates about him in Job, those fearful and terrifying things: his ribs are bronze, his spine is iron, his innards are emery stone, and everything else of that kind by which the word sketches that fearsome nature. This being, then, so terrible and so great, the general of the legions of demons: how is he named by the true and only Power? "A little fox." And all those around him, the army under his command, are all belittled alike and named in the same way by the one who urges the hunters on to hunt them. These hunters might perhaps be the angelic powers, which escort the Master's coming to earth, lead the King of glory into our life and show him to those who do not know him: "Who is this King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty in battle." Perhaps one might also say they are the ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation. Or perhaps one might say that the hunters are the apostles, sent out to hunt these beasts, to whom he said, "I will make you fishers of men." For they could not have carried out their fishing for human beings, netting the souls of the saved in the encircling net of the divine words, unless they had first driven these beasts out of their dens, those little foxes. I mean out of the hearts where they had made their lairs, so as to make room for the Son of God where he might lay his head, once the breed of foxes no longer lurked in those hearts. But whoever the word supposes the hunters to be, we are taught the greatness and ineffability of the divine power by what they are commanded to do. For he did not say, "Hunt the boar out of the forest that ravages God's vine," or "the wild solitary beast," or "the roaring lion," or "the great sea monster," or "the dragon beneath the waters." By such words the word would have shown the hunters that the adversaries have some power. Instead he says, in effect: all those earthly powers against which human beings wrestle, the principalities and authorities, the world rulers of darkness and the spirits of wickedness, are little foxes, crafty and wretched, when compared with our power. If you overpower them, you will recover the grace that belongs to you. Our vineyard, human nature, is already beginning to bear its clusters through the blossom of a virtuous life. "Catch for us, then, the little foxes that ruin the vineyard, and our vines will blossom." The vine heard the divine command. She is the wife of whom David says, "Your wife is like a flourishing vine." She saw herself cleansed of the damage done by these beasts through the power of the one who gave the order, and at once she gives herself to the vinedresser who broke down the dividing wall of the fence. For the wall of the law no longer walls her off from union with the one she longs for. Instead she says, "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine, who shepherds among the lilies, until

the day breathes and the shadows move." This means: "I have seen face to face the one who is eternally what he is, who for my sake rose up in human form from my sister the synagogue. I rest in him and become his dwelling place. For he is the good shepherd, who does not make grass the pasture of his flocks but feeds his sheep on pure lilies, no longer feeding grass with grass." For grass is the proper food of irrational nature. But the human being, being rational, is fed by the true Word. If he gorges himself on grass, he becomes grass himself. For "all flesh," it says, "is grass," as long as it remains flesh. But if someone becomes spirit, being born of the Spirit, he will no longer graze on a grassy life. The Spirit will be his food, and the purity and fragrance of the lily point to this. He himself, then, will become a pure and fragrant lily, transformed into the nature of his food. That is the day that [?] with its rays, or "breathes through." The divine voice gave the name "breathing through" to the spreading out that comes about through the breath of the rays. By this the shadows of life are moved away. Those who have not yet lit up the eye of the soul with the light of truth stare eagerly at these shadows: they see the shadow and what is empty as if it were real, and pass over what truly is as if it were not. But those fed on lilies, that is, those who fatten their souls on pure and fragrant food, will have removed themselves from every deceptive and shadowy illusion of the things people strive after in this life. They will look to the true reality of things and become sons of light and sons of the day. The bride sees these things and presses the Word to turn the hope of good things into reality quickly. "Turn back, my beloved," she says, "be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of the hollows." Look like a gazelle, you who see the thoughts of human beings and read the reasonings of their hearts. Wipe out the brood of evil, like a young stag destroying the race of serpents. You see the hollow mountains of human life, whose heights are not ridges but ravines. So the Word runs swiftly to the hollow mountains. For everything that exalts itself against the truth is a pit and not a mountain, a hollow and not a height. "If you run over these," she says, "every such ravine will be filled and every such mountain will be brought low." These are the words of the soul whom the Word shepherds, not among thorns or grass but in the fragrance of the lilies of a pure life. May we too be filled with these lilies as we are shepherded by the Word, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and power for ages of ages. Amen.

[?] my soul loved. I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me. I will rise and go around in the city, in the marketplaces and in the broad streets, and I will seek him whom my soul loved. I sought him and did not find him. I called him, and he did not answer me. The watchmen who go around in the city found me. "Have you seen him whom my soul loved?" It was only a little while after I had passed them that I found him whom my soul loved. I held him and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, into the chamber of her who conceived me. I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the forces of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases. Who is this coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the powders of the perfumer? Behold the bed of Solomon; sixty mighty men surround it, of the mighty men of Israel. All of them hold the sword and are trained in war. Each man has his sword on his thigh because of terror in the nights." Once again, through the present reading, we are taught great and lofty doctrines by the Song of Songs. For the bride's narrative, in which she tells about herself, is philosophy: it teaches how those who love the beauty beyond this world ought to be disposed toward the Divine. What we learn from the words before us is as follows. I think we should first set out the meaning contained in the words, and then fit the inspired words to what we have first considered. To put it briefly, the doctrine revealed through these words is something like this. At the very highest level of division, the nature of beings is divided in two. One part is sensible and material, the other intelligible and immaterial. We call sensible whatever we apprehend by the senses, and intelligible whatever lies beyond the grasp of the senses. Of these, the intelligible is infinite and unbounded, while the other is in every case enclosed by certain limits. For all matter is bounded by quantity and quality, and so what we observe about it, its bulk, form, surface and shape, becomes the limit of our understanding of it. Anyone who investigates matter can grasp nothing in imagination beyond these. But the intelligible and immaterial, being free of such circumscription, escapes all boundary and is limited by nothing. The intelligible nature is in turn divided. One part is uncreated and makes all beings; it is eternally what it is and always the same, above all addition and diminution, and cannot receive any further good. The other part, brought into being through creation, always looks toward the first cause and is continually preserved in the good by participation in what transcends it. In a sense it is always being created, being changed for the better through growth in good things, so that no limit is seen in it either, and its growth toward the better is not circumscribed by any boundary. Rather, the good it presently has, however great and perfect it may seem, is always the beginning of something higher and

greater. So in this too the apostle's word proves true: by straining forward to what lies ahead, what has already been traveled passes into forgetfulness. For what is always found to be greater and surpassingly good holds the disposition of those who share in it fixed on itself and does not allow them to look back at what is past; through the enjoyment of more precious things it drives out the memory of lesser ones. This, then, is what we think the philosophy of the bridal narrative teaches us. It is time first to recall the actual wording of the inspired oracles, and then to fit the meaning contained in the words to what we have already considered. "On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loved; I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me. I will rise and go around in the city, in the marketplaces and in the broad streets, and I will seek him whom my soul loved. I sought him and did not find him. The watchmen who go around in the city found me. 'Have you seen him whom my soul loved?' It was only a little while after I had passed them that I found him whom my soul loved. I held him and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, into the chamber of her who conceived me." How, then, do we find in these words what we first set out as doctrine? [?] has come about in the earlier ascents, in proportion to the growth she achieved at each stage. For she is always changing for the better and never stops at the good she has grasped. At one point she is compared to the horse that overthrew the Egyptian tyrant; at another she is likened to necklaces and turtledoves in the adornment around her neck. Then, as though not content with these, she advances still higher. Through the sweet nard she recognizes the divine fragrance, and she does not stay even there. Next she hangs the beloved himself about her like a fragrant spice between the rational breasts from which the divine teachings pour forth, clothing herself with him in the space of her heart. After this she makes the vinedresser her own fruit, calling him a cluster that gives off a sweet and gentle fragrance through its blossom. Having grown in this way through such ascents, she is called beautiful, she draws near, and the beauty of her eyes is compared to doves. Then she moves on again to something greater. Having become more clear-sighted herself, she perceives the beauty of the Word and marvels at how he comes down, shaded, to the bed of this lower life, overshadowed by the material nature of the human body. Beyond this she describes in words the house of virtue, whose roofing material is cedar and cypress, woods that do not rot or decay; by these she expresses the permanence and unchangeableness of a disposition toward the good. After these things

her change for the better is shown by comparison, and she appears as a lily among thorns. She in turn perceives how the bridegroom differs from the others. He is called an apple tree in a fruitless wood, made lovely by the fair color of its fruit. Coming under its shade she enters the house, is sustained with perfumes and is heaped about with the fruit of the apple tree. Receiving the chosen arrow in her heart through that sweet wound, she herself in turn becomes an arrow in the hands of the archer: his left hand aims her head at the target above, while his right hand draws the arrow back to himself. After this, as though she had already reached perfection, she uses her words to lead the other maidens into eagerness for the beloved, stirring up their love by a kind of oath. Who would not say that a soul raised so high had reached the very highest boundary of perfection? And yet the end of what has been traveled becomes the beginning of guidance toward what lies beyond. For all those things were taken to be the sound of a voice, while the soul was being turned through hearing toward the contemplation of the mysteries. Now she begins to see the beloved, who appears to her eyes in another form. He is likened to a gazelle and compared to a young stag. What appears does not stand still, either in our sight or in its own place, but leaps upon the mountains, bounding from the heights to the tops of the hills. And again the bride rises to a higher state when a second voice comes to her. It urges her to leave the shadow of the wall and come out into the open, to rest in the shelter of the rock that adjoins the outer wall, and to delight in the springtime. There she plucks the flowers of the season in their prime and beauty, ready for cutting, and enjoys whatever else the season grants for the delight of those who take pleasure in it, amid the voices of the songbirds. Through these the bride becomes more perfect still and asks to see clearly the very face of the one speaking and to receive the word from him directly, no longer spoken through others. At this point, again, it seems right to call the soul blessed, since by her lofty ascent she has reached the highest of all that is desired. For what greater blessedness could one imagine than seeing God? Yet this too is the end of what has been traveled and becomes the beginning of the hope of what lies beyond. For again she hears the voice ordering the hunters, for the salvation of the rational vineyards, to catch the beasts that damage the fruit, those little foxes. When this is done, the two pass over into each other: God comes to be in the soul, and the soul in turn moves to dwell in God. For she says, "My beloved is mine, and I am in him," in him who shepherds among the lilies and has moved human life from shadowy illusions to the truth of what really is. Do you see to what a height she has climbed, she who goes from strength to strength, in the words of the prophet,

as though [she had reached] the summit of good things? [?] she [?] and is distressed, and she makes this perplexity of the soul public in her narrative and describes in words how she found what she was seeking. We learn all this through contemplating the words set before us. They teach us clearly that the greatness of the divine nature is not bounded by any limit, and that no measure of knowledge becomes a boundary to our understanding of what we seek, at which the one who reaches for lofty things must halt his forward course. Rather, the mind that runs upward through ever higher understanding should be so disposed that every perfection of knowledge attainable by human nature becomes the beginning of a desire for higher things. Consider carefully the passage set before us for contemplation, first understanding this: the bodily outline of the text is a bridal chamber, and a kind of wedding setting supplies the material for contemplation. Philosophy transfers the images these things suggest to what is pure and immaterial, advances the doctrines through what takes place in them, and uses the riddles of the events to make clear what they signify. The word has made the soul the bride, and God, whom she loves with all her heart and soul and strength, is called the bridegroom. Accordingly, having come, as she thought, to the summit of her hopes, and supposing herself already united with the one she longs for, she calls her more perfect participation in the good a "bed," and she calls the time of darkness "night." By the name "night" she points to the contemplation of things invisible, like Moses, who entered the darkness where God was, God who, as the prophet says, "made darkness his hiding place all around him."

Having entered it, she is then taught that she is as far from attaining perfection as those who have not even begun. "I thought," she says, "that I had already been counted worthy of perfection, and was resting, as on a bed, in my grasp of what I had come to know. When I had entered the realm of the invisible and left the senses behind, when I was enfolded in the divine night and was searching for the one hidden in the darkness, then I did have love for the one I longed for, but the beloved himself flew beyond the grasp of my reasonings. For I sought him on my bed by night, to know what his essence is, where it begins, where it ends, and in what it has its being. But I did not find him. I called him by name, as far as I could find a name for one who cannot be named. But no meaning of any name reached the one I was seeking. For how could

he who is above every name be found by calling him by a name?" That is why she says, "I called him, and he did not answer me. Then I knew that there is no limit to his majesty, his glory and his holiness." So she rouses herself again and goes about in thought through the intelligible nature beyond this world. She calls it a city; in it are the principalities and dominions and the thrones assigned to the authorities. She calls the festal assembly of the heavenly beings the marketplace, and she signifies their multitude, which no number can encompass, by the name "broad streets." She searched to see whether the beloved might perhaps be found among them. So she went around searching through every rank of angels, and when she did not see what she sought among the good things she found there, she reasoned to herself: "Can it be that what I love is comprehensible to them?" And she says to them, "Have you seen him whom my soul loved?" But they were silent at such a question, and by their silence they showed that what she sought was beyond their comprehension too. When she had gone through that whole city beyond this world with the restless search of her mind and had not recognized the one she longed for even among the intelligible and bodiless beings, then she left behind everything she had found. In this way she came to know what she was seeking: she knew that he is, solely by not comprehending what he is, since every sign by which one might comprehend him becomes an obstacle for those who seek to find him. That is why she says, "It was only a little while after I had passed them." Having let go of all creation, passed by everything conceived within creation and left behind every approach by comprehension, "I found the beloved by faith. And I will no longer let go; I hold fast with the grip of faith to what I have found until he comes into my chamber." The chamber is surely the heart, which becomes able to receive the divine indwelling when it returns to the state it was in at the beginning, when it was formed by her who conceived it. And anyone who understands the mother to be the first cause of our existence will not go wrong. It is time to set out the divine words once more in their actual wording, so that the words may be fitted to what we have contemplated. "On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loved. I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me. I will rise and go around in the city, in the marketplaces and in the broad streets, and I will seek him whom my soul loved. I sought him and did not find him. The watchmen who go around in the city found me. 'Have you seen him whom my soul loved?' It was only a little while after I had passed them that I found him whom my soul loved. I held him and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, into the chamber of her who conceived me." After this, out of love for humanity, she also speaks to the daughters of Jerusalem, whom earlier, when compared with the beauty of the bride likened to the lily, [the word called] simply thorns

St. Gregory of Nyssa. [?] …he named, and by the oath sworn by the powers in the world he rouses them to an equal measure of love… so that the will of the bridegroom may take effect in them too. We have already said in the earlier discussion what the world is in which the strengths and powers are, and what the will is of the one who is loved with the whole heart and soul. There is no need to lengthen the discourse on these points again, since the meaning we considered earlier in those words makes clear enough what is to be understood in this place. Let us instead go on to what follows in the text, if it should be possible for us too to rise together with the perfect dove as she flies up to the height, and to hear the voice of the bridegroom's friends as they marvel at her ascent from the wilderness. What heightens the onlookers' amazement still more is that the wilderness should send up such a one, so that she resembles the beauty of trees, trees cultivated in the wilderness by the vapours of incense. The incense was myrrh and frankincense. With their vapour a kind of dust, made of finely ground spices, was stirred up and rose along with it, so that instead of dust mixed into the air there was a fine diffusion of the spices, by which the dust stood upright and hovered aloft [?] …acting out a story for them. Yet they are thought to appear as different people one after another, changing their appearance by the variety of their masks. One who now appears as a slave and a commoner is seen a little later as a champion and a soldier; and again, laying aside the subordinate role, he takes on the look of a general, or even puts on the form of a king. So it is with progress in virtue. Those who are transformed from glory to glory through desire for higher things do not always remain in the same character. Rather, in proportion to the perfection of good that each has achieved at any time, a particular character shines out in their life, one after another, as the good increases. That is why the friends of the bridegroom seem to me to be astonished at what they see. Earlier they knew her as beautiful, but beautiful as among women; after that they adorned her beauty with a likeness of gold with studs of silver. But now they see none of the earlier marks on her, and describe her instead by loftier ones, and they marvel not only at her ascent but also at the place from which she ran up. For this is what heightens their amazement: the one who ascends is seen as one, and yet the sight is compared to a grove of trees, for they seem to see stems shooting up and growing to a height. And what nourishes these stems is not rich, well-watered soil, but parched, thirsty desert. In what, then, are these stems rooted, and from what do they grow? Their root is the dust of the spices; their watering is the vapour of the incense,

which bedews this grove with its fragrance. How much praise [?] the text contains of the one to whom such testimony is given! For the fact that they question one another about the one they see, as though she were shown in another form and not in her former shape, is the most perfect praise of progress in virtue. It testifies to a great change and transformation in her for the better. For this is the voice of people astonished at a form unlike the familiar one, marvelling at the beauty that has blossomed on her: "This woman coming up from the wilderness was seen by us before as black. How has she washed away that dark form? How does her face now flash white as snow? The wilderness, it seems, is the cause of this. It has made her shoot up to a height like a sapling and changed her into such beauty." For this running up to the height did not happen by some chance accident, nor by an arbitrary lot. She acquired her beauty by her own labours, through self-control and diligence. In the same way the Prophet's soul once became thirsty for the divine spring, when it became for him a desert, trackless and waterless, and received the divine thirst into itself. Her coming up from the wilderness, then, bears witness that through attentiveness and self-control she ran up to so great and so lofty a height that she became a marvel even to the friends of the bridegroom. They interpret her beauty through many images, since it could not all be grasped through one. First they liken her loveliness to stems, and not to one of them; the comparison is drawn from the multitude of trees in the grove [?], so that the many forms and the variety of the virtues might be shown by the picture of the grove. Then smoke from incense is brought into the image of her beauty, and this too is not simple but blended of myrrh and frankincense, so that from both vapours a single grace arises, by which the bride's beauty is depicted. The mixture of these spices is a further praise of her. Myrrh is suited to the burial of bodies, while frankincense, for some reason, is dedicated to the honour of God. So whoever means to dedicate himself to the service of God will not become frankincense burned to God unless he first becomes myrrh. That is, he must put to death his members that are on the earth, being buried with the one who took our death upon himself, and receive in his own flesh, by putting his members to death, that myrrh which was used at the Lord's burial. When this has happened, every kind of spice of virtue in the course of his life, ground fine as in a mortar, produces that sweet dust. Whoever takes it in with his breath becomes fragrant, filled with the perfumed breath. After this testimony to her beauty, the friends of the bridegroom, who prepare the pure bridal chamber and act as matchmakers for the spotless bride, show her the beauty of the royal bed, so that they may lead the bride to a greater longing for the divine and undefiled [?] with him…

[?] …to take the text with more careful consideration, drawing the mind away from the material image to spiritual contemplation. For what adornment could a bridal bed get from armed men [?]? Their lessons are the terrors of war, their ornament is a sword held out before the body, and around them is a dread in the night. By the word "dread" the text indicates the fearful panic caused by certain terrors of the night, which it says attends these armed men. So we must look by every means for a meaning in these words that is consistent with what we have already considered. What, then, is the meaning? It seems that divine beauty has its loveliness in what is fearsome, and is shown by the opposites of bodily beauty. For here below what draws us to desire is what is gentle and sweet to the sight, free of anything fearsome or fierce. But that pure beauty is a fearsome and undaunted courage. The passionate and filthy desire of bodies lodges in the members of the flesh and lies in ambush for the mind like a band of robbers, and often seizes it and carries it off captive to its own will. What results is hostile to God, as the Apostle says: "The mind of the flesh is enmity against God." It follows, then, that divine love arises from the opposites of bodily desire. If that desire is led by slackness, laxity and soft dissipation, then here a formidable and undaunted courage becomes the material of divine love. For when manly spirit has terrified and routed the principle of pleasure, the pure beauty of the soul appears, defiled by no passion of bodily desire. Necessarily, then, the king's bridal bed is surrounded by armed men. Their experience in war, and the sword kept ready on the thigh, bring dread and panic upon the darkened thoughts that lie in ambush in the nights and the moonless dark to shoot at the upright in heart.

That the arming of those who surround the bed destroys filthy pleasures becomes clear from the text's description, which says: "All of them taught in war, each man with his sword on his thigh." For having the sword fitted on the thigh truly belongs to those who know how to wage war against flesh and blood. Anyone not unfamiliar with the ideas and riddles of Scripture certainly understands what is meant by the mention of the thigh, and that the sword is the word. So whoever has girded on the fearsome weapon, I mean the sword of chastity, is the one beloved by the incorruptible bed, one of the mighty of Israel, and worthy to be listed among the sixty. We do not doubt that this number has some mystical meaning, but it is clear only to those to whom the grace of the Spirit reveals hidden mysteries. For our part, we say it is good to fill ourselves with the meanings of the text that lie ready to hand, just as Moses legislates for the Passover that we eat the flesh that lies exposed, and to leave without prying into it what is hidden in the bones of obscurity. If anyone longs for the hidden marrow of the text, let him seek it from the one who reveals hidden things to those who are worthy. But so that we may not seem to pass over the text without exercising ourselves on it, or to neglect the divine command that bids us search the divine Scriptures, let us consider the meaning of the sixty in this way. Twelve rods, one for each of the tribes of Israel, were taken by Moses at the divine command, but one of them all was preferred, since it alone budded and the others did not. Again, Joshua son of Nun took from the Jordan stones equal in number to the tribes of Israel, and not one of them was rejected; all were taken alike, with equal honour, as witnesses to the mystery at the Jordan. And there is a clear sequence in these narratives. The text shows a certain progress of the people toward greater perfection. At the beginning of the giving of the law only one rod was found alive and budding, and the rest were rejected as dry and fruitless. But when more time had passed and they had come to understand the commandments of the law more precisely, they were able both to understand and to accept the second circumcision that Joshua brought upon them, when the knife of stone cut away all their uncleanness. (The attentive listener surely understands what is meant by the rock and the knife.) Since the lawful and virtuous life had, as was to be expected, become firmly established in them, none of the stones taken in the names of the tribes of Israel was found worthy of rejection. But since we must always seek growth in good things, when time had gone on and the power of Israel had grown greater (for so the text before us says: "from [?] Israel"), then it is no longer one stone or one rod that is taken from each tribe, but five

men of war from each tribe, in place of rods or stones, "taught in war, from the mighty of Israel," bearing swords and surrounding the divine bed. None of them is rejected, because the five are the firstfruits of every tribe, and their number, taken twelve times, makes up the full sum of the sixty. So five fearsome armed guards of the king's bed must come from each tribe, so that if a tribe fell short of the number five, what remained would be unacceptable too. May we then venture on the thought? How are five from each tribe armed, so that they may become guards of the royal bed? How does each of these five become fearsome to the enemy through his arms, holding out the sword from his thigh? Or is it not clear that the one stone is these five armed men, each sense holding out the sword fitted to it to strike terror into the enemy? The eye's sword is to look always toward the Lord, to see rightly, and not to be defiled by any filthy sight. Likewise the hearing's weapon is listening to divine teachings and never admitting an idle word. In the same way one can arm taste, touch and smell with the sword of self-control, equipping each of the senses with its own breastplate. Through these, dread and panic come upon the dark thoughts, whose time for plotting against souls is the night and the darkness. For in this, the Prophet said, the beasts of the field seek out their evil food from God's flocks: "You made darkness, and it was night; in it all the beasts of the forest will prowl, young lions roaring to seize their prey." Now everyone who is saved becomes Israel. For "not all who are of Israel are Israel"; rather, all who see God are properly called by this name, on account of what they do. And it is the mark of one who sees God that he looks toward sin with none of his senses. For no one can look to two masters; one must be hated if the other is to be loved. For this reason all who are saved become one bed of the king. For all who have become pure in heart will see God; those who have seen God properly become Israel and are called so; and this name is divided into twelve tribes for some unspoken reason. So the full number of those saved is fittingly summed up in the number sixty: one is taken from each part, and this one is divided into five armed men according to the number of the senses. Therefore all who have put on the divine armour surround the one bed of the king, all having become Israel; and through the twelve tribes of excellence, understood in every respect, the whole company of the champions is summed up in the number sixty.

All will become one battle line and one army, one bed (that is, one Church), one people and one bride, joined under one commander, one leader of the assembly and one bridegroom, into the fellowship of one body. That the bed is the rest of those who are saved we also learn from the voice of God, who says to the man shamelessly knocking at the door at night: "The door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed." The text rightly calls children those who have achieved freedom from passion through the weapons of righteousness. By this it teaches us that the good which comes to us through diligence is nothing other than what was placed in our nature from the beginning. For when someone has girded on the sword and, through attention to the life of virtue, has got rid of passion, he becomes an infant in age and has no sense of such passion, since the unripeness of that age has no room for passion. So it is the same thing to learn that there are armed men around the bed and that infants are resting on the bed. For freedom from passion is one and the same in both: in those who never admitted passion and in those who have driven it out. The former have known no other state [?]; the latter have brought themselves back to their first condition by turning and becoming children in freedom from passion. How blessed it is, then, to be found among these, having become a child, or an armed man, or a true Israelite: as an Israelite, seeing God with a pure heart; as an armed man, guarding the king's bed, that is, his own heart, in freedom from passion and in purity; and as a child, resting on the blessed bed, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

"King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon. Its pillars he made of silver and its back of gold, its seat of purple. Inside it is a mosaic pavement, love from the daughters of Jerusalem. Daughters of Zion, come out and look at King Solomon, at the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of his heart's gladness. See, you are beautiful, my close one; see, you are beautiful. Your eyes are doves, apart from your silence. [?] like flocks of goats that have been revealed from Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none among them is barren. Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is lovely. Your cheek is like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your silence. Your neck is like the tower of David, built for Thalpioth; a thousand shields hang on it, all the darts of the mighty. Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows move. I will go [?]

by myself to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense. You are wholly beautiful, my close one, and there is no blemish in you." King Solomon is taken in many respects as a type of the true King, in many, I mean, of the better things that holy Scripture records about him. He is called peaceful; he has boundless wisdom; he builds a temple; he reigns over Israel and judges the people in righteousness; and he is of the seed of David. Even the queen of the Ethiopians comes to visit him. All these things and others like them are said of him figuratively, but they sketch in advance the power of the Gospel. For who is as peaceful as the one who killed the enmity and nailed to the cross us, his enemies, or rather reconciled the world to himself, and broke down the dividing wall, so that he might create the two in himself into one new man, making peace; who proclaimed peace to those far off and to those near through those who bring the good news? And who is such a builder of a temple as the one who lays its foundations on the holy mountains, that is, on the prophets and apostles, and who builds on them, as Paul says, upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, the living and ensouled stones, which, as the prophetic word says, roll of themselves into the fitting together of the walls? So, fitted together in the unity of the faith and the bond of peace, they make the holy temple grow through themselves, to become a dwelling place of God in the Spirit. No one who looks at both the history and the truth would deny that Solomon, by his own wisdom, points to the true Wisdom. History testifies of him that he surpassed the limits of human wisdom, holding the knowledge of all things in the breadth of his heart, so that he outran those before him and could not be reached by those after him. But the Lord, in his own nature, is in very essence truth, wisdom and power. That is why, when David said, "In wisdom you have made all things," the divine Apostle, interpreting the Prophet, says that all things were created in him, since by "wisdom" the Prophet meant him. That the Lord is King of Israel is attested even by his enemies, who wrote on the cross the acknowledgement of his kingship: "This is the King of the Jews." We accept this testimony, even if it seems to belittle the greatness of his power by limiting his rule to the kingdom of the Israelites. But that is not so. Starting from a part, this inscription ascribes to the cross the rule over all, because it does not add that he is king of the Jews only. By testifying without qualification to his rule over the Jews, the text also took in, by what it leaves unsaid, his power over all in this acknowledgement. For the King of the whole earth is certainly also [king] of the part…

…thus holds the lordship. Solomon's zeal for just judgment points to the true Judge of the whole world, who says: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son"; and: "I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just." For this is the highest [?] of just judgment: not to hand out a verdict to those on trial from oneself, out of some partiality, but first to hear those who are subject to the judgment and only then to pronounce sentence on them. That is why the power of God admits that there is something it cannot do. For truth cannot turn judgment aside from what is just. That the Lord is of the seed of David according to the flesh, and was foreshadowed by the one born of David, we shall pass over, since it is acknowledged by all. But the mystery of the Ethiopian woman will become clear to anyone who considers which of the wonders of the Gospel it points to. She left the kingdom of the Ethiopians, crossed all that distance between, and hurried to Solomon because of the fame of his wisdom, greeting the king with precious stones and gold and sweet spices. Who does not know that the Church from the Gentiles was at first black from idolatry, before it became the Church, separated from the knowledge of the true God by the great gulf of ignorance? But when the grace of God appeared, and wisdom shone forth, and the true light sent its ray to those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, then, while Israel shut its eyes to the light and cut itself off from sharing in good things, the Ethiopians come. These are the Gentiles who run to the faith. Those who were once far off become near, washing away their blackness in the mystical water, so that Ethiopia hastens to stretch out her hand to God and to bring gifts to the King: the spices of piety, the gold of the knowledge of God, and the precious stones, which are the works of the commandments and of the virtues.

But I shall now explain in my discourse what I have in view as I begin the contemplation of the words before us. First I shall set out the very wording of the divine oracles, which runs thus: "King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon. Its pillars he made of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple. Its inside is paved with stones, love from the daughters of Jerusalem." In what we examined earlier about Solomon, our discourse found passages in which the mystery of the temple is sketched in his person. In the same way, the building of the litter points to God's plan for us. For God comes to be in those worthy of him in many ways, and he comes to be in each according to that person's capacity and worth. One person becomes a place of God, another a house, another a throne, and another a footstool. Someone may also become a chariot, or a horse that answers well to the rein, taking the good rider upon himself

and running the course wherever the one guiding him pleases. And as we are now taught, someone may also become his litter. Such a person is built according to his wisdom, not only from the wood of Lebanon but also with gold and silver and purple and stones, each fitted to its proper part, and through them his love becomes active. Not everyone has room for the working of love, but only one whose life shows that she is a daughter of the Jerusalem above, the free one. Even before we say anything, it is clear that whoever carries God within himself is a litter for the one who dwells and sits in him. According to holy Paul, such a person no longer lives himself but has Christ living in him, and gives proof that Christ speaks in him. He is properly called, and truly becomes, a litter of the one who is borne within him and carried by him. But that is not what we are asking. Rather, we should consider carefully what the variety and many kinds of material mean. How is the nature of wood joined with gold and silver and purple and stones in the building of the litter? After all, Paul, the wise master builder, judges that wood, together with hay and straw, should be rejected from the building of the house, since it is consumed by the devouring power of the fire that tests the work. But we know of a kind of wood that does not stay what it is, but changes itself into gold or silver or some other precious thing. For the Apostle says that in the great house of God some vessels are gold and silver by nature. By these he hints, I think, at the bodiless and intellectual creation. Others are of wood and clay, and by these he perhaps means us, whom disobedience made earthy and turned into clay. Sin, which came through the tree, made us wooden vessels instead of golden ones. The use of the vessels is also divided according to the worth of the material. Those of more precious material are set apart for honor, and the others are thrown aside for menial service. But what does Paul say about these things? That the vessel has the power, by its own choice, to become gold instead of wood, or silver instead of clay. "For if anyone," he says, "cleanses himself, he will be a vessel for honor, useful to the Master [?], prepared for every good work." Perhaps, then, what has been said brings us somewhat closer to the contemplation before us. In many places in holy Scripture, Mount Lebanon is mentioned to signify the adversary power. For example, it says through the prophet: "The Lord will shatter the cedars of Lebanon and grind them fine, them and Lebanon too, like the calf." This means the calf that Moses ground to powder in the desert, which became fine enough for the Israelites to drink. Here the prophecy shows that not only the evils that sprang from the adversary power, but also the mountain itself, Lebanon, the first root of evil, which feeds the timber of such trees, will be brought to nothing.

We, then, were once the wood of Lebanon, while we were rooted in it through a wicked life and the deceit of idols. But when we were cut away from there by the axe of the Word and came into the hands of the Craftsman, he made us his litter. Through rebirth he transformed the nature of the wood into silver and gold, into richly blooming purple, and into gleaming stones. As the Apostle says, God has distributed the gifts of the Holy Spirit fittingly to each. To one he gives prophecy in proportion to faith, and to another some other working, according to what each is naturally suited and able to receive of grace. One becomes an eye of the body of the Church, another is assigned to be a hand, another gives support as a foot. So also in the building of the litter: one becomes a pillar, another the seat, another the part at the head, which he called the back, and some are placed inside. For all of these the Craftsman, for some reason, does not devise a single kind of material for their adornment. All are adorned with beauty, but a different and fitting loveliness is devised for each. The pillars of the litter are silver, their seats purple, and the back that supports the head, on which the Bridegroom rests his head, is of gold. The whole interior is richly decorated with precious stones. By the pillars, then, we must understand the pillars of the Church, for whom the word is truly pure silver, refined in the fire. The purple are those who have mounted to the height of the royal way of life, for purple is regarded as the special mark of kingship. The headrest, on which the maker of the litter rests his head, is the gold of pure doctrines. Whatever is hidden and secret is made beautiful by the precious stones of a pure conscience. Through all these is formed the love from the daughters of Jerusalem. If someone wishes to call the whole Church a litter, and to assign the parts of the litter to particular persons according to their different activities, as was said above, our discourse can easily do this too and fit the parts of the litter to each rank of those appointed in the Church. As the Apostle says, "God has appointed in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers," and then each of the other gifts for the equipping of the saints. So the names of the things that go into building the litter may be understood as priests and teachers, and as holy virginity inside the litter, flashing with the purity of the virtues as with the gleam of stones. But enough about these things. The next passage contains an exhortation addressed by the bride to the daughters of Jerusalem. For the great Paul thought it a loss if he did not share his own good things with everyone,

and so he said such things to his hearers as: "Become as I am, for I too was once as you are," and: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." In the same way this bride, who loves humankind, was made worthy of the divine mysteries of the Master. When she saw the bed and became the King's litter, she cries out to the maidens, who would be the souls of those being saved: "How long will you be shut up in the cave of this life? Come out from the veils of nature and see this marvelous sight! Become daughters of Zion and behold the crown that encircles the King's head, which his mother placed on him." This agrees with the words of the Psalmist, who says: "You have set on his head a crown of precious stone." No one trained in judging words about God will quibble over the force of the name, that "mother" is mentioned instead of "father," for he will take one meaning from either word. The Divine is neither male nor female. How could such a thing be conceived of the Godhead, when even for us human beings it does not last forever? When we all become one in Christ, we strip off the marks of this difference together with the whole old man. For this reason every name we find has equal force in pointing to the incorruptible nature, and neither "female" nor "male" stains the meaning of that undefiled nature. That is why in the Gospel the father is said to give the wedding feast, while the prophet says to God, "You have set on his head a crown of precious stone," and here it says the crown is placed on the Bridegroom by the mother. Since there is one wedding and one bride, and the crown is put on the Bridegroom by one person, it makes no difference at all whether we call the only-begotten God the Son of God or, in Paul's words, the Son of his love. Under either name it is one and the same power that adorns him as a bridegroom for his union with us. "Come out, then," says the bride to the maidens, "and become daughters of Zion." Then from a lofty watchtower (for that is what Zion means) they may be able to see the marvelous sight of the Bridegroom wearing his crown. The Church becomes his crown, ringing his head with living stones. The one who weaves such a crown is love, and whoever calls her mother or love will not be wrong, for, as John says, God is love. The bride says that he rejoices in this crown and delights in his bridal adornment. For he who has made the Church his wife truly rejoices, crowned with the virtues of those who are outstanding in her. It would be better to set out the divine words themselves exactly as they stand: "Come out and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon [?] with which [?] crowned him, on the day of his wedding,

on the day of the gladness of his heart." The Word welcomes such love for humankind in the bride, since she too, in imitation of the Master, wants all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. So he makes her still more glorious by becoming the herald and painter of her beauty. The praise of her loveliness is not given in a simple way, as a general tribute to beauty. Instead, the discourse lingers lovingly over each part, granting each member its own praise through comparisons and likenesses. He speaks thus: "Behold, you are beautiful, my close one; behold, you are beautiful." For she imitated the Master's loving will, and like Abraham she urged the maidens to come out, each from her own land and from her kinship with the senses, so that they might see the pure Bridegroom crowned with the Church. She truly comes close to the Master's goodness, having drawn near to God through love of her neighbor. "You are beautiful," the Word says to her, "because by your good choice you have drawn near to the Good." The repetition of the praise shows that the testimony is true, for the divine law declares that truth is confirmed by a double testimony. That is why he says: "Behold, you are beautiful, my close one; behold, you are beautiful." But the whole Church is one body of Christ, and, as the Apostle says, in the one body there are many members, and not all the members have the same function. God created the eye in the body, and another was planted as an ear. Some become hands through the working of powers, and some, who carry burdens, are called feet. There may also be the work of taste and of smell, and all the other parts that make up a human body. In the common body of the Church one can find lips and teeth and tongue, breasts and belly and neck, and, as Paul says, even the parts of the body that seem less presentable. For this reason the exact judge of beauty picks out, from the whole body, the members that pleased him, and gives each its own fitting [?].

He begins his praises with the more important members. For which of our members is more precious than the eyes? Through them we perceive light. By them we recognize friends and enemies, and with them we tell what is our own from what belongs to others. They are the guides and teachers of every task, and the natural, inseparable leaders on a journey that does not go astray. Their position above the other senses shows that the benefit we gain from them is greater. My hearers will surely see at once which members of the Church the praise of the eyes refers to. Samuel was an eye,

the seer, for that is what he was called. Ezekiel was an eye, appointed by God as a watchman for the safety of those he guarded. Micah the seer was an eye, and so was Moses the beholder, who for this reason was even called god. All those appointed to guide the people were eyes, and the people of that time called them seers. And now those who fill their place in the body of the Church and are appointed as overseers are properly called eyes, if they look steadily at the Sun of righteousness and are never dimmed by the works of darkness. They are eyes if they can tell what is our own from what belongs to others, knowing that everything visible and temporary is foreign to our nature, while what is truly ours is what lies before us in hope, whose possession endures forever and cannot be taken away. It is also the work of the eyes to tell friend from enemy, so as to love the true Friend with all one's heart and soul and strength, and to show perfect hatred toward the enemy of our life. Whoever guides others in what they should do, teaches what is profitable, and leads them by the hand on the way to God, does with precision the work of a pure and healthy eye. Like the eyes of the body, he shines out ahead of the rest by his lofty way of life. That is why the Word begins his praise of the bride's beauty here, saying: "Your eyes are doves." For he sees that those set in the rank of eyes are innocent of evil, and approving the simplicity and innocence of their character, he called them doves, since innocence is the special trait of doves. Or perhaps the discourse bears witness to the eyes with praise of this kind. Sight is accomplished when the images of all visible things fall on the clear pupil. So whatever someone looks at, he must take on its form through the eye, which receives the shape of what appears as a mirror does. When, then, the one who has received this power of sight in the Church looks at nothing material and bodily, the spiritual and immaterial life is achieved in him. Such a life is shaped by the grace of the Holy Spirit. So the most perfect praise of the eyes is that the form of their life has been shaped after the grace of the Holy Spirit, for the Holy Spirit is a dove. The eyes are praised as a pair, so that the whole person, both visible and intelligible, may be praised. That is why he added yet another surpassing note to his praise, saying: "apart from your silence." For one part of the good life is plain to see, so that it is known even to men, while another part is hidden and unspeakable, seen by God alone. He, then, who sees what is not yet formed and looks into hidden things bears witness that in the one he praises, what is kept silent is greater than what appears. He does this by saying: "Your eyes are doves, apart from your silence." For what is admired in silence lies beyond what has already been praised.

He goes on with his praise of her beauty, turning his discourse to the hair, and says: "Your hair is like flocks of goats that have been revealed from [?]." We should first understand the nature of hair, and then recognize the praise that the discourse gives the bride through her hair. Paul calls hair the glory of a woman's head, and says that long hair has been given to a woman as a covering. He also says that the fitting covering for women is modesty and self-control, writing in these words: "As befits women who profess godliness, they should adorn themselves with modesty and self-control." From this, Paul's wisdom lets us understand the hair on the head, which a woman grows long, as modesty and self-control. For no other glory ought to be thought proper for a soul that professes godliness except modesty and self-control, which he called long hair. When she lacks it, she disgraces her head, as the Apostle says. Since Paul reasoned in this way about hair, we should apply the Apostle's words to the praise of the Church in our discussion of hair, following the text before us, which says: "Your hair is like flocks of goats that have been revealed from Gilead." Through these words the Word praises a virtuous way of life. But one more point should be added to what we say about hair: locks of hair have no share in any living sensation. This adds not a little to the praise, that hair feels neither pain nor pleasure. The body from which hair grows feels pain when it is plucked, but the hair itself feels nothing of what is done to it, whether it is cut or burned or smoothed with some cosmetic care. To lack sensation is the special trait of the dead. So whoever has no feeling for anything that people strive after in this world, who is neither puffed up by glory and honor nor pained by insult and dishonor, but keeps himself the same in either of these opposites, is the bride's hair that is praised. He has become simply dead and unmoved toward the affairs of the world, whether they go one way or the other. The excellence of the hair is compared to flocks of goats revealed from Gilead. What we ought to know precisely about these things we have not yet been able to grasp. But we conjecture that, just as the King changed the wood of Lebanon into gold and silver and purple and built himself a litter, so the Good Shepherd knows how to take flocks of goats and change them into flocks of sheep

working at virtue together with one another. That such flocks should have been revealed from Gilead raises the marvel still higher, because our turning to the philosophy that accords with God came about from the very opposite [?]. For it was not Mount Zion, his holy mountain, that led the way into such a way of life; rather, the nation dedicated to idols came to so great a change of life that it adorned the head of the bride with the excellences of virtue. Next in the sequence of praises the Word places the teeth, passing over the praises of the mouth and the lips. This deserves not to be passed over unexamined: why ever are the teeth placed before the lips in the praises? Perhaps someone wishing to bring out the beauty more elegantly might say that through the depiction of the teeth the smile of the mouth is covertly indicated as well. But I, looking to something else, reckon that the beauty of the teeth comes first in the praises, ahead of the praises of the mouth. For after this he did not leave even the lip unpraised, saying that her lips are scarlet and her speech lovely. What, then, is my conjecture about this? The best order in learning is first to be taught and only then to speak; and whoever says that lessons are the food of the soul will not miss the mark. For just as we grind bodily food with our teeth and so prepare it to become suited to the inward parts, in the same way there is in the soul a certain power that breaks teachings down fine, through which the lesson becomes profitable to the one who receives it. So I say that the teachers who discern and distinguish teachings, through whom instruction becomes easy for us to grasp and profitable, are figuratively called teeth by the Word. That is why the praise of the teeth comes first, and only then is the praise of the lips brought in. For the lip would not be praised for the beauty of reason unless those teeth, through a more diligent understanding of the lessons, imparted to the lips the grace that is in words. This, then, is the reason we have perceived for the order of the praises in the case of the teeth. Now it is time to examine the praise itself: how it compares the beauty of the teeth to flocks of shorn ewes which have just come up from the washing, all of them

rejoicing alike in twin offspring. The praise runs, word for word, as follows: Your teeth are like flocks of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, and there is none barren among them. Now if we look to the bodily sense of the comparison, I do not know how anyone could say that the teeth are praised by being compared with prolific flocks. For the praise of teeth lies in firmness and harmonious placement, and in being set solidly in the gums in an even and orderly arrangement. But what beauty of teeth flocks depict by their own example, coming up from the washing with their twin young and scattering over the glens, is not easy to see at first glance. Teeth stand in a row, holding harmoniously to one another; but those flocks scatter from one another, spreading out for the needs of grazing. Besides, a wool-bearing creature is no fitting comparison for a tooth, which is bare by nature. We must therefore inquire how the one who adorns with praises the good order of the teeth compares their beauty to flocks that bear twins, that have been shorn of their wool, and that have washed the dirt from their bodies in the washing. What, then, shall we understand by these things? Those who break down the divine mysteries finely through clearer exposition, so that this spiritual food becomes easy for the body of the Church to receive, are the ones who perform the work of the teeth. They take into their own mouth the coarse and solid bread of the word, and through more detailed interpretation make it easy to eat for the souls of those who receive it. For instance (since it is better to present the idea by examples), blessed Paul at one point sets before us the commandment of the law plainly and without elaboration, like an unchewed morsel, saying: You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain. Then, softening it by explanation, he makes the intent of the law easy to take in, saying: Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Or was it not written entirely for our sake?
