And there are many other such cases, for instance: Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. This is the unprepared bread. But see how, grinding it fine, he makes it edible for those who are fed: he transfers the story to two covenants, the one bearing children into slavery, the other setting free from slavery. In the same way, so that we need not dwell on each point, he takes the whole law as a coarse body and refines it through contemplation, making it spiritual instead of bodily: We know, he says, that the law is spiritual. What we have observed in Paul, then, that the Church needs teeth who do their work by grinding the doctrines down fine into clarity, we say also of everyone who, in imitation of him, makes the mystery clear to us. So the teeth of the Church are those who break down for us the unprepared grass of the divine oracles and chew it over like cud. Just as, then, the divine Apostle describes the life of

those who aspire to the good work of the episcopate, stating point by point what sort of person the one who has taken up the priesthood ought to be, so that along with everything else he has the gift of teaching, so here the Word wants those appointed to the service of teeth in the Church first to be shorn, that is, stripped of every material burden; then, through the washing of conscience, to be clean of every defilement of flesh and spirit; besides this, to be always going up through progress, and never to be dragged back down into the pit; and above all, to rejoice in double offspring of good conceptions in every kind of virtue, and to be barren in none of the good pursuits. The double conception is a riddle signifying good repute in each of the two parts we recognize in ourselves, so that such teeth bear twins, bringing forth dispassion in the soul and decorum in the life of the body. After these he adds, in due sequence, the praise befitting the lips, likening their beauty to a scarlet thread. He himself supplied its interpretation, calling the thread lovely speech. We have already considered above how the beauty of the lips is made lovely by the service of the teeth. For it is with the teeth, that is, with the guidance of teaching, that the mouth of the Church speaks clearly. That is why the teeth are first shorn and washed, are not childless, and bear twins, and only then do the lips bloom with the hue of scarlet, when the whole Church, in harmony toward the good, becomes one lip and one voice. The image of beauty here is twofold. For he does not simply say that the lips are a thread, but adds the bloom of a fine color as well, so that the mouth of the Church is beautified by both, the thread and the scarlet, each in its own way. By the thread it is taught unanimity, so that the whole Church becomes one thread and one cord twisted together out of various thoughts. By the scarlet it is taught to look to the blood by which we were redeemed, and always to carry in its mouth the confession of him who bought us with his blood. For through both of these the comeliness of the Church's lips is made complete, when faith shines out in confession and love is woven together with faith. And if we must encompass the image in a kind of definition, we will define what was said thus: the scarlet thread is faith working through love, so that the scarlet signifies faith and the thread is interpreted as love. The truth bears witness that the bride's lips are adorned with these. The lovely speech needs no subtler contemplation or further interpretation. For the Apostle has already made it clear that this speech is the word of faith which we proclaim: If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that

God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation. This is the lovely speech through which the lips of the Church bloom becomingly, like that scarlet thread. After the beauty of the mouth, the bridegroom delights also in the blush of the cheek. Common usage loosely calls this part of the face the 'apple'. So he likens the apple of the cheek to the rind of a pomegranate, writing his praise of it word for word thus: Your cheek is like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your silence. That what is praised here is modesty, anyone can easily reckon from the sequence of what we have considered. For the Word, having given the Church a body in the form of the bride and having distributed the individual virtues suitably across the depiction of the beauty of her face, now, through the blush glowing on the cheeks, fittingly praises self-control, adorning it with modesty in the riddle of the pomegranate. For this fruit is astringent, and it grows inside an inedible surface. It is therefore well and fittingly transferred, through contemplation, to the accomplishment of self-control. For as the astringency of the pomegranate's rind nourishes and guards the sweetness of the fruit contained within, so an austere, continent and hardened life becomes the guardian of the good things of self-control. Here too the praise of this virtue is twofold: through what appears outwardly in a decorous life, and through what is accomplished in the dispassion of the soul. The praise of these, as the Apostle says, is not from human beings but from God. For the modesty that shines out in what is done has its praise readily from what is plain to see; but apart from this are the wonders kept silent and hidden, which are seen only by that eye which sees what is hidden. From what follows we learn that everything done by the God-bearing saints became a type and a teaching of what is accomplished in virtue. Their marriages, their migrations, their wars, their constructions of buildings all prefigured, according to some principle, an admonition for the life that came after. For these things were written, he says, for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. The war against the foreigners counsels us to be brave against evil. Their eagerness for marriages suggests to us in riddles a dwelling together with the virtues. Likewise the migration hints at the settling of the virtuous life; and all their zeal for constructing buildings bids us take care of our own houses, which are built through virtue. That is why it seems to me that the famous tower in which David dedicated the choicest of the spoils was built with an eye to the Church's progress, and that by this work he prefigured something of what is pursued in virtue. This tower stands out,

rising to a height on a mountain ridge; and at that time it was thought suitable for guarding the spoils, all that the king, having subdued the foreigners, had made his own gain along with the rest of the plunder. The king, then, through his wisdom, showed what good for human life David had in view when, by building the tower, he laid down beforehand, as it were, a counsel for the life that came after. For he is about to praise the beauty of the whole body of the Church, member by member, by comparison and likeness to something; and next, describing in words what those among the people who hold the place of the neck ought to be like, he mentions this tower, which is named after David and is also known for its battlements. For the battlements are called Thalpioth. The text reads thus: Your neck is like the tower of David, built in Thalpioth; a thousand shields hang upon it, all darts of the mighty. The bodily structure of the tower is admired because it is the work of that [?] king, because of the prominence of its site, and because of the weapons dedicated in it, shields and darts, whose great number the text indicates by the word 'thousand'. Our aim, however, is to understand the force of the divine word: how that part of the Church whose name is 'neck' is compared to this tower. First, then, we should examine what part of our own body is called by the name 'neck', and then fit the name to the member of the Church. Well then, what is rooted between the shoulders, holds up the head upon itself and serves as the base of what lies above it, is called the neck. Its back is supported by bones, while its front [?] is free of any covering of bones. The bone there is not by nature continuous with itself and undivided, like that of the forearm or the shin. The bones are divided at many points in the form of vertebrae, and they are united with one another by the sinews, marrow and ligaments that grow on them, and by the spinal [?] marrow running through the middle, whose sheath is joined to the membranes and whose inner substance is joined to the brain. In front, the neck contains the windpipe, which is the receptacle of the breath that enters and flows into us from outside, by which the fire of the heart is fanned toward its natural activity. It also contains the passages for food, through the gullet and throat, conveying everything brought in through the mouth to the cavity that receives it. The neck also has something else that sets it apart from the other members. For at the upper end of the windpipe lies the workshop of the voice, in which all the vocal instruments are made ready, through which sound is produced as the windpipe is set vibrating all around by the breath rising up through it. With the bodily member thus described, it would be easy

from what we have considered here to understand also the neck of the Church's body: who it is that properly takes this name through activities corresponding to it, being called a neck and likened to the tower of David. First, then, and this truly comes first: if someone bears upon himself the true head of the universe, I mean that head which is Christ, from whom the whole body is joined and knit together, he properly bears this name. Further, if he is receptive of the Spirit that makes our heart fiery and warms it, and if with a resonant voice he serves the word. For God built the human voice into human nature for no other reason than that it should be an instrument of speech, articulating through itself the movements of the heart. Let this neck also have the nourishing activity, I mean teaching, by which the strength of the whole body of the Church is maintained. For as long as food keeps flowing in, the body remains in being; but when it fails, the body wastes away and perishes. Let it also imitate the harmonious arrangement of the vertebrae, by making the individuals among the people who belong to it into one member through the bond of peace, a member that bends and straightens itself and turns nimbly to either side. Such a neck was Paul, and anyone else who has shaped his life in imitation of him. He bore the name of the Lord, having become a chosen vessel for the Master, and the head of all things was fitted to him so exactly that whatever he said, it was no longer he who spoke but his head that uttered it, as he showed the Corinthians that Christ was speaking and uttering words in him. So melodious and resonant was his [?] windpipe, articulating the word of truth through the Holy Spirit; so was his throat always sweetened by the divine oracles, as through himself he nourished the whole body with those life-giving teachings. And if you ask about the vertebrae as well: who so joined everyone into one body by the bond of peace and love? Who so taught the neck to bow down in humble things, and to turn again in setting its mind on things above, and to look about to either side readily and nimbly, so as to avoid and guard against the various wiles of the devil? Such a neck, then, is truly built by David. By David understand the King who is the Father of the King, who from the beginning made man to be a tower and not a ruin, and through grace built him up again, securing him with many shields, so that he would no longer be easy prey to the attacks of enemies. For the hanging shields, not lying on the ground but seen suspended in the air around him, and along with the shields the darts of the mighty, strike fear into those who make war on it, so that they do not even attempt to assault the tower at all. I think the multitude of shields signifies to us the angelic guard that encircles such a tower like a wall. The mention

of the darts also points to this meaning. For he did not simply say 'darts', but by adding 'of the mighty' he indicated those who fight on our behalf, so that the saying is fulfilled: The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them. As for the number 'thousand', it does not seem to me to signify exactly ten hundreds; rather, the text adopted it to indicate a great number. For it is customary in Scripture's loose usage to indicate a great number by this figure, as David says, meaning a multitude: Thousands of those who prosper, and: Above thousands of gold and silver. This, then, is how we have understood the neck that is rooted upon the shoulders. By the shoulders on which it grows we mean practical and active endeavors, through which our arms work out their own salvation. Anyone who has followed attentively what has been said has surely perceived the soul's growth toward greater things as it is lifted up toward God. Before, the bride was content to be likened to the mare that defeated the Egyptian tyrant, and to have the comeliness of her neck resemble necklaces. But now see how great a perfection in the good he bears witness to in her: he does not liken the beauty of her neck to necklaces worn around it, but because of its greatness it is called a tower. The tower is made conspicuous and visible even to those standing far off, not only by the lavishness of its construction, raising it as high as possible, but also by its site, which naturally rises above its neighbors. When, then, the tower is the work of a king and happens to stand upon a lofty way of life, the saying of the Lord is shown to be true: A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden. Understand 'tower', if you will, in place of 'city'. Now it is time to consider also the two fawns of the gazelle that dwell around the bride's heart, which the Word calls breasts when it says: Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that feed among the lilies. The heart lies between them, and their pasture is not grass or thorns but lilies, which keep their bloom through the whole season of grazing, neither blooming for a season nor withering in season, but providing through themselves lasting food for the fawns. So the shadows of the deceit pursued in this life no longer prevail; the light now shines everywhere, and all things are lit up by the day, which breathes the light wherever it wills. For so the Word says: Until the day breathes and the shadows move away. You surely know, having learned it from the Gospel, that it is the Holy Spirit who, by breathing on whomever he wills, produces light in those [?] whence it comes and where it goes. Concerning this the text now proceeds thus: Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that feed among the lilies, until

…until the day breathes, and the shadows are stirred. Now, that the Holy Spirit is called “day”, a light that breathes on those in whom it comes to dwell, I do not think anyone with sense would hesitate over the statement. For if those born of the Spirit become sons of light and sons of the day, what else should we take the Holy Spirit to be but light and day, whose breath puts to flight the shadows of vanity? When the sun appears, the shadows cannot possibly remain; they must withdraw and depart. It would also be timely to add to our examination of the text the mystery of the two fawns of the gazelle. They were born as twins, their food is the lily, and their pasture is the good and rich ground. According to the Lord's parable, this ground is the heart. By grazing in it and gathering pure thoughts from it like flowers, they grow fat. The lily has a double grace from nature, fragrance mingled with lovely colour, so that it delights those who pick it in both ways, whether they bring it to their nose or feast their eyes on the beauty of its bloom. The sense of smell is filled with the fragrance of Christ, while the flower's appearance displays what is pure and spotless. Perhaps what the text means has already been made clear by what we have said. Two human beings are seen in each person, the one bodily and visible, the other intelligible and invisible. The birth of the two is twin, since they enter life together at the same time. The soul does not exist before the body, and the body is not fashioned before the soul; they come to be in life simultaneously. Their natural food is purity and fragrance and all the other things that the virtues bear in abundance. But sometimes people eagerly pursue poison instead of nourishment. They do not graze on the flowers of the virtues but take pleasure in thorns and thistles. For we have heard the Gospel parable give this name to sins, whose evil growth was produced by the curse on the serpent. There is need, then, of discerning eyes, able to tell the lily from the thorn precisely, to choose what saves and to reject what destroys. For this reason he gave a name to the one who, like the great Paul, became a breast for infants and nursed the newborn of the Church with milk. He called them a pair of breasts born together and likened them to the fawns of the gazelle. By all this he bears witness to the excellence of such a member of the Church. In both respects it makes its way well to the pasture of pure lilies, sharp-sightedly telling the thorn apart from what nourishes. It dwells near the ruling faculty, whose symbol is the heart, which by its own means [?] the breasts. And beyond this, it does not shut grace up within itself but offers the nipple of the word to those who need it, as a nurse cherishes

her own children, as the Apostle both did and said. After carrying the praise forward with these members of the Church, the Word in what follows makes his praise of her whole-bodied. This happens when through death he has destroyed the one who holds the power of death and has brought himself back to his own glory of divinity, which he had from the beginning, before the world existed. For he said, “I will go my way to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense,” and so displayed the glory of divinity. Then he added: “You are wholly beautiful, my close one, and there is no blemish in you.” By these words he teaches two things. First, no one takes his life from him; he has authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. He goes by himself to the mountain of myrrh, not because of our works, so that no one may boast, but by his own grace, accepting death on behalf of sinners. Second, human nature cannot be cleansed of its blemish in any other way than by the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world and wipes out all evil through himself. So he said, “You are wholly beautiful, my close one, and there is no blemish in you,” and introduced the mystery of the Passion through the riddle of the myrrh. Then he mentioned the frankincense, which points to the divine. By this he teaches us that whoever shares the myrrh with him will certainly share the frankincense too. For whoever suffers with him will certainly also be glorified with him. And whoever has once entered the divine glory becomes wholly beautiful, having passed beyond the blemish that opposes it. May we too be separated from that blemish through Christ Jesus our Lord, who died and rose for us, to whom belong glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.

“Come from Lebanon, bride, come from Lebanon. You will come and pass through from the beginning of faith, from the head of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards. You have heartened us, my sister bride; you have heartened us with one of your eyes, with one ornament of your neck.” The great Apostle recounted his great visions to the Corinthians. He said that he was uncertain about his own nature at the time of his initiation in paradise, whether he was body or mind. Yet he solemnly declares: “I do not yet consider that I have laid hold of it, but I still strain forward to what lies ahead, forgetting what has already been accomplished.” He clearly shows that even after that third heaven, which he alone knew (for Moses said nothing about it in his account of creation), and after he had heard the ineffable mysteries of paradise, he still presses on toward what is higher. He does not stop ascending and never makes the good he has already grasped the limit of his desire. By this, I think, he teaches us that in that blessed nature of the good, much

is always being found, yet what lies beyond is infinitely greater than whatever is grasped at any moment. This continues forever for the one who participates, through the whole everlastingness of the ages, as the participants keep growing through ever greater things. For, according to the Master's voice, which does not lie, the pure in heart see God. Each always receives understanding in proportion to his capacity, as much as he is able to contain. But the boundless and incomprehensible nature of the Godhead remains beyond all comprehension. For that whose majestic glory has no limit, as the Prophet testifies, always stays the same and is always seen at the same height. Great David set fair ascents in his heart and always went from strength to strength, and he cried out to God: “But you, Lord, are most high forever.” I think he meant this: through the whole everlastingness of the endless age, the one who runs toward you always becomes greater and higher than himself, always growing in proportion as he ascends through good things. But you remain the same, most high forever. You can never appear lower to those who ascend, because you are always equally above and beyond the power of those who are being raised up. We take the Apostle to be teaching these things about the nature of the ineffable goods when he says of that good that the eye has not known it, even though it always sees. For the eye does not see as much as the good is, but only as much as the eye can receive. And the ear has not heard it in the full measure of what is meant, even though it always takes in the word by hearing. And it has not entered the human heart, even though the pure in heart always see as much as they can. For what is grasped at any moment is greater than everything grasped before, yet it does not put a limit on what is sought. Rather, for those who ascend, the end of what has been found becomes the beginning of finding higher things. The one who ascends never stops, receiving one beginning after another, and the beginning of ever greater things is never complete in itself. The desire of the one who ascends never comes to rest in what is already known. Through another, greater desire the soul rises in turn toward another good that lies beyond, and so it always journeys through higher things toward the infinite. Now that we have laid this out, it is time to add our contemplation of the divine words: “Come from Lebanon, bride, come from Lebanon. You will come and pass through from the beginning of faith, from the head of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” What, then, have we understood in these words? The fountain of good things always draws the thirsty to itself, as the fountain says in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” In these words he set no limit to the thirst, or to the impulse toward him, or to the enjoyment of drinking.

Instead, by the continuous form of the command he makes the summons perpetual: to thirst, to drink, and to keep pressing toward him. And for those who have already tasted and learned by experience that the Lord is good, the taste itself becomes a kind of summons to share in more. This is why the summons toward himself, which always draws toward the greater, never fails the one who ascends. Let us recall how often the Word has already urged the bride in what came before. “Come, my close one,” he says; and again, “Come, my dove”; and, “Come yourself into the shelter of the rock.” The Word has spoken to the soul in other such words too, urging her on and drawing her toward the desire for greater things. He has already testified that she who listens to him is blameless in every respect, saying, “You are wholly beautiful, and there is no blemish in you.” Now, so that she may not grow puffed up by this testimony and be hindered from ascending to greater things, he again uses this voice of summons and bids her rise to the desire for what lies beyond. He says: “Come from Lebanon, bride.” The meaning is something like this: “You followed well in what went before,” he says. “You came with me to the mountain of myrrh, for you were buried with me through baptism into death. You came with me also to the hill of frankincense, for you were raised with me and exalted into fellowship with the divinity, which the name frankincense indicates. Go up with me from these to other mountains also, advancing and being exalted through active knowledge. Come, then, from Lebanon,” he says, that is, from the frankincense, “no longer betrothed but a bride. For no one can live with me who has not been changed through the myrrh of death into the divinity of the frankincense. Since you have now reached this height, do not stop ascending, as though you had already [?] perfection through these things. For this frankincense, which you shared in through the resurrection, becomes for you the beginning of faith, and also the beginning of the journey toward the higher goods. From this beginning, then, which is faith, you will come and pass through.” That is, she will both come and forever pass through such ascents, not

The text reads: “You will come and pass through, from the beginning of faith, from the head of Sanir and Hermon.” By these words he hints at the mystery of the birth from above. For it is said that the springs of the Jordan pour out from here. This mountain is their [?], and it is divided into two ridges that bear the names Sanir and Hermon. The stream from these springs has become for us the beginning of our transformation toward the Divine. For this reason she hears the one who calls her to himself, saying: “Come from Lebanon, from the beginning of faith, and from the head of these mountains, from which the springs of the mystery have come to you.” He fittingly adds mention of lions and leopards, so that by setting painful things beside them he may make the enjoyment of joyful things sweeter. For since

man [?] rejected the divine form, he became beastlike and came to resemble irrational nature, turning into a leopard and a lion through his wicked practices. For the one who is dragged off by the lion lying in ambush in its den, as the Prophet says, and is brought low in its snare, is transformed into its nature, because the nature of the beast has overpowered him. “May those who make them become like them,” he says, “and all who trust in them.” In the same way, whoever has spotted his soul with the stains of his life becomes a leopard. There was a time when humanity lived among these beasts, led astray by idolatry, by the Jewish deception, and by the varied wickedness of sinners. Afterward, through the Jordan, the myrrh and Lebanon, it was raised so high that it now walks the heights together with God. For this reason the text heightens the joy of present goods by setting the sorrows of the past beside them. It recalls the state the soul was in before Lebanon and the beginning of faith, and before the mysteries made known to us at the Jordan. Life in peace becomes sweeter after war, sweetened by grim stories. And the good of health delights our bodily senses all the more when nature returns to itself after the misery of some illness. In the same way, the good Bridegroom arranges a heightening and increase of joy in good things for the soul that ascends to him. He not only shows the bride his own beauty first; he also uses his word to remind her of the most dreadful form of beasts. In this way she may delight all the more in the present goods, learning by comparison what she has received in exchange for what. Perhaps these words also providentially prepare another good for the bride. We are changeable by nature, and the Word does not want us to slip away toward evil through our changeability. He wants us instead, through constant growth toward the better, to have change as a helper in our ascent to higher things. In this way the very changeability of our nature can achieve unchangeableness with regard to evil. For this reason the memory of the beasts that once overpowered us serves as a kind of tutor and guardian, keeping us estranged from evils. [?] … so that, by [?] from worse things, we may achieve steadfastness and constancy in good things, neither stopping in our change toward the better nor being altered toward evil. This is why he both bids the bride come from Lebanon and reminds her of the den of lions in which she once lodged. He also mentions the mountains of leopards where she spent her time when she lived among beasts. But the voice of the Word is always a voice of power. At creation the light shone forth together with the command, the firmament came to stand together with the word that commanded it, and all the rest of creation likewise appeared along with the creative Word. In the same way now too, when the Word

had bidden the soul, now made better, to come to him, she was empowered by the command and at once became such as the Bridegroom wished. She was transformed toward what is more divine, and through this good alteration she was changed from the glory in which she was to a higher glory. As a result she became a wonder to the choir of angels around the Bridegroom, and all of them, praising her, spoke to her in wonder: “You have heartened us, our sister bride.” For the mark of impassibility [?] shines on her and on the angels alike. It raises her, who has achieved impassibility in the flesh, to kinship and [?] with the incorporeal beings. That is why they say to her: “You have heartened us, our sister bride.” She is rightly honoured with both names: our sister because of the kinship of impassibility, and bride because of her union with the Word. We think that “You have heartened us” means something like “You have given us a soul,” as if they were saying to her, “You have put a heart in us.” To make what we are saying clearer and more evident, we shall call on the divine Apostle to interpret these mysteries. Somewhere in his writings, in his letter to the Ephesians, he describes for us the great economy of God's appearing in the flesh. There he says that not only was human nature taught the divine mysteries through this grace, but that the manifold wisdom of God was also made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, revealed through the economy in Christ among human beings. The text runs: “so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, according to the eternal purpose that he carried out in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through faith in him.” For truly the varied wisdom of God is made known through the Church to the powers above the world. This wisdom worked its great wonders through opposites. How did life come through death, righteousness through sin, blessing through a curse, glory through dishonour, and power through weakness? In earlier times the powers above the world knew only the simple, uniform wisdom of God, which worked its wonders in a way that matched nature. Nothing in what they saw was varied. The divine nature, having power, made the whole creation at will. By the mere impulse of its will it brought the nature of beings into existence and made all things very good, springing up from the fountain of the good. But this varied form of wisdom, made up of an interweaving of opposites, has now been clearly shown through the Church: how the Word becomes flesh, how life is mingled with death, how by his own bruise he heals our

wound; how by the weakness of the cross he overthrows the power of the adversary; how the invisible is made manifest in the flesh; how he ransoms the captives, being himself both the buyer and the price, for he gave himself to death as a ransom for us; how he enters into death without departing from life; how he takes part in slavery and yet remains in his kingship. The friends of the Bridegroom learned all these and similar works of wisdom through the Church, works that are varied and not simple. They were heartened, because in the mystery they perceived another character of the divine wisdom. And if it is not too bold to say so, perhaps they too saw the beauty of the Bridegroom through the bride and marvelled at what is invisible and incomprehensible to all beings. For he whom no one has ever seen, as John says, and whom no one can see, as Paul testifies, made the Church his own body. Through the addition of those who are being saved he builds it up in love, until we all attain to the perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. If, then, the Church is the body of Christ, and Christ is the head of the body, forming the face of the Church with his own character, perhaps the friends of the Bridegroom were heartened by looking at this, because in her they see the Invisible more clearly. People who cannot look at the disk of the sun itself can look at it through its gleam in water. In the same way the friends look into the face of the Church as into a pure mirror and see the Sun of righteousness, who is perceived through what appears. For this reason the friends do not say only once to the bride, “You have heartened us,” which means, “Through yourself you have created in us a soul and an understanding for perceiving the light.” They repeat the same words again and lend credibility to what they say by the repetition. For they say again: “You have heartened us with one of your eyes.” This above all produced in the friends their wonder at the bride. The soul's power of sight is twofold: one kind sees the truth, while the other wanders among vain things. The bride's pure eye is open only to the nature of the good, while the other eye is wholly idle. For this reason the friends direct their praise to the one eye, through which alone she contemplates the One alone. I mean the One who is apprehended in the unchangeable and eternal nature: the true Father, the only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit. For that alone is truly one which is contemplated in one nature, since the difference of hypostases creates no separation or estrangement. There are some who, with eyes that differ, sharply and wrongly see what does not exist. In the fantasies of their distorted eyes they divide the One into many natures. These are the ones called “much-seeing”, who by seeing many

[?] seeing nothing. And those who now look toward God, but then wander off again after material imaginings, are unworthy of the angels' praise, because they waste themselves on imaginings of things that have no real existence. But someone who is sharp-sighted toward the Divine alone is blind to everything else that the eyes of the many look at. That is why the bride makes her friends marvel with one of her eyes. So the many-eyed person, who looks at empty things with many eyes, is blind. But the person who looks toward the good alone with the single eye of the soul is sharp-sighted and discerning. It would not be hard to work out from what we have examined what that "one" is, or what the ornament of the bride's neck is, even if the phrasing seems somewhat [?] obscure. For the text says: "You have ravished our heart with one of your eyes, with one, with an ornament of your neck." So "with one" agrees with "one of your eyes," and we understand it with a word left unstated: "with one soul." For many souls come to be in each uneducated person. In such people the passions gain mastery and take over the place of the soul, and the character of the soul shifts toward grief and pleasure, anger and fear, cowardice and rashness. But the soul that looks to reason is said to live with one soul, because the virtuous life has a single form. So we must divide the passage like this: "with one" is joined in sense to what comes before [?], and we take it to mean either "with one soul" or "with one settled state." The next phrase, "with an ornament of your neck," has a different meaning. Someone rephrasing the whole verse more clearly might say: "Your eye is one, because it looks toward one thing, and your soul is one, because it is not divided among different dispositions. And the setting of your neck has perfection, because it has taken the divine yoke upon itself." In the ornament of your neck, then, we see the yoke of Christ, and in your disposition toward the truly good we see one eye and one soul. That is why we confess that you have ravished our heart with your wonders, showing one eye and one soul in the ornament of your neck. As has been said, the ornament of the bride's neck is the yoke. This, then, is the praise that the angels have given for the bride's beauty, for we have understood them to be the bridegroom's friends. And so that their praise may not seem uncritical and mistaken, the Word adds his own vote and confirms the friends' judgment of the bride's beauty. He himself also adds greater wonders to the testimony about her beauty, describing in words the loveliness that shines out in her very limbs. God willing, we will set this out in what follows, if some power for understanding the mysteries should come to us from our ally above, for the knowledge of the Church's beauty and for the praise of the glory of his grace in Christ Jesus, to whom belongs all glory forever. Amen.

"How beautiful your breasts have become, my sister, bride! How beautiful your breasts have become from wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes [?] is above all spices! Your lips drip honeycomb, bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense. A garden locked, my sister, bride, a garden locked, a fountain sealed. Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruit of fruit trees, henna with nard; nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon, myrrh and aloes with all the finest perfumes. A fountain of the garden, and a well of living water, rushing down from Lebanon." "If, then, you have been raised with Christ, set your minds on the things above, not on the things on earth." This is what the one who speaks in Paul says to us. "For you have died," he says, "and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, is revealed, then you too will be revealed in glory." We have become dead to the lower nature and have moved our hope of life from earth to heaven. Our life through the flesh has been hidden in us, as the proverb says: "The wise hide perception." And we wait for the true life, which is Christ, to be revealed in us, so that we too may be revealed in glory, transformed into something more divine. If all this is so, then let us listen to the present words as people who have died to the body and are not dragged down by what is said toward fleshly [?]. For the one who is dead to the passions and desires will carry the meanings of the words over to what is pure and undefiled. He will set his mind on the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of the Father, in whom there is no passion, and he will forget lowly and earthbound thoughts. Let us listen, then, to the divine words in which the Word sketches the beauty of the undefiled bride. And let us listen as people who have gone outside flesh and blood and have been transformed into the spiritual nature. "How beautiful your breasts have become, my sister, bride! How beautiful your breasts have become from wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes is above all spices!" Everyone who does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother. And the pure virgin betrothed to the Lord, so as to share in the undefiled bridal chamber, is properly called bride. Anyone who knows the divinely inspired words will see this clearly. But as I search out the meaning of these divine sayings, I do not see the Word offering the bride mere praise by giving her such a title. Rather, I say that the bridegroom is recounting the causes of her growth in beauty. For she would not have been made beautiful in the springs of good teachings, which he figuratively

calls breasts, if she had not first made herself the Lord's sister through good works, and been renewed into virginity through birth from above, and so become the betrothed and bride of the one who joined her to himself. So he who called her his sister and bride states the cause of the change in her breasts toward something better and more perfect. They no longer gush with milk, the food of infants, but pour out pure wine for the gladness of the more perfect, and the water of the tavern-keepers has not spoiled its charm. In these words a loving affection is preserved, as at a wedding feast, with each partner returning the other's love in turn. For the bridegroom greets the Church in return with the same words with which she had earlier hymned his beauty at the opening. Right at the first words, she longed for the Word from the divine mouth to come into her own mouth, and she signified this by the riddle of the kiss. She then stated the cause of her desire: his breasts are good, surpassing the nature of wine by what they supply, and exceeding every fragrance of perfumes and spices. She put it this way: "For your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes is above all spices." In all other matters too we learn this teaching from the divine philosophy: the Divine always becomes toward us whatever we show ourselves to be toward God by our free choice. David in his prophecy testifies that he is good to the good. But another of the prophets calls him a bear and a leopard to those who have turned into beasts through the way they live, setting out in advance in riddles the [?] teachings. In these teachings the King's words are seen to take one character toward those on the right and another toward those on the left. To the one group he is good and gentle, to the other fearful and implacable, since he adapts himself to the choice of those being judged. For this reason the Word now makes a fitting return to the bride. The Lord repays her praise in the same terms in which she hymned the Master's beauty. He too welcomes the change for the better that her breasts have undergone through their activity. They have stopped bearing milk and pour out wine instead. Through this wine gladness comes to more perfect hearts, those that are no longer tossed about by infancy but can fill their mouths from the mixing bowl of wisdom and draw good things into themselves. So, having praised her breasts for producing wine, he also adds praise for her fragrance, saying: "And the fragrance of your garments is above all spices." To understand such praise, we must learn from Holy Scripture the nature of the spices named. Every sweet-smelling spice gives pleasure to the sense of smell. So let us understand that by "spices" the Word means all the things that Scripture has taught us are fragrant. For example, Noah offers the sacrifice to God, and the Lord smelled an odor of

sweetness. So sacrifice becomes a spice to God. Later, many sacrifices of atonement are offered to God under the law: thank-offerings and peace-offerings, purification offerings and offerings for sin. Count all these among the spices. Count the offerings of whole fruits and the burnt offerings, and the partial dedications of the portions set apart: the breast of the victim, the lobe of the liver, the fat over the kidneys. Count, besides these, the frankincense, the fine flour soaked in oil, the compounded incense, and everything else that was consecrated through fire. Let all of it be in the list of spices. So when we hear that the bride's perfume is judged worthy of greater acceptance than all spices, we learn from this that the mystery of the truth, accomplished through the teaching of the gospel, is the only thing fragrant to God, and is preferred above all the spices of the law. It is no longer veiled by any type or shadow, but becomes fragrant through the revealing of the truth. For if the Lord did smell any of the earlier spices as an odor of sweetness, each was judged worthy of acceptance because of the meaning shown in it, not because of the obvious and bodily form of what was done. This is clear from the great voice of the Prophet, who says: "I will not accept bulls from your house, or goats from your flocks; for I will not eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats." And yet animal sacrifices took place many times. But even when they take place, what is laid down for you in riddle through them is something else: the passions in you must be slaughtered. "For a sacrifice to God," it says, "is a broken spirit; God will not despise a broken and humbled heart." From this comes our sacrifice of praise, which glorifies the one who smells such an odor. The soul that is spiritually fragrant surpasses all the symbolic spices of the law. As Paul says, he was the aroma of Christ. Such a soul has itself become fragrant through its way of life. Through a varied blending and mixture of the virtues it has given off a fine scent, the scent of the priestly anointing oil and of the compounded incense, and so it has proved worthy to reach the bridegroom's sense of smell as an odor of sweetness. Therefore the divine sense, as Solomon calls it, prefers to the bodily spices of the law that immaterial and pure fragrance which the virtues blend like perfume, saying: "And the fragrance of your perfumes is above all spices." The next passage raises the praise higher, testifying to the wealth of spiritual gifts that came to her through study and attentiveness. For the proverb wants the disciple of wisdom to keep company with the bee (and you surely understand from the disciples who the teacher is). It says to the lovers of wisdom: "Go to the bee and learn how hardworking she is, and what a noble work she trades in,

whose labors kings and ordinary people use for their health." It says that she is desired by all and held in honor, weak in strength but having honored wisdom, and for that reason raised up to be a model of life for the virtuous. "For having honored wisdom," it says, "she was raised up." Through these words it advises us to hold back from none of the good teachings. Instead, alighting on the meadow of the divinely inspired words, we should gather from each something toward acquiring wisdom and mold the honeycomb for ourselves, storing up this industry in our own heart as in a hive. Just as there are cells in a honeycomb [?], we should build in our memory separate chambers for the many kinds of teaching, so that they are not confused. And so, imitating that wise bee, whose honeycomb is sweet but whose sting does not strike, we should carry on this noble work of the virtues continually. For such a person truly trades, exchanging the labors of this life for eternal goods and sharing his own labors with kings and ordinary people for the health of the soul. In this way such a soul becomes desirable to the bridegroom and held in honor by the angels, perfecting power in weakness because it honors wisdom. The stories about that wise bee, then, are a model of learning and diligence. And the various distributions of spiritual gifts come to those who have labored, in proportion to their zeal. That is why he says to the bride: "Your heart has become full of the honeycombs of every kind of learning. From the good treasure of your heart you bring out the honeyed drops of words, so that your speech is honey mixed with milk." For it says: "Your lips drip honeycomb, bride; honey and milk are under your tongue." Your speech has been prepared so that it does not offer the same kind of benefit to every hearer, but is adapted to the capacity of those who receive it. In this way it suits both the more perfect and those who are still infants, becoming honey for the perfect and milk for infants. Paul was like this. He nursed the newborn with gentler words, but among the perfect he spoke wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom hidden from the ages, which this age cannot contain, nor its rulers. So he says that this store of honey and milk lies under the tongue, and by this phrase he points to the measured and timely use of words. For the one who knows how he ought to answer each person keeps this varied power of speech under his tongue. He brings out what each hearer needs, suitably and at the right time

[?] of the virtuous life is likeness to the Divine. For this reason the virtuous take care to cultivate purity of soul and freedom from every passionate disposition, so that through their more refined life some imprint of the transcendent nature may come to be in them too. The virtuous way of life is not of a single form or a single kind. In making fabrics, the weaver's art produces a garment from many threads, some stretched straight and others running crosswise. In the same way, many things must come together in the virtuous life, and from them the refined life is woven. The divine Apostle lists such threads, from which the weaving of pure deeds is made up: love, joy and peace, patience and kindness, and all such things. With these a person is adorned who exchanges a corruptible and earthly life for the incorruption of heaven. For this reason he welcomes the adornment of the bride's garment, as resembling frankincense in its fragrance. And yet before this he said that the fragrance of the bride's perfume surpasses all spices. So this might seem to lower the praise: she who was ranked above every spice is now compared to one of the spices, for the Word says: "The sweet smell of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense." But for some reason frankincense incense was specially set apart for the honor of the Divine. That is why she, who was judged to be above all spices, is thought worthy to be likened to the one spice that is dedicated to God. So the meaning of the riddle is this: "Your clothing of virtues, O bride, imitates the divine blessedness, and through purity and freedom from passion it is made like the inaccessible nature." For the fragrance of the divine garments is such that it resembles the frankincense dedicated to the honor of God. Again, the praises that follow teach us how someone might become the Lord's sister and spouse, when he says: "A garden locked, my sister, bride." So if anyone aspires to become a bride by being joined to the Lord, and a sister by doing his will, as the Gospel says, let him become a flowering garden, holding within himself the beauty of every plant: the sweet fig, the fruitful olive, the high-crowned palm, the flourishing vine. Let there be no thorny bush or fleabane, but cypress and myrtle in their place. This is how the great David and the lofty Isaiah know how to beautify such a garden. David says: "The righteous will flourish like a palm"; and, "But I am like a fruitful olive"; and, "Your wife is like a flourishing vine." In another prophet, the one who rests under his own fig tree is called blessed. And Isaiah says that instead of the bush the cypress, and instead of the fleabane the myrtle, will

come up. It would be superfluous to set out in detail the riddles about each of these trees that the prophecy has shown us, since everyone can see what they mean. The fig's sweet fruit is ripened from the sharpest sap: at first it is bitter and inedible, but later it becomes a peaceable fruit and sweetens the senses of the soul. Everyone can see, too, what the olive's fruit-bearing gives us. At first a very sharp and bitter juice is nourished in the fruit, but afterward, through proper ripening and cultivation, it is changed into the nature of oil. Oil becomes fuel for light, relief from weariness, rest from labor, brightness for the head, and a help in contests for those who compete by the rules. It is plain how the palm makes its fruit hard for thieves to reach, storing it up high rather than bearing it close to the ground. And it is plain what the grace of the vine means, and the fragrant cypress, and the sweetness of the myrtle. When all these are understood figuratively as speaking of virtue, it is plain to anyone who listens with understanding what each of them points to. So whoever has become a flourishing, well-planted garden of such trees, and is secured on every side by the fence of the commandments, gives the thief and the wild beasts no way in against him. For whoever is enclosed all around by the hedge of the commandments cannot be reached by the solitary wild beast, and the boar from the forest does not ravage him. If anyone, then, is a garden, and a secured one, he becomes the sister and bride of the one who says to such a soul: "A garden locked, my sister"

But this garden also needs a fountain, so that the grove may stay flourishing, constantly enriched by water. That is why, in his praises, he joined the fountain to the garden, saying: "A garden locked, a fountain sealed." Proverbs teaches us the meaning of the fountain in a riddle, where it says: "Let the fountain of water be sweet to you, and let it be yours alone, and let no stranger share it with you." There it forbids the fountain's water to be spent on strangers. In the same way, here it testifies that the fountain is never poured out to strangers, by calling it "sealed," which amounts to saying "guarded." What is meant is this. In my view, the fountain properly stands for the thinking power of our soul, which gushes and wells up with thoughts of every kind within us. But the movement of the mind becomes truly ours when it moves toward what benefits us and gives us every help in acquiring good things. When someone turns the activity of his thoughts toward devising evil, then the stream is spent on strangers. The thorny life thrives, watered by its alliance with wicked thoughts, while the better planting dries up and withers, receiving nothing from good

…the moisture of [?] thoughts nourishing the root. Since, then, a seal makes whatever it guards inviolable, frightening the thief with its mark, and whatever is not stolen stays intact for its master, the praise here seems to testify to the bride's supreme virtue: her mind remains untouched by her enemies, guarded in purity and freedom from passion. Purity seals this fountain for its own Master, and no [?] of thoughts muddies the clear, airy brightness of the heart. To bring out the meaning more clearly, it is this. Of the things within us, some are truly ours, namely whatever belongs properly to the soul. Others we claim as ours, by which I mean what concerns the body and external things, because some mistaken assumption leads us to think that what is foreign to us is our own. For what does the immaterial nature of the soul have in common with the grossness of matter? For this reason the word of Proverbs advises us not to spend the fountain of our mind on what is foreign to us, that is, on what concerns the body and external things. Instead we should busy ourselves with our own garden and enrich God's planting. We have learned that God's planting is the virtues. When the thinking power of our soul is occupied with them and flows away toward nothing external, it is sealed with the stamp of truth and takes its form from its relation to the good. But let us also look at the meaning of the praises that follow. "What you send forth," it says, "is a paradise of pomegranates with the fruit of orchard trees, henna with spikenard; spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes with all the chief perfumes; a fountain of gardens, a well of living water, rushing down from Lebanon." The plain wording alone makes it clear that some immense and extraordinary meaning lies in these words. Through them the beauty of the one exalted according to God becomes a thing of wonder, as she is extolled with every kind of extravagant praise. But the true sense these words point to could be clearly known only by someone who, like the holy Paul, knows how to speak the divine mysteries in the Spirit. For how is what the bride sends forth a paradise of pomegranates? How does the fruit of orchard trees come from pomegranates? And how do orchard fruits turn into a list of perfumes and spices? For among the fruits of the orchard trees we find henna and spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, and every tree of frankincense, so that no variety of frankincense fragrance is missing from the list. Myrrh and aloes and all the chief perfumes are added to these. And the one who was called a garden above, by the one who praises her, is now called a fountain of gardens and a well of living water rushing down from Lebanon. As I said before, the true account of these things would be seen by those who are able to search out the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God. As for us, so that we may not be left entirely without a taste or enjoyment of the good things set before us in this passage,

we will offer a few words of our own on the text, taking God the Word himself as the guide of our effort. The whole list of praises, both those spoken earlier and those the text has now set before us about her, seems not to aim mainly at mere commendation. Rather, through what is said, it seems to give power for the heart's ascent to greater and higher things. For example, she is called sister and bride of the Word, and each of these names joins the soul to the Bridegroom. The meaning of "bride" makes her one body with the incorruptible Bridegroom, as Paul says, while her eagerness to do his will brings her into a sister's kinship, as the Gospel says. Next her breasts are praised for pouring out wine instead of milk, and clearly the praise becomes a reality, for no one praises what does not exist. Besides this, her perfume is judged superior to all spices. It would not have been judged so unless she had truly run up to that height by progressing in what is better. After this the honeycombs of the word dripping from her mouth are admired, along with the mixed provision of wisdom that lies under her tongue, milk mixed with honey. These things too are power, not mere words. For the Word led her by the hand toward the ascent to higher things, and she grew so much that she made her mouth a fountain of honey and her tongue a storehouse of mixed wisdom, in which the land of promise flowing with milk and honey can be seen. Having raised her so high through these ascents, the Word leads her higher still. He says that her garment smells sweetly with the scent of frankincense, and by this the Word testifies that she has put on Christ. For the goal of every virtuous life is participation in God, and frankincense signifies the divine. Even here the soul did not stop, since the Word always leads her by the hand toward what is higher. After she has been made like the fragrance of frankincense, she becomes a garden in the likeness of paradise. She is not a garden like the one the first human beings had, open and unguarded, but one walled in on every side by the remembrance of the commandment…

Do you see how much power she has gained for rising upward? Now see the ascent beyond this. She did not only become an enclosed garden bearing sweet fruit for food. She also becomes drink for the thirsty, changed into the nature of a fountain, and a sealed fountain at that. Nor did she stop even there. She reached such a degree of growth toward what is greater that a paradise springs up from her mouth. For someone who pays closer attention to the meaning of the Hebrew says, in place of "What you send forth," "What you send forth from your mouth is a paradise of pomegranates." This means that the word sent forth from your mouth is a paradise of pomegranates. The pomegranates produce a whole harvest of orchard fruits, and the orchard fruits are henna

with spikenard, and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, every kind of frankincense, myrrh, aloes, and the chief perfumes. According to the blessing in the Psalm, help came to her from God, and she set these fair ascents in her heart, going always from strength to strength. Since this is so, the things sent forth from her mouth, now that she is in a more perfect state, are rightly called a paradise of pomegranates. The phrase "sending forth" also fits the underlying thought well. What is sent passes from the sender to the one who receives it. This can be learned from the ordinary use of the word, and so the Gospel says that the Word called the disciples who were sent out to preach the truth "apostles," that is, "ones sent forth." What, then, does the bride's mouth send forth? Clearly the word of faith. When it comes to be in those who receive it, it is planted in their hearts through hearing and becomes a paradise. Ordinary usage calls a grove thickly planted and shaded with trees a paradise. So that we may also learn what kind of plants the Word cultivates in the souls of believers, the text names pomegranates as the trees grown by the Word sent forth from the bride's mouth. The pomegranate is hard for a thief to get at, because it puts out thorny branches. It encloses and nourishes its fruit inside a covering that is harsh and bitter to the taste. In its own season, when the fruit has ripened, the rind bursts and the fruit shows itself from within. It is pleasant to look at and neatly arranged, honey-sweet and agreeable to the taste, and it sweetens the palate with its winelike juice. That, it seems to me, is why the word sent forth from the bride's mouth produces a paradise of pomegranates in the souls of the hearers. These words teach us not to grow soft in this present life through slackness and luxury, but to choose a life hardened by self-control. In this way the fruit of virtue becomes inaccessible to thieves. It is fenced in by the astringent covering of self-control, and through a grave and unsmiling bearing it pricks those who approach with evil intent, as if with the points of thorns. But when the season gives the signal to enjoy the fruits, the pomegranate becomes a full harvest of delight, yielding every kind of orchard fruit. The enjoyment it offers is not in sloes or acorns or the like. Instead, a varied and manifold nature of spices is found among the orchard fruits. Henna with spikenard makes a fair pairing, the one warm and the other fragrant. Warmth is not praiseworthy in itself when the heat is a foul-smelling burning. The purity of the warmth must be attested by its fragrance, so that the person who has been cleansed of unpleasant heat may become fervent in the Spirit. Among these orchard fruits one can also find the other spices: "spikenard," it says, "and saffron." We learned about the fragrance of spikenard in the earlier discourses,

so it remains to explain the riddle of the saffron. Those who have studied the properties of this flower say that it holds a middle place between cold and heat and avoids excess in either direction. Perhaps, then, the text uses this riddle to teach us philosophically about virtue. For every virtue is a mean between vices, between falling short of the good and overshooting it. For instance, they say that courage is seen to lie between cowardice and rashness, and generosity between stinginess and extravagance. Cowardice and stinginess, they say, become vices by falling short of what is fitting, while extravagance and rashness do so by excess and overshooting. The mean between the excesses on either side is what they call virtue. So the account of saffron, with the middle character of its properties, might well apply to virtue, expressing the virtuous state that neither falls short nor goes too far. But I would say, though my explanation is rather homely, that the riddle of the saffron is perhaps more properly taken to refer to the doctrine of faith. The flower is nourished inside a threefold calyx, and the calyx itself, with its airy colour, is a flower. When the covering of the calyces is opened, three flowers hidden inside them are always found, fragrant and useful for healing. They are alike in size, beauty, fragrance and the particular quality of their power, and the three are shown to be one in every respect: in colour, as has been said, in fragrance, and in the quality of their power. Alongside them grow three others, yellow to look at but of no value for any healthful use. Here the inexperienced go astray. Fooled by the fine colour, they pick the counterfeit instead of the better. This is just what those who err in matters of faith do now, choosing clever deceptions over sound doctrines. Let the hearer judge between the two interpretations and choose either one or both. For in a sense both are one: the possession of perfect virtue and the possession of the Godhead. Virtue does not lie outside the Godhead. But let us move on to consider the remaining spices, which the text mentions in order. "Calamus," it says, "and cinnamon, and" [?]

[?] to have the nature of living things, and they tell other such stories about it which seem too much for their hearers to believe. They say that if it is placed in the mouth of someone asleep, the sleeper is not prevented from answering those who question him. He stays asleep, yet gives sober and clearly spoken answers to the point. For someone who has not learned the truth of these reports by experience, it would be rash and thoughtless to affirm that they are so. Nevertheless, this spice too has been counted in the list of orchard fruits for some mystical reason. Pomegranates do not really grow here, for the bride's mouth does not put forth paradises that can be seen with the senses. Rather, the spice is listed so that it may become a symbol of some idea that adds to the bride's praise. So I do not think it right to pass over the tales told about cinnamon, either those just related or any others that those who describe it see fit to tell. For what is said may add something to the praise of virtue, if each of the reports is fittingly taken over to show the perfection of the virtuous life. Among educated and reasonable people, one may find this cinnamon in the soul when someone seething with desire or blazing with anger quenches the passions by reason. Or again, someone in the sleep of this life may hold in his mouth this sober cinnamon of reason. Like the sleepless and wakeful angels, he displays an unerring and unconfused understanding of what is said, imitating through the truthfulness of his speech the sleepless nature of the angels, whom no force of illusion can move from the truth. Such a person might be said to pour forth cinnamon from his mouth. By it the burning of desire and the seething of anger around the heart are quenched, and his speech is pure of all the dreamlike illusion and confusion of this life. Let no one look at how implausible the stories about cinnamon are and then slander the text for praising the bride with things that are untrue. Holy Scripture often knows how to borrow certain myths from outside to serve its own purpose. It does not hesitate to mention names from mythical stories to show more clearly the meaning it intends. Take the daughters of Job. The text, greatly admiring their beauty, showed through their names how extraordinarily wonderful they were. It said that one was called Day, another Cassia, and the third Amalthea's Horn. Everyone knows that the tale about Amalthea was invented by a Greek myth. They tell how she was a goat who became the nurse of that Cretan, and the myth has every kind of fruit pouring out of the hollow of one of her horns after it broke off. Did Holy Scripture, then, believe the tales told about Amalthea?

Not at all. Rather, by this name it testifies to the abundant fruitfulness of Job's daughter in the goods of virtue. A reasonable listener to Scripture is meant to grasp the aim of the praise from the name alone and dismiss the mythical marvels. In the same way, when we heard "Cassia" and "Day," the names did not teach us about the aromatic substance or about the sun's course above the earth. Instead, we say that the names contain an indication of their virtuous way of life. Cassia indicates the purer and fragrant quality of their pursuits, and Day indicates their good conduct, since the Apostle says that those who live purely are called children of light and sons of the day. In the same way here, what is said about cinnamon, taken by figurative interpretation as material for praise, does contribute to the praises of the bride. Someone who has become such a person, and has reached through his life this height of praise, displays in himself the features of the divine image in every respect. This is what the one who said "with all the trees of frankincense" indicates. For those who have observed such things say that the tree from which frankincense flows is not of a single kind. There is variety among the trees, and the character of the fragrance changes with the kind of tree. So whoever marks himself with godlikeness in all the pursuits of life displays in himself the beauty of all the frankincense trees, by which the divine form is expressed. But no one becomes a sharer in God's glory without first being conformed to the likeness of his death. For this reason the praise also says, in the list of spices, that the orchard fruits of the pomegranates include the other spices the text has listed, and with them myrrh and aloes and the chief perfumes. The first of these, myrrh and aloes, show a share in his burial. As the lofty Gospel says, with these the burial was prepared for the one who tasted death for us. By the chief perfumes the text indicates what is pure and unmixed with any trickery of dishonest dealers. In the same way Amos reproaches those who live in luxury with such things: "Those who drink strained wine and anoint themselves with the chief perfumes." Before that he says, "Those who eat kids from the flock and suckling calves from the midst of the herds, and who clap to the sound of instruments." In such things the wine is not muddied by dregs, and no admixture spoils the perfume's pure fragrance. But there, one must surely suppose, the prophecy reproaches the Israelites. They were filled with the undiluted word of Scripture, strained of all dregs, and had the unadulterated fragrance of perfumes, and they feasted fully at the spiritual banquet. Yet they gained nothing from such luxury, because their evil will turned even the clear wine into a muddy mess

and corrupted the purity of the chief perfumes by mixing in wicked thoughts. Here, however, the text testifies through the fruit of the chief perfumes that the bride's doctrines are pure and unadulterated. Even here neither of them stopped: not the bride, who strains forward to higher things, nor the Word, who helps her ascend. The bride whose sendings forth from her mouth are paradises of pomegranates and spices now becomes a fountain, watering the paradises that have sprung up from her. It is not as we have learned in the case of Paul and Apollos, where one plants and another waters. She does both, producing the paradises and watering them at the same time. Or perhaps the praise contains an even loftier meaning. It says she is a fountain not of some stream that pours out, but of gardens. What springs and gushes from her is not outflows of water but the gardens themselves. In this way the divine Apostle made living gardens spring up wherever he went, producing the paradise of the Church through his teaching. Then the Word leads the bride to the very summit through his praises, calling her a well of living water rushing down from Lebanon. Consider what we have learned about the life-giving nature from Holy Scripture. At one point the prophecy says in the person of God, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water." Again, the Lord says to the Samaritan woman, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water." And again: "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from within him. This he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive." Since the divine nature is understood everywhere by living water, here the truthful testimony of the Word declares that the bride is a well of water whose stream comes from Lebanon. This is the most astonishing thing of all. All other wells hold water that stands still, but the bride alone has water flowing through her, so that she has both the depth of a well and the ceaseless motion of a river. Who could do justice to the wonders shown by the likeness now coming to be in her? Perhaps there is nowhere further for her to go beyond herself, since she has been made like the archetypal beauty in every respect. She has imitated it exactly, fountain with fountain, life with life, water with water. The Word of God is living, and the soul that has received the Word lives too. That water flows from God, as the Fountain himself says: "I came forth from God and am here." She holds what flows into the well of the soul, and so she becomes a storehouse of that living water which flows, or rather rushes, as the text puts it, from Lebanon. May we too come to share in it by acquiring that well, so that, as Wisdom instructs, we may drink our own water and not another's, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

"Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind, and blow through my garden, and let my spices flow. Let my kinsman come down into his garden and eat the fruit of his fruit trees. I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices. I have eaten my bread with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, my neighbors, and drink, and be drunk, brothers. I sleep, and my heart keeps watch." The contemplation of the divine sayings now set before us from the sequence of the Song of Songs holds thoughts that are hard to reach and veiled in obscurity among hidden things. So it calls for greater attention on our part, or rather for more help from your prayers and for the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Otherwise our amazement at these lofty wonders may leave us as we usually are with the stars. We admire their beauty from afar, but we can devise no means of knowing what they are made of; our enjoyment of them through their beauty lies only in marveling at what we see. The gleams and flashes of these divine oracles are simply stars of this kind, shining beyond the eyes of the soul and lying above them, "as high as heaven is above the earth," as the Prophet says. But suppose what we hear of Elijah were to happen to our soul as well, and our mind were taken up in the fiery chariot and carried aloft to the heavenly beauties. (We shall understand the fire to be the Holy Spirit, which the Lord came to cast upon the earth and which was divided among the disciples in the form of tongues.) Then it will not be beyond hope for us to draw near to these stars, by which I mean the divine thoughts that flash around our souls through the heavenly and spiritual oracles. For I say to you, the hearer, in the words the Lord spoke to the patriarch: look up with the eye of the soul; look up into this heaven and see the stars, and see whether you can measure the height of its thoughts. See the authority of the queen, and recognize her power from her commands, for a kind of imperial sovereignty shows itself in what she says. She does not achieve what she wishes by prayer. She achieves it according to the unerring voice of him who promised, who says that the faithful and wise steward becomes lord of all the Master's possessions. Laying hold of this authority, she royally disposes the two winds as she pleases. The north wind she banishes from herself by command; the south wind she calls kindly and urges to come to her. The text runs thus: "Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind." Perhaps something akin to these words can be found in the words of the centurion, which God the Word himself

marveled at, as the Evangelist related: "When Jesus heard it, he marveled." And he ranked the centurion's words above the faith of Israel. It seems to me that the comparison with the centurion in the matter of faith is made not with the people of Israel but with Israel himself. In his wrestling with the adversary, Israel barely escaped a fall even with God as his ally, and he did not get entirely clear of the adversary's harm, for he received the injury in his thigh. But this centurion of whom we are now speaking, with a kind of royal power, dismisses by his authority what is alien and takes to himself what he desires. It seems to me that the man won admiration above all for this: he says that among the soldiers under his command he sends away whomever he wishes with sovereign authority, summons the one he wants, and assigns the servant his proper service. There is a kind of philosophy in the centurion's words here as well. The one he has once sent away he no longer brings back to himself; when that one has departed, he brings in another in his place. For after saying, "Go," and he goes, he says he calls another, not the one he dismissed. The text, I think, teaches this doctrine: things opposed to one another by nature cannot dwell together in the same place. "For what fellowship has light with darkness?" says the Apostle. When darkness withdraws, it is entirely necessary that light should be what is seen in its place, and when evil is removed, virtue is brought in instead. Once this has been accomplished, the mind of the flesh no longer rises up against the spirit. Indeed it cannot, since its power to resist has been put to death. Instead it becomes fit for every proper service, obedient and subject to the dominion of the spirit. For the soldier allied with evil may be driven out, and in his place the hoplite of virtue may enter, clad in the breastplate of righteousness, bearing the sword of the Spirit in his hand, holding before him the protective armor, the helmet of salvation and the shield of faith, and wearing the whole spiritual armor. When that happens, the slave, which is the body, fears its own lord and readily receives the commands of its ruler, and through these virtue is accomplished by the body's service. This is what the centurion's word shows when he says, "And to my servant I say, Do this, and

But let us hear the queen, and how she drives the north wind away from herself and turns its blast back the other way. She does not order it to be still, as the Lord on the surging sea commanded the storm to be quiet and enjoined silence on the waves. Rather, she bids it withdraw and flee, so that the south wind may flow unhindered, with no contrary wind blocking its course. "Awake," she says

to the north wind. What is the reason for removing this wind? On this point the word of Proverbs says, "The north wind is a harsh wind, but by name it is called 'on the right.'" Yet the north wind is on the right of no one except a person who has the east at his back and is making his way toward the west. You surely grasp the riddle in these words.
