A person who has turned away from the East (for so Christ is named by the prophecy) and drives himself toward the setting of the light, where the power of darkness is, has the north wind on his right. It greets him with right-hand welcome and wicked provisions for the road, and by these he makes his way toward the darkness. In this way the licentious man finds the north wind on his right, blowing along with him toward the passion of dishonor. In this way this spirit of wickedness becomes favorable to the greedy man, when it heaps up the stuff of greed around him like sand or dust. In this way, by lending its help to every kind of sin, it becomes "on the right" to those it attaches itself to. It is harsh by nature, but it hides its harshness beneath pleasures. For this reason the soul that has taken up power against the passions banishes the north wind from her own realm, saying, "Awake, O north wind." Anyone who has observed the nature of visible things will see clearly that the opposing power is signified by this name. Who does not know the motion of the sun, how it makes its course from the east through the south and then declines toward the west? The earth is spherical in shape, as those who have studied such matters say. So whatever part of it is illuminated by the sun, the opposite part is necessarily darkened, shaded by the interposition of what lies between. That region therefore remains forever without light and frozen, neither lit nor warmed by the sun's rays. For this reason the Word calls the ruler of the power of darkness both "north wind" and "harsh." He turns the soft nature of souls to stone by freezing them like water and makes them hard. He is the worker of winter's gloom, and I mean that winter in which, the Gospel says, flight from danger is impossible, for in it the season of those who flower in virtue withers away. Rightly, then, the queen's voice drives him away with authority. She calls instead the southern wind, warm and ever-bright, which she names the south wind and through which the torrent of delight flows, saying, "And come, O south wind, blow through my garden, and let my spices flow." By its violent blast, like the one we have heard came upon the disciples in the upper room, it was to fall upon the living plants and stir God's planting to bear spices. It was to make the fragrant prophecy flow from the mouth, together with the saving doctrines of the faith, pouring out the fragrance of the teachings unhindered in every kind of tongue. So the hundred and twenty disciples, planted in the house of God, at the breath of such a south wind put forth the teaching given through tongues

as their blossom. That is why the bride says to such a south wind, "Blow through my garden." She has [?] become a garden through the voice of the bridegroom who made her, as the passage about the garden and the fountain relates. For this reason she wishes her garden, the Church, which teems with living trees, to be blown through, so that spices may flow from them. The Prophet says, "He will blow with his wind, and waters will flow." But the bride, adorned with royal wealth, changes the streams into something more magnificent, making rivers of spices flow out from the trees of the garden through the force of the wind. From this we may learn the difference between the Old Covenant and the New: the prophetic river was filled with water, but the gospel river with spices. Such a river of spices, flowing from the garden of the Church through the Spirit, was the great Paul, whose stream was the fragrance of Christ. Such also were John, Luke, Matthew, Mark and all the others, the noble plants of the bride's garden. Blown upon by that bright southern wind, they became springs of spices, gushing with the fragrance of the Gospels. "Let my kinsman come down," she says, "into his garden, and eat the fruit of his fruit trees." O bold voice! O generous and bountiful soul, outdoing every extreme of magnanimity! Whom does she welcome to a feast of her own fruits? For whom does she prepare a banquet from her own good things? Whom does she invite to dine on what has been made ready? She invites him from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things. He gives food to all in due season; he opens his hand and fills every living thing with his good pleasure. He is the bread that comes down from heaven and gives life to the world, and he pours life from his own spring upon all that exist. For him the bride sets a table. The table is the garden, planted with living trees. And we are the trees, if indeed we too set before him the salvation of our souls as food. For the one who feasts on our life has said, "My food is to do the will of my Father." The aim of the divine will is clear: he wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. This, then, is the food prepared for him: that we be saved. Our free choice becomes the fruit. Through it, as through a branch, the soul is handed over to God, who gathers us. We should notice here that first the bride is sweetened by the fruit of the apple tree, when she says, "And his fruit was sweet in my mouth." Only then does she herself become fruit, ripe and sweet, set before the husbandman for his delight. The words "Let him come down" have the force of a prayer. They are expressed in the same way as "Hallowed be your name" and "Your will be done." For just as there the form of those phrases carries the sense of a prayer,

so here too "Let him come down" is the prayer of the bride as she shows God how richly the fruit trees of virtue are bearing. The descent signifies the work of his love for humanity. There is no other way to be taken up to the Most High unless the Lord, who lifts up the meek, bends down toward what is lower. For this reason the soul that is rising upward calls on the guiding hand of the one above and prays that he come down from his own greatness, so that he may be within reach of those below. He who said through the prophet, "While you are still speaking, behold, I am here," did not wait for the bride to finish her prayer. He heard what she asked, heeded the readiness of her heart, and was in the garden that the south wind had blown through. He gathered the fruits of the spices, ate his fill of the fruit trees of virtue, and gave an account of the feast, speaking thus to the bride: "I came down into the garden, my sister, my bride. I gathered my myrrh with my spices. I ate my bread with my honey. I drank my wine with my milk. Eat, my neighbors, and drink, and be drunk, my brothers." Do you see how far his generosity exceeds the request? The bride prayed that her plants in the garden, blown through by the south wind from the midday quarter, might become springs of spices and might welcome the husbandman with the fruit of the fruit trees. Everyone knows that every fragrance is a pleasure to the sense of smell, and that fruits, as food, are weaker than the power of bread for keeping those who eat them in good health. But he came down into his own garden and changed the nature of the fruits into something greater and more precious. From the garden he gathers myrrh, finding it together with his spices, for the prophetic word has sung that whatever good there is, wherever it is found, comes from him. In place of fruits he makes the trees teem with bread, mingled with his honey. And let the prophetic word be voiced along with this too: the honey is his, as is everything else. He draws wine from them as well, mixed with his milk. For from him and through him and to him are the [?] of those blessed gardens, whose plants [?] teem with such fruits that they are fittingly transformed into every kind of food, according to the desire of the one who enjoys them. To one who delights in fragrance it becomes myrrh, through the putting to death of the earthly members, preparing like a perfumer the pure and fragrant life that is blended from the many and various spices of virtue. To one who seeks more perfect food it becomes bread. This bread is no longer eaten with bitter herbs, as the law commands, for the bitter herb belongs to the present life. Instead it takes honey as its relish, when in its own time the fruit of virtue sweetens the senses of the soul. The proof of this is the bread that appeared to the disciples after the Lord's resurrection, sweetened with the comb of

honey. To one who thirsts it becomes a bowl full of wine and milk. It is not a sponge soaked in gall and vinegar, such as the Jews held out on the reed to their benefactor when they showed him their "friendship cup." We are surely not unaware of the riddles in these words. Paul was a myrrh-bearing tree: he died daily, passed the sentence of death on himself, and gave off the scent of spices through purity and freedom from passion, becoming a fragrance of life to those being saved. The living plants of the garden make bread for the master of the garden, as he who sits on the throne testifies: "I was hungry, and you gave me food." For doing good is the bread of gladness, sweetened with the honey of the commandment. And again, the fruitful plants of the garden pour wine for the bridegroom, who says to them, "I was thirsty, and you gave me drink." They mix the wine with milk, not with water as innkeepers usually do. Milk is the first food of human nature, pure and simple, truly childlike and guileless, and free of every cause of evil. Having said these things to the bride, the Word sets the mysteries of the Gospel before his neighbors, saying, "Eat, my neighbors, and drink, and be drunk, my brothers." Anyone who knows the mystical words of the Gospel will see no difference between these sayings and the initiation given to the disciples there. For both here and there the Word says, "Eat and drink." Many might think that the encouragement to drunkenness which the Word gives his brothers here goes somewhat beyond the Gospel. But anyone who examines it carefully will find that this too agrees with the gospel. What he urged on his friends here in words, he did there in deeds. For all drunkenness tends to produce ecstasy in a mind overcome by wine. So what he urges here happened then through that divine eating and drinking, and it always happens, since a change and ecstasy from the worse to the better enters together with the eating and drinking. In this way, as the prophecy says, those who drink the richness of God's house and are given drink from the torrent of delight become drunk. So the great David was once drunk, when he went out of himself, came into ecstasy, and saw the invisible beauty. He cried out that famous saying, "Every man is a liar," meaning anyone who entrusts the interpretation of the ineffable treasures to words. So too Paul, the younger Benjamin, was drunk when he was in ecstasy and said, "For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God" (for his ecstasy was directed toward God himself), "if we are in our right mind, it is for you." He showed this in his words to Festus, that he was not mad but was speaking words of soberness and righteousness. I know also that blessed Peter, in this kind of drunkenness,

was hungry and drunk at the same time. Before he had taken any bodily food, when he became hungry and wanted to eat and his people were preparing the table for him, the divine and sober drunkenness came upon him. Through it he went out of himself and beheld the gospel sheet, let down from above by four corners. It held every race of humanity in countless forms, as birds, four-footed beasts, creeping things and wild animals, shaped according to the differences in what they worshiped. The Word commands Peter to sacrifice their bestial and irrational form, so that once they have been purified, what remains may become fit to eat. At that point the word of true religion is also handed over unveiled. The divine voice did not say only once, "What God has cleansed is not common." This proclamation was made three times. By the first voice we learn that the Father is God who cleanses. By the second, likewise, we learn that the only-begotten Son is God who cleanses. By the third, similarly, we learn that the God who cleanses everything unclean is the Holy Spirit. Such, then, is the drunkenness that comes from the wine the Lord sets before his fellow drinkers, through which the soul is carried out of itself toward diviner things. Rightly, therefore, the Lord addresses his invitation to those who have come near through the virtues and not to those who stand far off: "Eat, my neighbors, and drink, and be drunk." For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself. And rightly he called those who are worthy of this food brothers. For whoever does his will is named by the Word brother and sister and mother.

Sleep follows drunkenness in natural sequence, so that through digestion the food's strength may be distributed to the banqueters for their good health. For this reason, after that lavish banquet, the bride falls asleep. But this is a strange sleep, foreign to what nature is used to. In ordinary sleep the sleeper is not awake and the one who is awake does not sleep. Sleep and waking each end in the other, giving way to each other in turn. Here, however, a new and paradoxical mixture and union of opposites is seen in her. "For I sleep," she says, "and my heart keeps watch." How, then, should we understand these words? Sleep is a likeness of death. In sleep all the sensory activity of the body is suspended: neither sight, nor hearing, nor smell, nor taste, nor touch performs its own work while sleep lasts. It also relaxes the tension of the body. It makes a person forget his cares, lulls fear, calms anger, and eases the tension of those who are embittered. As long as it holds sway over the body, it makes a person insensible to all ills. From what has been said, then, we learn that she who boasts of these things and says, "I sleep, and my heart keeps watch," has risen higher than herself. For truly, in those in whom the mind alone lives by itself,

…undisturbed by any of the sense organs, as if the nature of the body were paralysed by a kind of sleep and torpor. One can truly say that sight sleeps from inactivity, since those spectacles that usually amaze childish eyes are held in no esteem. I do not mean only the things that belong to earthy matter, such as gold and silver and those stones which stir greed in the eyes by some fine colour, but also the wonders that appear in the heavens: the rays of the stars, the disc of the sun, the many shapes of the moon, and whatever else brings pleasure to the eyes. None of these stays forever; all of them shift and revolve with the passing of time. When all such things are disregarded for the sake of contemplating the true goods, the bodily eye is paralysed. The more perfect soul is not drawn down to anything the eye points out to it, because with the mind it sees only what lies beyond visible things. In the same way hearing becomes dead and inactive, since the soul is occupied with things beyond speech. As for the more bestial senses, it is not even worth saying that they are cast far from the soul like the stench of a corpse: smell, which tracks down odours; taste, which sits in attendance on the service of the belly; and touch as well, that slavish and blind sense, which nature perhaps made only for the blind. When all these are held fast by inactivity as if in a kind of sleep, the activity of the heart is pure, and reason looks upward, unclouded and untouched by the din of sense-motion. For pleasure in human nature is twofold: one kind is worked in the soul through freedom from passion, the other in the body through passion. Whichever of the two our free choice prefers gains mastery over the other. So if someone looks to sense and draws to himself the pleasure that sense implants in the body, he will live out his life without tasting divine joy, because it is somehow natural for the better to be overshadowed by the worse. But for those whose desire inclines toward the Divine, the good remains unovershadowed, and everything that bewitches the senses is thought something to be fled. That is why the soul, when it delights only in the contemplation of true Being, is awake to none of the things that sense works for pleasure. Instead, having put every bodily movement to sleep, it receives the manifestation of God with a naked and pure mind through divine wakefulness. May we too be made worthy of it, attaining the soul's wakefulness through the sleep we have described, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.
The voice of my beloved knocks at the door: “Open to me, my sister, my close one, my dove, my perfect one; for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the
night.” “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly was stirred [?] for

This too is one of the Lord's great commandments, by which the mind of those who are disciples of the Word shakes off from itself, like dust, everything material in nature and is lifted up to desire the things above. The commandment is this: those who look to the life above must be stronger than sleep and stay awake in mind at all times, driving drowsiness from their eyes as a deceiver of souls and a plotter against the truth. I mean the drowsiness and sleep that fashion these dreamlike phantoms for those sunk deep in the deceit of life: offices, riches, powers, pride, the bewitchment of pleasures, the love of glory, of enjoyment and of honour, and everything in this life that the unreflecting pursue in vain because of some fantasy. These things flow past with the passing nature of time, and their being lies only in seeming. They are not what they are thought to be, nor do they last forever even in being thought so. They seem to come into being and perish at the same moment, like the waves that crest on the water. For a moment the movement of the winds swells them up, but their bulk has no stability or permanence. Having risen with a brief gust of wind, they subside along with the wind and leave the surface of the sea smooth again. So that our mind may be free of such phantoms, he bids us shake this heavy sleep from the eyes of the soul, so that we do not slip away from what subsists and truly is through our concern for what has no existence. For this reason he also suggests to us a way of staying awake, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands.” Light shining on the eyes drives sleep from them, and loins bound tight with a belt make the body unreceptive to sleep, since the feeling of discomfort does not allow the relaxation that sleep brings. What these riddles signify is entirely clear. One who is girded with self-control lives in the light of a pure conscience, and the lamp of confidence lights up his life. When the truth shines forth, the soul remains sleepless and undeceived, and is not made foolish by any of these futile dreams. If this is achieved according to the guidance of the Word, a kind of angelic life takes us over. For the divine command likens us to the angels when it says: “And be like people waiting for their master, when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks they may open to him at once.” For they are the ones who wait for the Lord's return from the wedding, keeping watch with wakeful eye at the heavenly

gates, so that the King of glory may enter through them again when he returns from the wedding to that blessedness above the heavens. As the psalm says, the bridegroom came forth as from his chamber and, through the mystical rebirth, betrothed us to himself as a virgin, though we had played the harlot with idols, and refashioned our nature into virginal incorruption. So when the wedding had been accomplished, and the Church had been espoused by the Word (as John says, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom”) and received into the bridal chamber of the mysteries, the angels awaited the King's return, as the Church was brought back to the blessedness that belongs to its nature. He said, then, that our life must also be made like theirs. They live far from evil and deceit and are ready to receive their Master when he comes. In the same way we too should keep vigil at the doorways of our dwellings and make ourselves ready to obey when he stands there and knocks at the door. “For blessed,” he says, “are those servants whom their master will find doing so when he comes.” Since it is blessed, then, to obey the one who knocks, the soul that always looks toward blessedness and keeps good watch over its own treasures perceives the one standing at the door and says: “The voice of my beloved knocks at the door.” How could anyone worthily grasp, from these words, the bride's ascent toward more divine things? She had banished that harsh north wind from herself with such authority and confidence, and drawn the luminous breeze to herself. She had produced an orchard of pomegranates through her mouth, whose fruits were spices. She had set her own garden as a table before the Master of creation, and none of the dishes offered was found worthy of rejection; all were declared good: the myrrh, the spice, the bread with honey, the wine with milk. The Word bore witness to her perfection when he said, “You are all fair, and there is no blemish in you.” Yet she is now disposed as though she were about to receive the manifestation of God for the first time. As though she had not yet received the Word who now stands before her doors or welcomed him into her house, she marvels at the power of his voice. That is why she says the bridegroom's voice touches not yet her, but her door. “For the voice of my beloved,” she says, “knocks at the door.” Do you see how boundless the course is for those who ascend to God, and how whatever is grasped becomes, every time, a beginning toward what lies beyond? For when did we expect, from what had been said to her, any halt in the course of her journey to the heights? What more could anyone seek after the testimony to her perfection? Yet we see her still within, not yet gone out of her doors, not yet delighting in the face-to-face manifestation, but still being led by hearing toward a share in good things. This, then, is the teaching we learn from what has

been said: to those who keep [?] advancing to greater things, the Apostle's saying applies: “If anyone thinks he knows, he does not yet know as he ought to know.” In the earlier stages the soul knew him as far as it had grasped him. But what has not yet been grasped is infinitely greater than what has been grasped. That is why the bridegroom has often appeared to the soul, and yet, as though he had never come into view, he promises the bride with his voice that he will be seen. To make the teaching clearer, I will add an image by way of illustration. Suppose someone came near that spring which, Scripture says, rose up from the earth in the beginning, so abundant that it watered the whole face of the earth. Whoever approached the spring would marvel at that limitless water, which is always gushing up and pouring forth. Yet he could not say he had seen all the water. How could he see what lies hidden in the bosom of the earth? So however long he stays beside the gushing source, he is always at the beginning of his contemplation of the water. For it never ceases flowing and is always beginning to gush. It is the same for anyone who looks to that divine and boundless beauty. Whatever he finds at each moment is seen to be altogether newer and more wonderful than what he had grasped before, so he marvels at whatever is being revealed, yet he never stops desiring to see, because what he expects is more magnificent and more divine than all he has seen. That is why here too the bride, always marvelling and astonished at what she knows, never lets her longing for contemplation come to rest in what she already knows. And so now too she perceives the Word still knocking at the door, rises to listen, and says, “The voice of my beloved knocks at the door.” Then, quieting her ears, she hears the Word who sounded through the voice, and his word is this: “Open to me, my sister, my close one, my dove, my perfect one; for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.” Its meaning might be grasped through contemplation as follows. God's manifestation to the great Moses began with light. After that he speaks to him through a cloud. Then, when Moses has become loftier and more perfect, he sees God in darkness. What we learn from this is the following. The first withdrawal from false and mistaken notions about God is a passage from darkness to light. Next comes a closer understanding of hidden things, which leads the soul by the hand through what appears toward the invisible nature. This becomes like a cloud, overshadowing all that appears while guiding the soul and accustoming it to look upon what is hidden. The soul that journeys upward by these steps leaves behind the things below, as far as human nature can attain. It comes within the sanctuary of the knowledge of God and is surrounded on all sides by the divine darkness. There, everything that appears and is

grasped is left outside, and only the invisible and incomprehensible remains for the soul to contemplate, and in that is God. As the text says of the lawgiver: “Moses entered the darkness where God was.” Having considered these things in this way, we should examine how the words before us are related to what has been said. There was a time when the bride was black, darkened by unenlightened doctrines. The sun had glared at her, the sun that through temptations scorches the rootless seed on the rocks. She had been defeated by those who fought within her and did not guard her own vineyard, and, not knowing herself, she shepherded flocks of goats instead of sheep. But when she cut herself off from her kinship with evil and longed to bring her mouth to the fountain of light through that mystical kiss, she became beautiful, bathed in the light of truth, and washed away the blackness of ignorance in the water. Then she is likened to a horse for her swift running, and to a dove for the swiftness of her mind. Running through everything that is grasped and appears like a horse, and flying through it like a dove, she first rests with longing in the shade of the apple tree, calling what overshadows her an apple tree instead of a cloud. But now she is enveloped by the divine night, in which the bridegroom draws near but does not appear. For how could what is unseen appear at night? He gives the soul a certain sense of his presence, but escapes clear comprehension, hidden in the invisibility of his nature. What, then, is the initiation that this night brings to the soul? The Word touches the door. By the door we understand the mind that reaches by conjecture toward things that cannot be spoken, through which what is sought is brought inside. Truth, then, stands outside our nature, since our knowledge is partial, as the Apostle says, and knocks at the door of the mind with hints and riddles, saying, “Open.” And with encouragement it suggests the way the door should be opened, as if holding out keys: these fine names by which what is shut is opened. For the meanings of these names are plainly keys that open what is hidden: sister, close one, dove, perfect one. “If you wish,” he says, “for the door to be opened to you and the gates of your soul to be lifted up, so that the King of glory may come in, you must become my sister by receiving my will into your soul.” For in the Gospel he says that whoever lives according to his will becomes his brother and sister. “You must also draw near to the truth and become close to it, so that nothing stands between us like a wall, and you must have the perfection that belongs to the nature of the dove, that is, lack nothing and be filled with all innocence and purity.” Take these names, then, O soul, as keys, and with them open the entrance to the truth, becoming sister, close one, dove and perfect one. And your

gain from receiving me and taking me into your house will be the dew from my head, of which I am full, and the drops of the night that flow from my locks. That the dew is healing we have learned clearly from the prophet, who says: “The dew that comes from you is healing to them.” The drops of the night belong with the meaning we have already contemplated. For one who has come within the sanctuary of what cannot be seen cannot meet with a downpour or a torrent of knowledge. He may be content if the truth sprinkles knowledge of itself in fine and faint thoughts, as the drop of the Word flows down through the saints and those inspired by God. For I think that the locks hanging from the head of the universe is a figurative name for the prophets, evangelists and apostles. Each of them drew as much as he could hold from the dark, hidden and invisible treasures, and for us they become rivers. Yet compared with the truth itself they are drops of dew, even though they overflow with the abundance and greatness of their teaching. Paul was such a river. The waves of his thoughts crested above the heavens, up to the third heaven, up to paradise, up to words that are unspeakable and cannot be uttered. Yet though his discourse spreads out like a sea in all this grandeur of speech, he shows again that this word of his is a drop of dew compared with the true Word, when he says: “We know in part and we prophesy in part,” and, “If anyone thinks he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know,” and, “I do not consider that I have yet grasped it.” If, then, the moisture of the dew and the drop from the locks seem like rivers and seas and waves when measured against our capacity, what must we think of the fountain that said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink”? Let each listener form some idea of the wonder by analogy with what has been said. For if the drop was enough to give rise to rivers, what can one reckon, by way of this drop, about the very [?] of God?

Let us see, too, how the bride obeys the Word and how she opens the entrance to the bridegroom. “I have taken off my tunic,” she says; “how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” She listened well to the one who bade her become sister and close one, dove and perfect one, so that through these the truth might dwell in the soul. For she did what she heard. She took off the tunic of skin that she had put on after the sin. She washed from her feet the earthiness in which she had become wrapped when she departed from the life of paradise to the earth and heard, “You are earth, and to earth you shall return.” That is why she opened the entrance into the soul for the Word: the veil of the heart, that is, the flesh, was drawn aside. By “flesh” I mean the old

self, which the divine Apostle bids those to take off and put away who are about to wash the filth from the feet of the soul in the bath of the word. So having taken off the old self and removed the veil from the heart, she opened the entrance to the Word. Once he has come in, the soul makes him her own garment, following the instruction of the Apostle, who bids anyone who has taken off the fleshly covering of the old self to put on the tunic created after God's likeness in holiness and righteousness. And he says that this garment is Jesus. The bride declares that she will not take up again the tunic she cast off, but will be content with the one tunic, according to the law given to the disciples, the tunic she put on when she was renewed by birth from above. In this she confirms the word of the Lord. He bids those who have once been adorned with the divine garment never again to put on the tunic of sin over it, nor to have two tunics, but only one, so that the same person may not wear two tunics that are incompatible with each other. For what fellowship does the dark garment have with the luminous and immaterial one? The law says not only that one should not have two tunics, but also that one should not sew new cloth onto an old garment. Otherwise the shame of the person wearing it becomes worse: the patch does not hold, and the old garment suffers a worse tear that is hard to mend. “For the new patch,” he says, “pulls away from the old, and a worse tear results,” so that what is shameful is exposed by it. That is why she says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” For who, seeing himself clothed in the Lord's tunic, bright as the sun, put on him through purity and incorruption, like the one the Lord showed at the transfiguration on the mountain, would then consent to put on the poor and ragged cloak which, as the proverb says, the drunkard and the fornicator wear? Nor, having washed her feet, does she let her steps take up the defilement of the earth again. “For I have washed my feet,” she says; “how shall I soil them?” Neither is Moses recorded as binding his feet in sandals again, after he had freed them at God's command from their dead covering of skins when he stepped onto the holy and illumined ground. When he skilfully made the priestly vestment after the pattern shown on the mountain, he blended in the weaving the radiance of gold and purple, fine linen, blue and scarlet, so that a beauty mingled from them all flashed out. Yet he devised no adornment for the feet. The adornment of the priestly foot was to be bare of all covering, and free. For the priest must stand entirely on holy ground, and it is not lawful to walk on it in dead skins. That is also why the Lord forbids sandals to his disciples, since he bids them not to go on the road of the Gentiles but to go forward by the holy road. And surely you are not unaware

[?] So, with her feet cleansed, she keeps herself on the royal road, turning aside neither to the right nor to the left, so that she will not set her footprint off the road on either side and soil her foot. You surely understand what these words point to: that through baptism the soul [?] the sandals. For it is the proper work of the one who baptizes [?] to loose the sandals, as John [?]. [?] sets his own feet upon the rock, as he says in the psalm: “He raised me up out of the pit of misery and out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and directed my steps.” By the rock we understand the Lord, who is light and truth and incorruption and righteousness. These are the paving stones of the spiritual road. Whoever does not turn aside from them to either side keeps his footprint safe, and the mud of pleasure soils it nowhere. These, at least in my account, are the means by which the bride opens the door to the Word. For the pledge never again to take up the mud once it has been cast off, and never to let earthly defilement into the journey of life, becomes the way in for sanctification into the soul that has been prepared in this way. And the Lord is sanctification. So the meaning of what was said has been confirmed. After this the soul reaches the still higher ascent. Now the voice is no longer knocking at the door of the heart. Instead the divine hand itself slips in through the opening to the inside. For “My beloved” [?]

[?] the footprint. So she heard his voice and obeys the command. She opens the door, having taken away the veil from her heart. She tore apart the curtain of the flesh at the door [?], and the whole gate of the soul was opened, so that the King of glory might come in. But the wide gate turned out to be a small opening, narrow and short, through which not the bridegroom himself but only his hand could barely pass. Through it the hand came inside and touched her who longed to see the bridegroom. From this she gained only enough to know that the hand belonged to the one she longed for. We may learn what doctrines are shown to us through the philosophy in these words if we spend a little longer on the discussion. The human soul stands on the border between two natures. One is incorporeal, intellectual and pure; the other is corporeal, material and irrational. As soon as the soul has been cleansed of its attachment to the gross, earthy life and through virtue looks up to what is akin to it and most divine, it never stops searching and inquiring after the first principle of all that exists. It asks what is the source of the beauty of existing things, where their power springs from, and what pours out the wisdom that shows itself in existence. It stirs up every line of reasoning and every power of inquiring thought, and labors to grasp what it seeks. Yet the limit it sets to its grasp of God is only his activity, which comes down to us and which we perceive through life. Consider the air that rises from the earth with water. It does not stay at the bottom of the pool. It becomes a bubble and runs upward to what is akin to it, and when it has passed through the topmost surface of the water and mingled with the air, then its upward motion stops. Something like this happens to the soul that searches out divine things. When it stretches itself from things below toward the knowledge of things above and grasps the wonders of his activity, it cannot go any further by curious inquiry. Instead it marvels at and reverences the one who is known only to exist, through what he does. It sees the beauty of heaven, the rays of the luminaries, the swift revolution of the pole, and the orderly and harmonious circuit of the stars. It sees the yearly cycle returning on itself through four seasons, and the earth attuned to what surrounds it, changing its own workings as the motion of the things above it changes. It sees the many kinds of living creatures: those that live in the waters, those whose lot is to move through the air, and those that live on land. It sees every kind of plant and the various grasses, differing from one another in quality, power and shape, and the properties of fruits and juices, and all the other things through which the activity of God is displayed. Seeing these, the soul marvels at what appears, and from this it reasons in its mind that the one who is perceived through his works exists. Perhaps in the age to come, when everything that is seen has passed away, as the Lord says, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away,” and we have passed over into that life,

which is beyond eye and ear and thought, then we will no longer know the nature of the good in part, through its works, as we do now. Nor will the transcendent be understood through the activity of what appears. Instead, the form of that inexpressible blessedness will surely be grasped in another way, and there will be another mode of enjoyment, one that by nature cannot now enter the heart of man. Meanwhile, for now, the limit of the soul's knowledge of the inexpressible is the activity displayed [?] in existing things, which the text has signified figuratively by calling it a hand. This, then, is the doctrine that these divine words set out for us philosophically. In them the pure soul no longer treads on earthly and material life, so that she will not soil her footprint by [?] things below. She had expected to receive the bridegroom himself, come wholly into the house, but for the present she was content to see only the hand through the opening. The hand stands for his active power. “My beloved,” she says, “put his hand through the opening,” for human power cannot take into itself the boundless and incomprehensible nature. “And my belly,” she says, “was stirred for him.” The word “stirring” signifies astonishment and amazement at the wonder that appeared. Her whole [?] faculty was moved to wonder at the things worked by the divine hand. Our understanding of these is beyond our reach, and that very fact shows how incomprehensible and uncontainable is the nature of the one who works them. For the whole creation of existing things is the work of that hand which has been revealed to us through the opening, as John says, and the prophet agrees with the Gospel. The one says, “All things were made through him.” The other calls the power that made all things a hand, saying, “My hand has made all these things.” Consider the works of that activity, all the others and the beauties of heaven as well. The inquiring human mind has not yet grasped what man is in his essence, or the sun, or any other of the wonders that appear in creation. This is why the heart is stirred at the divine activity: if it cannot grasp these things, how will it grasp the nature that is above them? Perhaps someone may take the riddles in these words in a different way and still not stray from what is likely. For I think the bride's house can be understood as the whole of human life. This hand, the maker of all things, came to dwell in the brief and worthless life of human beings and contracted itself by sharing our nature in every respect, in likeness, without sin. And coming among us it caused stirring and amazement in souls: How is God manifested in the flesh? How does the Word become flesh?

How can there be childbirth in virginity? How is light mingled with darkness, and life blended with death? How can the narrow opening of life take into itself the hand that holds all existing things, the hand by which the whole heaven is measured and all the earth and all the water are contained? It is likely, then, that the bride is prophetically indicating to us the grace of the Gospel through the riddle of the hand. For when the Lord was seen on earth and lived among men, we came to know the bridegroom's pure and [?] beauty, the divinity of the Word, and the radiance of the true light through the hand of his works. By the hand we understand his miracle-working power, by which the dead were brought to life, the sight of the blind was restored, the disease of leprosy was driven out, and every kind of incurable and grievous illness left people's bodies at his command. So two interpretations of the hand have been set before us. The first holds that the divine nature is wholly incomprehensible and beyond comparison, and is known only through its activity. The second says that the bride is proclaiming the grace of the Gospel in advance through these words. We leave it to the hearer to choose whichever is more fitting and better suited to the subject. In any case, whichever is judged more profitable for the soul, either one gives us enough guidance toward the good. From the first we learn that what can be known of God, in Paul's words, is understood and clearly seen from the creation of the world. So we will refrain from curious meddling with things beyond comprehension, so that heresy does not gain material against the truth from speculation about the unattainable and unutterable nature. If instead we take the riddle of the hand as pointing to the Gospel, then our faith in the mystical doctrines will become firmer in this way too, gaining certainty from the advance proclamation of those doctrines, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory forever.

“I rose to open to my beloved. My hands dripped myrrh, my fingers were full of myrrh, on the handle of the bolt. I opened to my beloved; my beloved had passed by. My soul went out at his word. I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me. The watchmen who go about in the city found me; they struck me, they wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took my veil from me.” People set out on a voyage overseas in the hope of wealth. When they have already moved the merchant ship out of the harbor, and the one sitting at the tiller is using the rudders to turn the prow toward the open sea,

they make [?] the prelude to their voyage, asking God to guide them to a good passage. The sum of their prayer is that a gentle, favorable wind may fall on the sail, toward the goal set by the helmsman standing at the stern. When the wind blows steadily for them, the sea becomes pleasant, [?] smoothly with calm waves. The broad expanses of the open sea give no trouble, as the ship flies easily over them and glides across the waves. The wealth they hope to gain from their trading is already before their eyes, for they have known a good voyage before they have tried it. The more perceptive of my hearers will surely see what this preface is aiming at. A great sea of contemplation of the divine words lies before our discourse. Great wealth of knowledge is hoped for from this voyage. This living ship, the Church, with its whole complement, is waiting eagerly for the wealth of interpretation. But the Word, our helmsman, does not take hold of the tiller until prayer rises from the whole complement of the ship, so that we may receive the power of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit raises the waves of thought and through them carries the discourse forward on a straight and favorable course. In this way, having become [?] through contemplation, we may trade in the wealth of knowledge, if the Holy Spirit comes upon the discourse through your prayers and fills [?]. Let the discourse begin by recalling the inspired words, which read exactly as follows: “I rose to open to my beloved. My hands dripped myrrh, my fingers were full of myrrh.” The living Word cannot come to be in us in any other way. I mean the pure and [?] bridegroom, who joins the soul to himself through incorruption and holiness. He can come in only if someone puts to death his members that are on earth, takes away the veil of the flesh, and so opens to the Word the door by which he comes to dwell in the soul. This is clear not only from the divine teachings of the Apostle but also from what the bride now says. “I rose,” she says, “to open to my beloved,” by making my hands springs of myrrh that pour out the fragrance from themselves, and by showing my fingers filled with myrrh. In these words she states the way the door is opened to the bridegroom: “Because I was buried with him through baptism into death, I rose.” For the resurrection would not have taken effect if voluntary deadness had not come first. The drop of myrrh flowing from her hands, and her fingers filled with this fragrance, show that it was voluntary. She does not say that the myrrh came to her hand from somewhere else. In that case it might have been thought that what the myrrh signifies happened to her by circumstance and against her will. Instead she says that her hands (and by the hands she means

the active motions of the soul) dripped myrrh of themselves. This is the putting to death of bodily things that comes from within, by free choice. By this she means the myrrh that fills all the fingers. By the word “fingers” she means the particular kinds of virtue, each pursued separately. So the whole sense of the words is this: “I received the power of resurrection by putting to death my members that are on earth. I brought about the death of these members willingly. No one else put the myrrh into my hands; it flowed from my own choice. So in all the practices of virtue, which she has called fingers, this disposition is seen with nothing lacking.” For among those who pursue virtue one can see some who are dead to one passion but alive in others. We see some, for example, who put to death their own licentiousness but carefully nourish their conceit, or some other passion that harms the soul, such as love of money, or anger, or love of gain [?] and love of glory, or something else of the kind. While such a passion lives wickedly in the soul, it is impossible to show fingers full of myrrh, because the death of evil and estrangement from it do not appear in all the practices. But when all these fingers have been filled with the myrrh as we have understood it, the soul both rises and opens the way in to the bridegroom. Perhaps this is why the great Paul, rightly understanding the Master's saying that an ear of grain cannot grow unless the seed is first given over to death, preaches this doctrine to the Church: death must come before life, since life cannot come to be in a person in any other way unless it gains passage through death. For our nature is twofold. One part is fine, intellectual and light; the other is gross, material and heavy. It is wholly necessary, then, that the impulse in each is peculiar to itself and incompatible with the other. The intellectual and light part naturally moves upward, while the heavy and material part always sinks and is carried downward. Since their motions are naturally opposed, one cannot be strengthened unless the other is weakened in its natural course. Standing between the two is our power of self-determination and choice. By its own action it gives strength to whichever part is flagging and weakness to whichever prevails, and it gives the victory over the other to whichever part it joins. So in the Gospel the faithful and wise steward is praised, and in my view this steward is the choice that rightly presides over what is within us. He is praised because he feeds his master's household by putting to death what is opposed to it, for the destruction of the worse is the food and health of the better. But the wicked servant is condemned, who keeps company with drunkards and maltreats God's household with blows. For the prosperity of vice is truly a blow against the virtues. Therefore

it is good to follow the prophet's words and make morning for ourselves by killing all the sinners of the land. That is, we should destroy from the city of the Lord (and the city is the soul) all the thoughts that work iniquity, for their destruction becomes the life of the better ones. So we live through death when, as the Prophet says, the Word who said “I will kill and I will make alive” kills one of the things within us and makes the other alive. So too Paul, dying, lived; being weak, was strong; being bound, completed his course; being poor, made others rich; and having nothing, possessed all things, always carrying about in his body the dying of Jesus. [?] But let us return to our subject: that through death the soul rises from death. For unless it dies, it remains dead forever and unable to receive life. But by dying it comes into life, having put off all deadness. This doctrine is confirmed for us by the present text, where the bride says: “I rose to open to my beloved. My hands dripped myrrh, my fingers were full of myrrh.” No one familiar with the divine Scriptures would doubt that myrrh is a symbol of death. I think some are asking for a clearer explanation of how death raises us from death. So we will explain it as best we can, setting out the argument step by step. The account of the world's creation testifies that everything God made was very good. Man too was among the very good things; or rather, he was adorned with beauty beyond the other good things. For what could be as beautiful as the likeness of pure beauty? If everything was very good, and man was among them all, or even first of all, then death was certainly not in man. Man would not have been anything beautiful if he had borne in himself the gloomy stamp of death's dejection. But being the image and likeness of eternal life, he was truly beautiful, very beautiful, adorned with the bright stamp of life. He also had the divine paradise, teeming with life through the abundant fruit of its trees, and God's commandment was a law of life, commanding him not to die. In the middle of the planting of paradise was the tree that teems with life, whatever that tree must be understood to be, whose fruit is life. And the death-bearing tree, whose fruit Scripture declares to be at once good and evil, was also in the middle of paradise. Yet it is impossible for both trees to stand in the very middle. Whichever of the two we grant occupies the middle, the other is necessarily shut out from the place of the middle.

For the exact position of the middle is fixed relative to the circumference: it is the point [?] equally distant from the edge on every side. Since the center of a circle is exactly one point, there is no way to find room for two centers in the middle while the circle stays the same. If someone placed another center beside the first, the circle would necessarily shift along with it. The first point would then fall outside the middle, since the circumference would now be drawn around the second center. Yet Scripture says that both trees are in the middle of paradise, though their powers are opposed to each other. I mean the life-giving tree and the tree whose fruit was death, which Paul called sin when he said, “The fruit of sin is death.” So the philosophy of these words teaches us to understand this doctrine: the very center of God's planting is life, while death is unplanted and rootless and has no place of its own anywhere. Death is planted in the absence of life, when the living cease to share in the better. Life is in the middle of the divine plants, and the nature of death comes into being by falling away from life. This is why the one who taught this doctrine philosophically through riddles says that the death-bearing tree is also in the middle of paradise, and says that its fruit has a power mixed from opposites. He defined the same thing as both good and evil, hinting by this, I think, at the nature of sin. Some pleasure always leads the way in everything done through vice, and no sin can be found apart from pleasure, whether the passions arise from anger or from desire. This is why the fruit is called good: it seems so by a mistaken judgment of the good, to those who place the good in pleasure. Afterwards, though, it turns out to be evil from the bitter aftertaste of eating it. As the Proverbs say, honey drips from the lips of wickedness; for a time it soothes the throat, but afterwards it proves more bitter than gall to those who were wrongly sweetened by it. So man departed from the abundance of good fruits and through disobedience filled himself with the corrupting fruit, whose name is death-making sin. At once he died to the better life, exchanging the more divine life for an irrational and bestial one. Once death had been mingled with our nature, deadness passed down through the generations of those born. So a dead life has come down to us, as if our life itself had in a way died. Our life is plainly dead, because it has been deprived of immortality. For this reason the one who is known to stand in the middle between the two lives acts as mediator between them, so that by destroying the worse he may give the victory to the pure one. Just as man, then, by dying to the true life, [passed over] into this dead one

[?] fell into [?] life. In the same way, when one dies to this dead and bestial life, one passes over to the life that lives forever. So it is beyond doubt that no one can come to be in the blessed life without having become dead to sin. This is why the text teaches, with a philosopher's insight, that both trees stand in the same place, in the middle: the one is there by nature, while the other comes upon what exists by way of privation. For life and death take each other's place in the same subject, through participation and privation. The one who has been made dead to the good lives to evil, and the one who has become dead in evil has come back to life for virtue. So the bride does well to show her hands full of myrrh. She is rising up through deadness to all evil, so that she may open the way into herself to the Word. And the Word whom she brings in to dwell is Life. Yet although the soul that looks toward God has been lifted to such greatness by the things we have considered, she has not yet, as Paul says, known as she ought to know, nor does she reckon that she has laid hold of it. She still runs toward what lies beyond, stretching herself out to what lies ahead. The sequence of the following words leads us to understand this about her: "Upon the handles of the bolt I opened to my beloved." And she added: "My beloved passed by; my soul went out at his word." Through these words she teaches us that, where the power that surpasses every mind is concerned, there is only one way of grasping it: never to stop at what has been grasped, but always to seek more than what has been reached and never to stand still. She had become full of myrrh, and in all the pursuits of life, which she figuratively calls fingers, she showed her deadness toward evil. By the myrrh dripping from her hands of their own accord she showed that her virtue was freely chosen. Now she says that her hands touched the bolt. That is, she says that her works came near the narrow and constricted entrance, whose bolt the Word entrusts to those who are like Peter. So she opens the door of the kingdom for herself by both means: by her hands, which signify works, and by the bolt of faith. For it is through both of these, works and faith, I mean, that the Word fashions the key of the kingdom in us. When, then, like Moses, she hoped that the face of the King would be shown to her so that she might know it, the one she longed for passed beyond her grasp. For she says, "My beloved passed by." He did not abandon the soul that followed him; he drew her toward himself. "For my soul went out at his word." O blessed going-out, by which the soul that follows the Word goes out! "The Lord will guard your going out and your coming in," says the Prophet. This is truly the going out and coming in that God guards for the worthy. For the going out from where we are becomes the coming in to the good things that lie beyond.

This, then, is the going-out by which the soul went out. She took as her guide the Word who said, "I am the door" and "the way," and "If anyone enters through me, he will go in and go out." Such a one never ceases going in and never stops going out. He is always going in by progress toward what lies beyond, and always coming to be outside what he has grasped. In this way that longed-for face of the Lord passed by Moses too, and in this way the lawgiver's soul was always going out of where it was, following the Word as it went on ahead. Who does not know of the ascents that Moses made? He was always becoming great and never stopped growing toward the greater. He grew at the start, when he valued the reproach of Christ above the kingdom of the Egyptians and chose to suffer hardship with the people of God rather than enjoy sin for a season. He grew again when he killed the foreigner who was oppressing a Hebrew, fighting on behalf of the Israelite. You will surely understand how he grew in these events if you turn the history into figurative contemplation. Again he became greater than himself when he kept his life free from the world's noise through the philosophy he practiced in the desert for a long time. Then he is enlightened by the fire in the bush. He also bares his feet of their dead covering. With his rod he consumes the serpents of Egypt. He rescues his people from Pharaoh's tyranny. He is guided by a cloud. He divides the sea and drowns the tyranny beneath it. He sweetens Marah. He makes the rock yield abundance [?]. He is filled with the food of angels. He hears the trumpets. He dares to approach the burning mountain. He touches the summit. He goes beneath the cloud. He enters the darkness where God was. He receives the covenant. He becomes a sun that no one who comes near can approach, flashing with the light of his face. How could anyone go through all his ascents and his many kinds of divine appearances in words? And yet this man, so great and of such a kind, who had passed through so much and been exalted so high toward God, still has an insatiable desire for more and becomes a suppliant, asking to see God face to face. The Word had already testified that he had been granted converse face to face. Yet neither speaking with God as with a friend nor talking with him mouth to mouth puts an end to his desire for higher things. He says, "If I have found favor in your sight, show yourself to me, so that I may know you." And the one who promised to grant the favor he asked for, who said, "I know you above all," passes by him in a divine place in the rock, while the divine hand shelters him, so that after he has passed Moses can barely see his back. Through this, I think, the Word teaches that whoever desires to see God sees what he longs for by always following him, and that the contemplation of his face is the unceasing journey toward him,

which is accomplished by following behind the Word. So it is now with the soul too. When she rose up through death, when she was filled with myrrh, she brought her hands to the bolt through her works and hoped to bring the one she longed for in to dwell with her. Then he passes by, and she goes out. She no longer stays where she was, since the Word leads on ahead [?]. The words that follow confirm still further the idea we stated before: that the greatness of the divine nature is known not by comprehending it, but by going beyond every image and [?] that tries to grasp it. For the soul that has already gone out beyond nature is set free, as it were, from the usual ways of knowing things invisible. She neither stops seeking what is not found nor ceases calling on what cannot be uttered. For she says, "I sought him, and I did not find him." How could anyone find what none of the things we know can reveal? It has no form, no color, no outline, no quantity, no place [?], no shape; no conjecture, likeness or analogy reaches it. It is always found to be beyond every attempt to grasp it and wholly escapes the hold of those who seek it. That is why she says, "I sought him" with the soul's powers of discovery, in reasonings and thoughts, and he was wholly beyond, escaping the mind's approach. He is always found beyond every defining mark, so how could some designating name contain him? For this reason she devises names of every kind and force to signify the inexpressible good, but the power of speech to express is defeated and shown to fall short of the truth. So she says, "I called as best I could, devising words to point to that inexpressible blessedness, but he was greater than anything those words could point to." The great David does the same. He often calls on the Divine by countless names, and he confesses that the truth defeats him. "For you," he says, "are God, compassionate and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in mercy, and true, and strength, and firmament, and refuge, and power, and helper, and protector, and horn of salvation," and so on. And again he confesses that God's name is not known but marveled at in all the earth: "How marvelous," he says, "is your name in all the earth!" The one who gave Manoah the oracle about his child spoke in the same way when he was asked his name: it is marvelous and too great for human hearing to contain. This is why the soul too calls on the Word as she is able, but she is not able as she wishes. She wishes for more than she is able to do, yet she will never wish for as much as he is, only for as much as her will is able to wish. Since, then, the one called lies beyond the reach of the caller's longing, she says, "I called him, and he did not answer me."

The bride adds more to what she has said. At first sight it may seem rather gloomy, but to me it seems to look toward the same goal and to keep to the ascent to higher things. She says, "The watchmen who go about in the city found me. They struck me, they wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took my veil from me." Some may think these words, "they struck," "they wounded" and "they took away the veil," belong to someone lamenting rather than rejoicing. But to someone who has carefully examined their meaning, they are the words of one who boasts of the finest things. The point may become clear to us this way. A little earlier, in the preceding passage, the text testifies that she was free of every covering, where it says in the person of the bride, "I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?" But here she says again that her veil was taken from her. The veil is a bridal covering that hides the face along with the head, as the history also tells of Rebecca. How then does she, who was stripped of every garment, still have the veil that the watchmen now take from her? Is it not clear from these words how far she has risen by progress from that point to a still higher one? She had put off the old tunic and become free of every covering, yet she becomes so much purer than she was that, compared with the purity she has now reached, she seems not to have put off the covering at all. After that stripping she again finds something about her to put off. So the ascent toward the Divine shows that something coarse is always being found about her. Therefore, compared with her present purity, even the stripping of the tunic described earlier is taken off her once more as a covering by those who find her. These are the watchmen who go about the city, and the city is the soul. Those whose task is to guard the city's walls took away her veil by striking and wounding her. The removal of the veil is something good, for the eye, freed from its covering, can gaze without hindrance at the beauty it longs for. No one who looks to the Apostle could doubt this. He attributes the removal of the veil to the power of the Spirit when he says, "But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed; and the Lord is the Spirit." And no one who knows how to follow an argument would doubt that whatever brings about the good is itself surely good. If, then, the removal of the veil is good, the blow and the wound that accomplish its removal must surely be good as well. But on the surface these words suggest something unpleasant, for the words

"they struck me" and "they wounded me" suggest pain. So it is well first to consider how holy Scripture uses these words, and whether it speaks of them in a good sense, and then to examine the meaning of what is said here. How does Wisdom rescue the young man's soul from death? What does she advise doing so that the young man may not die? Let us hear Wisdom. "If you strike him with the rod," she says, "he will not die. For you will strike him with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death." So it seems that "they struck" signifies immortality, as the text says: "If you strike him with the rod, he will not die." And there is no other way for the soul to be delivered from death except by being struck with the rod. What we have said, then, shows that being struck is good, for it is truly [?] good for the soul to be delivered from death. In the same way the prophet says that God gives life by killing and heals by striking: "I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal." For this reason the great David also said that what comes from this rod is not a blow but comfort: "Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me." Through them come the preparation of a divine table and everything else the psalm goes on to list: the oil on the head, the unmixed wine of the cup that produces a sober drunkenness, the mercy that pursues him for good, and a long life in the house of God. If that sweet blow provides these things, as both the teaching of Proverbs and the voice of the Prophet say, then being struck with the rod is good, since from it comes an abundance of such good things. But let us rather examine what we passed over before these words. The Word passed by the bride and became beyond the grasp of the one who longed for him. Yet he passed by not to abandon the one he ran past, but rather to draw her toward himself. For she says, "My soul went out at his word." So the soul goes out from where it was, and in this way it is found by those who guard the city. "The watchmen who go about the city found me," she says. Now if the perils of Hades had found her, or if she said that robbers had found her, it would be grievous to become the find of such as these. For the thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. But if it is the watchmen who go about in the city who find her, she is surely blessed in being found this way. For one who has been found by the guard cannot be stolen by robbers. Who, then, are the watchmen? Who else but the ministers who guard Israel? Who else but the ministers of the one who is entrusted with sheltering the right hand by his watch [?], who guards both the coming in and [the going out] [?] [?]

guardian. He is the guardian of the city, of whom it is said, "Unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman stays awake in vain." By the watchmen who go about the city, then, the text means the ministering spirits who are sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation. And the soul, as the text has said, is God's dwelling place. By these, then, she says, the soul was found, as the sheep was once found by the good shepherd. According to the Lord's word, all the companies of the flock were stirred to joy over it. In the same way the coin was once found by the light of the lamp, and all the friends and neighbors rejoiced over it. David, the servant of the Lord, also becomes such a find, as the psalm says in the person of God: "I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I anointed him." And since he became the possession of the one who found him, let us hear what he is granted: "My hand," it says, "will support him, and my arm will strengthen him. I will cut down his enemies before his face, and put to flight those who hate him," along with everything else in the list of blessings. So it is good for the soul to be found by the angels who go about the city. For this is how the great David leads us to understand it when he says, "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them." So when she said, "The watchmen struck me," she was boasting that she had gained something more in her advance upward. And when she says that she has also been wounded, her words show the deep mark the divine rod has left in her. For the working of the spiritual rod did not touch her superficially, so that no one could tell where she had received it. The blow is made plain by the wound, and the bride boasts of it. What this means is as follows. That divine rod and comforting staff, which brings about healing by striking, is the Spirit. Its fruit is all the good things Paul listed, and among them self-control, the tutor of a virtuous way of life. So Paul too, who bore the brands of such blows and exulted in these wounds, said, "I bear the marks of Christ in my body." He was showing his weakness toward every evil, through which the power that is in Christ is made perfect in virtue. What we have said, then, has shown that the wound too is good, since through it her veil was removed. In this way the beauty of her soul was uncovered, and the covering no longer cast a shadow over it. But let us go back and sum up the meaning of what has been said. The soul that looks toward God and takes up that good longing for incorruptible beauty always has a fresh desire for what lies beyond. [?]

and she never lets satiety dull her longing. So she never stops stretching herself out to what lies ahead. She goes out from where she is and enters further within, where she has not yet been. Whatever seems marvelous and great to her at each stage she counts as lower than what comes next, because what she is always finding is far more beautiful than what she grasped before. In the same way Paul died daily, because he was always passing over into some new life. He was always becoming dead to the past and forgetting the ground he had already covered. So too the bride, running toward the Bridegroom, finds no point at which her progress toward the greater comes to a halt. Through her mouth she makes orchards of pomegranates that flow with spices. She prepares food for the Master of creation and welcomes him with her own fruits. She becomes a fountain for gardens and a well of living water. According to the testimony of the Word, she is shown to be all beautiful and without blemish. Rising above these things again, she perceives something still more glorious as the Word advances: his head filled with dew, and the drops of the night that are in his locks. She washes her feet, takes off her tunic, and drips myrrh from her hands. She brings her hands to the bolt, opens the entrance, seeks the one who cannot be grasped, and calls the one who is beyond reach. She is found by the watchmen and receives the striking rod upon herself. She imitates the rock of which the Prophet says, "He struck the rock, and waters flowed." Do you see to what height the bride [?] has run up? She is struck like the sheer rock struck by Moses, so that, like that rock, she too may pour out the Word for the thirsty as it gushes from the spring. After this she lays bare the beauty of her face, since the watchmen have taken away her veil. These are the things we have been able to grasp about this passage. But nothing prevents someone else from receiving from the one who reveals hidden mysteries a contemplation of this passage that is more profitable to the soul. Perhaps someone will say that Isaiah's vision also has some connection with the words before us. I mean the vision in which, after the leper king died, he says he saw the one seated in majesty on the high and lofty throne. He was not able to see his shape, size or form. If he had been able to, he would surely have said so, as he did with the other things he saw: he counted the wings and described the standing and the flight. He says that he heard only a voice, when the lintel was lifted by the hymn of the Seraphim and the house was filled with smoke, and one of the Seraphim put a burning coal to the Prophet's mouth. When this happened, not only his lips but his hearing too were purified to receive the word. For just as here the bride says that the watchmen struck and wounded her, and so stripped her of the covering of her veil, so there too, instead of the veil

the lintel is lifted, so that nothing may stand in the way of his seeing what is in the inner sanctuary. In place of the watchmen, the Seraphim are named; in place of the rod, the coal; in place of the blow, the burning. The outcome is the same for the bride and for the prophet's soul: purity. The prophet is not pained by the burning coal but glorified by being made radiant. In the same way the bride here does not complain of pain from the blow. Instead she boasts of the added freedom of speech and of the removal of the covering, which the text has called a veil. It is also possible to find another meaning in these words, one that does not conflict with what we have already considered. The soul that went out at his word, seeking the one who is not found and calling on the one who cannot be reached by the meaning of names, is taught by the watchmen that she loves the unattainable and longs for the incomprehensible. By this she is in a way struck and wounded, because she despairs of what she desires and thinks her longing for the Beautiful is incomplete and can never be enjoyed. But the veil of grief is taken away when she learns this: always advancing in the search and never ceasing from the ascent is the true enjoyment of what is desired, since desire is continually filled, and each fulfilment gives birth to a new desire for what lies beyond. So when the veil of despair was taken away, she saw that the beauty of the beloved is beyond hope and without limit, and through the whole eternity of the ages is always found to be greater. She is stretched toward him in a more intense longing, and through the daughters of Jerusalem she makes known to the beloved the state of her heart: she has received God's chosen arrow within herself and has been struck in the heart by the point of faith, taking love's arrow in a vital place. And God is love, as John says. To him be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field: if you find my beloved, what will you tell him? That I am still wounded by love. What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest among women, that you have so adjured us? My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of ten thousands. His head is gold of Kephaz; his locks are fir trees, black as a raven; his eyes are like doves by brimming waters, washed in milk, sitting by brimming waters.”

He who gave the mysteries of the law through Moses fulfilled the whole law and the prophets in his own person, as he says in the Gospel: “I did not come to abolish the law, but to ful-

fill.” By removing anger he did away with murder as well, and by wiping out desire he drove out the defilement of adultery along with it. In the same way he banishes from life the curse that comes from perjury: by forbidding oaths he binds perjury in idleness, for an oath cannot be broken where there is no oath. That is why he says: “You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform your oaths to the Lord. But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your word be Yes, yes, and No, no. Anything more than these comes from the devil.”

In the Song of Songs the soul has been attested as perfect. She has taken the covering from her soul by stripping off the old tunic, and she has thrown off the veil of her face, by which we understand every doubting and wavering thought, so that she may look at the truth purely and without ambiguity. This soul adjures the daughters of Jerusalem, but not by the divine throne, which Scripture calls heaven, nor by God's palace, whose name is Jerusalem, nor even by the precious head, whose hairs can become neither white nor black. Instead she moves the oath to the field and makes the adjuration by the powers in it, saying to the young women: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the forest.”

She who is wholly beautiful and free of every blemish utters nothing superfluous, nothing belonging to the devil's portion. She speaks from God, from whom, according to Micah, comes whatever is good and whatever is beautiful, and apart from these nothing. Anyone taught by the Lord's testimony can therefore see the advantages the bride possesses. She has set aside the forbidden kinds of oath. She did not make the royal city or the throne of the great King an oath for the young women, and this teaches us how far we must keep from making free with God in oaths, since we are not permitted [?] to invoke either the throne or the city in an oath. Besides this, she spared the precious head, which she will later describe in words as golden, and whose hairs are neither white nor black. How could gold turn black, or change its color to white? Clearly, then, she offers the virgins an adjuration that does not conflict with the law of the Gospel and that becomes a cause of praise for those who swear it. This agrees with the Prophet, who says that everyone who swears by him shall be praised. So the meaning of her words does not go beyond the double word by which the law of the Gospel wants truth to be confirmed when it says: “Let your

word be Yes, yes, and No, no.”

In matters of oaths, then, we are forbidden to invoke the King's throne, the city where the palace is, and likewise the true head. Only Yes and No are allowed, and in both the truth is seen equally through the Yes. It is clear, then, that the oath the bride now lays on the young women is written in the sense of the Yes, where the assent of our soul must be firmly fixed.
