The text reads: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field: if you find my beloved, what will you tell him? That I am wounded by love.”

We have already considered these words earlier, as the sequence of thought required, but what we find in them will now be stated briefly. The Apostle says that an oath is something unchangeable, which confirms the truth through itself, and he defines it as the end of every dispute, serving to confirm what is known. So the bride lays the adjuration on the virgins so that they will keep what she says without breaking it. But every oath is made by something greater, as the Apostle says, for no one would swear an oath by something less honourable than himself. We should therefore consider what greater thing the bride sets before the young women in her oath. “I adjure you,” she says, “O daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field.” What in these things is above us? We have no doubt that, in the figurative sense, the field means the world, since the Lord himself named the world so and interpreted it so. What, then, are the many powers and strengths of the world that are invoked in the oath? We must think them greater than ourselves, so that the oath, made by greater things, may have force to confirm the truth.

To make the passage clear, then, we must set beside it another translation of the words, which reads: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and by the harts of the field.” These names teach us in what the strength of this world lies and in what its power lies, the things invoked in the oath to confirm the truth. Two things make a human being akin to God. The first is an unerring conception of true Being, so that one is not carried off by mistaken notions into pagan and heretical opinions about the Divine. This is truly the Yes. The second is pure reason, which banishes every passionate disposition from the soul, and this too is not foreign to the Yes. The first of these two good habits makes us look up to true Being, and the second puts to flight the passions that ravage the soul. The mention of gazelles and harts makes their power known through symbols: the gazelle sees without error, and the hart has the power to devour and destroy wild beasts. This, then, is the Yes the bride sets before the virgins: to look toward the Divine with reverence, and purely

in freedom from passion to run the course of life. When these are achieved, the Yes is confirmed in us as something unchangeable. This is the oath that confirms the truth, by which everyone who swears is praised, as the Prophet says. Someone who has made himself secure in these two things, in the word of faith, by looking unerringly to the truth, and in his way of life, by keeping himself pure of every stain of wickedness, truly swears to the Lord. He swears not to go up onto the bed of his couch, not to give sleep to his eyes or slumber to his eyelids, until he finds in himself a place for the Lord and has become a tabernacle for the one who dwells in him.

If we too are children of the Jerusalem above, let us listen to the bride, our teacher, and learn how the one we desire can be seen. What does she say? If we make this our oath, to be among the powers of the clear-sighted gazelles and the strengths of the harts that destroy wickedness, then through these we can see the pure bridegroom, the archer of love, and each soul can say to him: “I am wounded by love.”

We have also learned from Proverbs that the wounds of love are good, for it says: “The wounds of a friend are to be chosen, but the kisses of an enemy are evil.” Who is the friend whose wounds are worth more than the enemy's kisses? This is clear to anyone who knows the mysteries of salvation. The true and steadfast friend is the one who did not stop loving us even when we had become his enemies. The faithless and savage enemy is the one who brought us to death though we had done him no wrong. To the first-formed humans, the prohibition of evil given in the commandment seemed a wound, for being kept from what was pleasant was thought a wound, while the urging toward what was pleasant and visible was thought a kiss. But experience showed that the supposed wounds of the friend were more profitable and more desirable than the enemy's kisses. The good lover of our souls proved his love, in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us. Therefore the bride, loving in return the one who loved her, shows that the arrow of love is lodged deep within her, that is, a share in his divinity. For love is God, as has been said, the love that enters the heart through the point of faith. If we must also name this arrow, we have found what we learned from Paul: this arrow is faith working through love.

But let each judge of these things as he thinks best. Let us look at the question the virgins put to their teacher: “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest among women? What is your beloved more than another

beloved, that you have so adjured us?”

As far as the sequence of what we have already examined lets us guess, this saying seems to me to have the following meaning. The virgins saw the beautiful going-out of the bride's soul when she clung to the Word, she who said, “My soul went out at his word.” They knew that, having gone out, she was seeking the one who is not found through signs, and was crying out to the one who did not answer to names. Therefore they say: “How shall we recognize him, when he is found by no identifying sign, does not answer when called, and cannot be grasped when sought? Now you, too, take the veils from our eyes, as the watchmen of the city did for you, so that we may have some guidance toward what we seek. Tell us who your beloved is, as he is in the account of his nature. Give us some way to come to know him through identifying marks, for you are filled with the Beautiful and have therefore become beautiful among women. Make known to us what we seek, and teach us the signs by which the invisible one is found, so that we may tell him about the arrow of love that has wounded you in the very centre of your heart, increasing your longing through the sweet pain.”

It would be better to take up the same saying again word for word, so that the meaning we have set out may be fitted to the words: “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us?” Let us listen, then, to her who has carefully taken off the veil and, unveiled, looks at the truth with the eye of the soul. How does she sketch for them what they seek? How does she paint in words the features of the one desired? How does she bring before the virgins' eyes the one they do not know?

In Christ one aspect is uncreated and another is created. We call uncreated what in him is eternal, before the ages, and maker of all things that exist. We call created what was conformed to the body of our lowliness in the economy carried out for our sake. Or rather, it would be better to set out the meaning of this in our discourse through the divine words themselves. We call uncreated the Word who was in the beginning, through whom all things came to be, and without whom nothing that has come to be exists. We call created the one who became flesh and dwelt among us. The glory that shone out when he was in the flesh shows that God was manifested in flesh, surely God, the Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, as John said: “We beheld his glory.” Yet what appeared was a man, but what was made known through it, he says, was “glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” His uncreated, eternal aspect, which is before the ages, is wholly beyond the grasp of every nature and cannot be put into words. But what was manifested to us through the flesh can come to some degree of knowledge. For this reason the teacher always looks to these things and speaks about whatever the hearers are able to take in. I mean

the great mystery of godliness, through which God was manifested in flesh: he who existed in the form of God lived among human beings through the flesh in the guise of a servant. Through the firstfruits he once drew to himself the perishable nature of the flesh, which he took up through incorruptible virginity, and he always sanctifies our common nature with incorruption through those who are united to him by sharing in the mystery. He nourishes his own body, the Church, and fits the members that grow through faith in him suitably into the common body. So he makes the whole beautiful, appointing believers fittingly and appropriately as eyes, mouth, hands and the other parts. Paul says: “There is one body, but many members.” Not all the members have the same rank. There is an eye in the body that does not despise the hand, and one who is a head does not reject the feet. The whole body is blended together with itself through its members in a variety of activities, so that the members may not be at odds with the whole. Having first set out these thoughts in riddles, Paul moves the discourse on to greater clarity, saying: “God appointed in the Church apostles, prophets, teachers and shepherds, for the equipping of the saints, for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” And again: “Let us grow up in every way into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and knit together by every joint that supplies it, according to the working in the measure of each single part, makes the growth of his body for building itself up in love.”

Whoever looks at the Church, therefore, looks directly at Christ, who builds himself up and grows greater by the addition of those who are being saved. She, then, who has put the veil away from her eyes sees with a pure eye the ineffable beauty of the bridegroom, and so has been wounded by the incorporeal and fiery arrow of eros. For intensified love is called eros. No one is ashamed of it when its arrows are not aimed at the flesh. On the contrary, one boasts of the wound when one receives the point of immaterial longing deep in the heart. This is exactly what the bride has done in saying to the young women, “I am wounded by love.”

[?] she leads the virgins by the hand toward clarity. The great John did the same: he kept silent about what was from the beginning, but carefully told what we have seen and heard and what our hands have touched concerning the word of truth.

So the bride says to them: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of ten thousands. His head is gold of Kephaz; his locks are fir trees, black as a raven; his eyes are like doves by brimming waters, washed in milk, sitting by brimming waters. His cheeks are like bowls of spice, putting forth perfumes. His lips are lilies dripping with abundant myrrh; his hands are turned work in gold, set with Tharsis stones; his belly is an ivory tablet upon sapphire stone; his legs are marble pillars set on bases of gold; his appearance is like choice Lebanon, like the cedars. His throat is sweetness, and he is altogether desire. This is my beloved, and this is my companion, daughters of Jerusalem.”

All these features, which make up the sketch of his beauty, do not point to the invisible and incomprehensible aspects of the Godhead. They point to what was manifested in the economy, when he was seen on earth and lived among human beings, having put on human nature. Through these things, as the Apostle says, his invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood through the things he has made, and they are made manifest through the building of the Church's world. The building of the Church is the creation of a world. In it, as the prophet says, a new heaven is created, which is the firmament of faith in Christ, as Paul says. A new earth is fashioned too, the earth that drinks the rain that falls on it. Another human being is formed, renewed through birth from above according to the image of the one who created him. Another kind of luminary also comes into being, of which he says, “You are the light of the world,” and, “among whom you shine as lights in the world.” There are many stars as well, rising in the firmament of faith.

Yet it is not the most wonderful thing that there are multitudes of stars in this new world, numbered and named by God, whose names, says the maker of such stars, are written in the heavens. For I have heard the creator of creation say to his own luminaries: “Your names are written in heaven.” The marvel of the new creation is not only that the Word fashions a multitude of stars in it. Many suns are also created, which light up the inhabited world with the rays of good works, as the maker of such suns said: “Let your light shine before men,” and, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun.” Just as someone who looks at the visible world and perceives the wisdom displayed in the beauty of things reasons from it by analogy

[?]…through the things that are seen, the invisible beauty, and the fountain of wisdom whose outflow brought the nature of existing things into being. In the same way, one who looks at this new world, the creation that is the Church, sees in it the One who is and is becoming all in all. Through what our faith can hold and grasp, his knowledge is led by the hand toward what cannot be held. This is why, when the virgin souls bring their request to the soul that has run up toward perfection, asking that the one they long for be made known to them, she uses the things revealed to us for our salvation to sketch for the virgins the marks by which the one they seek can be recognized. She makes the whole Church one body of the Bridegroom, and as she sketches his beauty she shows a particular meaning through each of the members, so that from all the parts contemplated one by one the beauty of the body is made complete. She begins her teaching, then, with what is nearest and most familiar to us. For she starts from the bodily part of the instruction, just as Matthew did. He traced the genealogy of the mystery according to the flesh from Abraham and David, and left it to the great John to proclaim, to those already taught the first elements through these things, the Beginning understood as eternal and the Word understood together with that Beginning. Through these ideas, then, the bride initiates the maidens into the mystery: our mind will not be led up to what is beyond grasp and without limit until it has first laid hold by faith of what was seen; and what was seen is the nature of the flesh. For when she says, "My kinsman is white and ruddy," she sketches in words the distinctive character of flesh through the blending of these two colors. She did the same earlier when she called him an apple, whose appearance is seen to be a blend of both colors. For the apple is white and also turns red, and its redness, I think, symbolically indicates the nature of blood. But all flesh comes into being in one way: marriage always prepares the way for the birth of those who enter this life by generation. Someone who accepts a birth of flesh in the mystery of godliness might let his thought slip down to the works and passions of nature, supposing that the birth of that flesh too was of the same kind as everyone else's. To prevent this, she declared that the one who shared in flesh and blood is white and ruddy, hinting at the nature of the body through the two colors, but she does not say that his delivery happened in the same way as an ordinary birth. Instead, out of all the myriads since human beings came to be, and up to whatever point nature will reach as it flows on through the births of later generations, he alone entered this life by a new kind of delivery. Nature did not work together to bring him into being; it only served. Therefore, she says, this white and ruddy one, who came to dwell in our life through flesh and blood, is the only one out of all the myriads "chosen out" (eklelochismenos), brought forth from virginal purity,

apart from childbed. His conception was without union, his delivery undefiled, his travail painless. His bridal chamber was the power of the Most High, overshadowing the virginity like a cloud; the wedding torch was the shining of the Holy Spirit; the bed was freedom from passion; and the marriage was incorruption. So the one born of such things is rightly called "chosen out of ten thousands," and this means that he did not come from a marriage bed. For he alone was born without childbed, just as he alone was conceived without marriage. One cannot properly use the word "childbed" of a woman who is uncorrupted and has no experience of marriage, because the words "virginity" and "childbed" cannot both apply to the same person. Just as a Son was given to us without a father, so the child was born without childbed. The Virgin did not know how the body that received God was formed within her body, and in the same way she did not feel the birth. Prophecy bears witness that her travail was painless, for Isaiah says: "Before the pains of travail came, she escaped and bore a male." Therefore he is "chosen out," born apart from childbed, departing from the course of nature in both respects: he neither began from pleasure nor came forth through pain. This follows fittingly and is not unreasonable. She who brought death into nature through sin was condemned to bear children in sorrows and pains, so it was entirely fitting that the mother of life should begin her pregnancy in joy and complete her childbearing through joy. For the archangel says to her, "Rejoice, you who are favored," and with that word he drives out the sorrow that sin had assigned to childbirth from the beginning. This, then, is the one who alone out of all the myriads came to be such through the new and unique character of his birth. He is rightly called white and ruddy because of his flesh and blood, and "chosen out of ten thousands" because, unlike all others, his birth was incorruptible and free from passion. Or perhaps the bride applied this word to him also because of his other kinds of birth, as distinct from those that come about through childbed. You certainly know how many times the firstborn of all creation was born: firstborn among many brothers, firstborn from the dead, the first to loose the pangs of death, who by his resurrection opened for everyone the way to birth from the dead. He was born in all these ways, yet in none of them did he pass into birth through childbed. Neither the birth from water, nor the rebirth from the dead, nor his being firstborn of this divine creation involved the experience of childbed; in all of these his birth is free of childbed. That is why she says, "chosen out of ten thousands." Now it is time to consider, from what she says, how she describes his beauty in each of his members. "His head is gold of Kephaz." The

Hebrew word, if translated into our language, signifies gold that is pure, unadulterated, and free from any admixture. It seems to me that those who rendered the Hebrew words into Greek left the word Kephaz untranslated because they found no Greek term that could express the force contained in the Hebrew word. Having learned that this word indicates what is perfectly pure, unmixed with any foul matter and unable to receive it, we are led to understand the following about the passage before us: Christ is the head of the body of the Church. By "Christ" we do not here refer to the eternity of the Godhead, but to the man who received God, who was seen on earth and lived among human beings, the shoot of virginity, in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily, the firstfruits of the common lump. Through him the Word clothed himself with our nature and made it undefiled, cleansed of all the passions that naturally belong to it. For this is what the prophet says of him: "He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth"; he was tested in every way in the likeness of our nature, yet without sin. So the head of the body of the Church, the firstfruits of our whole nature, is gold that is pure, unmixed with any evil and unable to receive it. The locks of hair were once gloomy and black and looked like ravens. I mean those ravens whose task, according to the proverb, is to peck out eyes and to provide those robbed of sight as food for young eagles. These locks become firs, tall trees reaching to heaven, because they have run up from earth to heavenly height, and hanging from his divine head they add to the beauty of the Bridegroom. Surely everyone knows the task of these locks, having learned it earlier from the Bridegroom's own voice: "My locks [?] with drops of water." His, then, are the dripping locks, which the prophets call clouds. From them comes the rain of teaching, which waters the lifeless fields so that God's farmland may bear abundant fruit. I think that in the divine word the locks figuratively signify the apostles. Some of them were once gloomy in their way of life: the robber, the tax collector, the persecutor, and anyone else of that kind, after the likeness of the black, flesh-eating raven that destroys eyes. By the raven I mean the ruler of the power of darkness, as he says who became a fir instead of a raven and was therefore named a lock of the divine head. Formerly he was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a man of violence while he was a raven; then he was transformed for this grace and became a lock drenched with heavenly dew, which sprinkles upon the whole body of the Church the word of the hidden and

dark mysteries. We took these to be the ones the bride calls locks. Hanging from the golden head and stirred by the breeze of the Spirit, they add no small beauty to it. They become crowns of beauty for the undefiled head, adorning it as they encircle it. It seems to me that the prophecy speaks of them when it says: "You set a crown of precious stone on his head." So they are understood under both images, as comely locks and as precious stones that adorn the head. Next our discourse should consider what is said about the eyes. The text reads: "His eyes are like doves by full pools of water, bathed in milk, sitting by full pools of water." The meaning of these words is beyond our comprehension, for whatever we think about them, we consider it less than the truth. But when we examined it carefully, it seemed to be something like this. The divine Apostle says somewhere in his writings that the eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you." With these words he teaches that the body of the Church must act rightly through both, joining the faculty that discerns truth with the faculty that acts. Contemplation by itself does not make the soul perfect unless there are also works that set the moral life right. Nor does practical philosophy give enough benefit unless true piety guides what is done. If, then, the eyes must be paired with the hands, perhaps what has been said leads us first to understand who the eyes are, and then to grasp in contemplation the praise given to them. We will save the discussion of the hands for its proper place. Seeing is the natural task proper to the eyes. That is why they are placed above all the other sense organs, set in front by nature to guide the whole body. In divine Scripture we hear those who lead the way to truth called by such names: one was called Seer, another One Who Sees, and another was named by the prophecy a Watchman appointed by God. From these we are led to think that those appointed to oversee, look out, and watch over are the ones here called eyes. We are taught that their wonder is expressed through a kind of likeness and comparison, which sketches their beauty by setting them beside something better. For she says, "Eyes like doves." Truly, guilelessness is fine praise for such eyes. It is achieved by those who are no longer defiled by the life of the flesh but live and walk by the Spirit. The spiritual and immaterial life is represented by the form of the dove, since the Holy Spirit himself was seen by John in this form, flying from heaven upon the water. [Ezek. 3:17.]

So the one appointed by God to serve as eyes for the body of the Church, if he wants to oversee and look out with purity, must wash away with water all the rheum of evil. And there is not just one water for washing the eyes; she says that there are many full pools of such waters. As many as the virtues are, so many springs of cleansing water should we picture, through which the eyes become ever purer than before. Self-control, for example, is a spring of cleansing water. Humility is another such spring, and so are truth, justice, courage, desire for the good, and estrangement from evil. These and others like them are waters from a single spring, flowing in different streams that gather into one full pool. Through them the eyes are cleansed of all the rheum of passion. The eyes that have become like doves through their purity and guilelessness are by the full pools of water, and she says that their bath is milk, for the text reads, "bathed in milk." It is fitting praise for such eyes that the dove is made beautiful by being bathed in milk. For it is true, as people have observed, that milk alone has this property: no image or likeness appears in it. Every liquid, like a mirror, reflects through its smooth surface the likenesses of those who look into it. Only in milk is there no room for such image-making. For this reason the most perfect praise of the Church's eyes is this: they do not deceive themselves by sketching anything unreal, mistaken, or empty apart from the truth of what exists. Instead they see the One who truly is and do not admit the wandering sights and fancies of this life. Therefore, for the purity of the perfect soul's eyes, the bath of milk is safe

The next phrase is a law for those who hear, concerning what the eyes should be eager for. For she says, "sitting by full pools of water." These words, by which she praises pure eyes, set before us continual, attentive devotion to the divine teachings. They also teach us how we may gain the beauty proper to eyes: by always sitting beside the full pools of water. For many of those appointed to be eyes have stopped attending to such pools and sit instead by the rivers of Babylon. They fulfill the accusation that God makes against such people: "They have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water." The lesson, then, is how an eye may become beautiful, fitting and in harmony with the golden head. It must be guileless like the dove, and free from wandering and deception like the nature of milk, with no wandering

fancies about unreal things. It must sit by the full pools of the divine waters with perseverance and constant attendance, like the tree that is planted by the streams of water and is not moved. In this way it will bear its fruit in its season, and its branch will stay evergreen, rustling with the fresh color of its leaves. As it is, though, the eyes neglect these spiritual waters and care little for constant attendance on the word. Instead they dig themselves the cistern of love of money, or quarry vainglory, or sink the well of pride, or carefully dig some other cisterns of deceit. By nature these cannot hold for long the water people strive for. Honor in this world, and power and glory, which most people are eager for, always drain away as soon as they are gathered and leave no trace of the empty effort in those who were deceived. The Word wants those who see and oversee to be like this. The security of the divine teachings must guard them in front like a fence of eyebrows, and self-control must cover the purity and brightness of their way of life like eyelids, so that the beam of conceit does not fall into the pure pupil and block their sight. What praise is given to the members of the Bridegroom that come after the eyes we will go through in what follows, God granting, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.

"His jaws are like bowls of spice, putting forth perfumes. His lips are lilies, dripping abundant myrrh. His hands are turned gold, filled with Tharsis. His belly is an ivory tablet on a sapphire stone. His legs are marble pillars set on golden bases. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars. His throat is sweetness, and he is altogether desire. This is my kinsman, and this is my close one, O daughters of Jerusalem."

The one who feeds with pure milk those who are still infants in spiritual age, becoming, as the Apostle himself says, a nurse to the newborn in the Church, saves the bread of wisdom for those made perfect in the inner man. He says, "Yet among the perfect we speak wisdom." Through the habit of good teaching, their soul's senses have been trained, so they are ready to receive the bread of wisdom. To take this food they need jaws, with teeth that grind the reasoning fine. So there must also be jaws in the body of Christ for those who no longer cling [?] to the breast of the Word but already long for more solid food. The bride now speaks of these, saying, "His jaws are like bowls of spice, putting forth perfumes." That the discussion of the jaws follows naturally from what was considered about the eye should be clear to anyone who

listens with understanding. This is why the eye that keeps constant watch by the full pool of the spiritual waters must be bathed in milk that neither misleads nor deceives, and be made like the innocent dove: so that it may share its own good things with all who make up the body of the Church. For this reason the great Isaiah also tells the one who has climbed the high mountain by his way of life to cry out in a loud voice. Through him, those who hear will come to know the Lord who comes with strength, and the arm that rules over all things; who shepherds his flock and gathers the lambs, and comforts those who are with child through good hopes; who has measured heaven with a span and holds the whole earth in his hand; and whatever else the prophecy says must be proclaimed by the one who has climbed to the summit. If, then, the eyes receive power from the waters and the milk for these purposes, so that they may come to know the truth, it follows naturally that the jaws are praised after them. Their task is to grind fine the food that preserves the nature and strength of the body. Let us see, then, what the praise of the jaws consists of. Let us hear what the bride says about them: "His jaws," she says, "are like bowls of spice, putting forth perfumes." The word "bowl" may refer to a kind of drinking vessel that is spread open, made in such a way that its hollowness is hidden. The shape is neither very deep nor laid out flat, so that it seems neither truly hollow nor flat. If the bride points to such a shape by the bowl, then the praise of the jaws would draw its own meaning from this shape. One might say that the word mentions the bowl because it wants to praise teaching that is simple, open, and guileless. In a bowl there can be no such depth as the Prophet rejected when he said, "May I be rescued from those who hate me, and from the depths of the waters." So we say that the name "bowl" signifies truth that appears in simplicity, without any deceitful hollow. Its material is spice, and its work is to put forth perfumes. For "his jaws are like bowls of spice," not from

[?]…testimony of the Lord is sure, making infants wise; the commandment of the Lord is radiant, giving light to the eyes. If the bowls of the Word are of this kind, they will clearly not be made of earthly material. Their nature will be of spice, and I mean the spice that the bride, at the opening of the Song, says is above all spices. Paul was such a bowl, who commended himself not by craftiness with the word but by the open statement of the truth. His material put off its earthly origin from the moment when, through baptism, he cast off the scales from his eyes together with the flesh. He was refashioned out of the fragrant spice and became a child of the Holy Spirit. Through this kind of smithing he was fashioned into a chosen vessel and became a bowl for pouring out the wine of the word, so he no longer needed any human being to pour the knowledge of the mysteries into him. He did not confer with flesh and blood. Instead the divine drink grew and welled up within him, and through the fragrance of Christ he blended the various flowers of the virtues into perfume for his hearers. As a result, the spice was found to suit the need of each seeker, according to the differences and particular traits of those who received the word: Jews, Greeks, women, men, masters, slaves, parents, children, the lawless, and those under the law. The grace of his teaching was truly manifold and blended with every virtue, since through his varied instructions the bowl prepared perfume for those who received the word, suited to the need of each. These are the cheeks, then, that the bride praises as she paints the beauty of the bridegroom's body in words. The next phrase confirms by its sequence that the praise of the cheeks looks to this, for after the cheeks come the lips, through which the fragrant word goes out. The praise runs: His lips are lilies, dripping abundant myrrh. Through this twofold image she bears witness to two virtues of the word at once. The first is truth, which is seen to be bright and luminous in what is said. That is what the lily looks like, and its brightness is a figure of the purity and truth of what is spoken. The second is that the teaching points only to the intelligible and immaterial life, while the life here below, which is carried on through flesh and blood, is put to death through the contemplation of intelligible things. The myrrh that flows from the body and fills the soul of whoever receives it is a sign that the body has been put to death. In many places in the usage of the divinely inspired words it has been observed that the word "myrrh" signifies death. So the perfect and pure eye, which makes the cheek a bowl from which the perfumes grow and spring up, also makes the lilies of words blossom through the mouth, words adorned with divine brightness. For this is how the text names those who are pure and through

virtue fragrant. From them comes the drop of myrrh that fills the minds of those who receive it without fail. This drop is contempt for material life: all the things pursued here become inactive and dead because of the desire for the goods above. Paul once poured such myrrh from his mouth, mixed with the pure lily of chastity, into the ears of the holy virgin. The virgin was Thecla. She received the flowing drops into her soul as she should, held the outer man fast in death, and shook off every fleshly thought and desire. After that good teaching her youth was dead, her visible beauty was dead, and all her bodily senses were dead. Only the word lived in her, and through it the whole world had died to her and the virgin had died to the world. In the same way the great Peter once spoke the bright lilies of the word in the house of Cornelius and made the souls of his hearers full of myrrh. They received the word at once and were buried with Christ through baptism, becoming dead to this life. Besides these, one can find countless examples of saints who became the mouth of the common body of the Church and filled their hearers with the myrrh that puts the passions to death. They blossomed with the lilies of the word, and through these lilies the great champions of the faith were anointed with the myrrh of the good confession during the time of their witness, in their contests for godliness. But why should we draw out our discussion of these things any further? What has been said has already made clear to us how the mouth of the Church becomes a lily, how the myrrh drips from the lily, and how the [?] of those who receive it is filled with such a drop.

But let us now go on to the next phrase. It says: His hands are chiselled work, golden, filled with tarshish. We have learned clearly from the great Paul that, in the body of the Church, the grace of the eye is incomplete when it is separated from the service of the hands. He says: The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you. The activity of the eyes is shown most fully when the works bear witness to the eye's keen sight, and the eye's good guidance becomes evident through zeal for what is good. Since we have set out to praise the hands of the divine body, we must be guided by these words as to how those who serve as hands in the Church ought to be equipped. So we will set out the divine saying itself and, as far as we can and with God's help, try to discern the meaning it contains. His hands, it says, are chiselled work, golden, filled with tarshish. For the moment, this much of the meaning is plain from what has been said: the hands are praised in the same terms as the form of the head. The head

we understood to be Christ, in whom God was reconciling the world to himself, in Paul's words, and who revealed himself in the flesh through mighty works and miracles. The text called this head, as we have understood it, pure gold, because it is free of all sin: who committed no sin, it says, nor was deceit found in his mouth. Since the text also says that the hands are golden, its meaning is plain. It lays down for the hand what is pure and sinless in every respect, unmixed with any evil and admitting none. By the hand we must understand whoever administers the common goods of the Church for the needs the commandments require. The praise of such a person is to be made like the nature of the head in purity and sinlessness. A hand becomes pure when chiselling scrapes away everything that hinders its beauty. Sculptors who shape marble into the form of some living creature carve and chisel away certain parts of the stone, and once those parts are removed, the copy takes on the form of its original. In the same way, many things must be scraped off by the chisel of reasoning for the hands of the Church's body to become beautiful, so that the hand may be truly golden and pure. Everyone can see which things spoil the hand's beauty if they are not removed: people-pleasing, love of glory, love of gain, looking only to appearances, seeking to win some distinction for oneself through what is entrusted to one's hands, and misusing the provision made for the commandments for one's own luxury and enjoyment. One must scrape away all these and the like with the tools of reasoning and leave only the pure, unadulterated gold of the will, which is made like the pure head. The Apostle's words will make our point clearer. Having called God faithful, he asks nothing else of stewards either but that they be found faithful, writing: Moreover, it is required of stewards that one be found faithful. So the faithful and wise steward, who acts as a hand for the Church, shows the hand of the body to be golden like the head, because he imitates his wise master in his way of life. No such hand was that pitiable and wretched man in the body of the apostles, or rather that hateful and abominable man. He was entrusted with the stewardship of the poor, but he did not scrape off the leprosy of avarice. He was guardian of the purse against thieves, yet he became his own thief, filching with his own hands what was in his hands, looking not to the commandment but to the money. And what did he get out of it? A noose of his own choosing, estrangement from life, the utter ruin of his soul, and an evil memory that stretches through all the time after him. So the hands must be chiselled and carved, so that once the evils that have grown into them are removed, what

remains may be gold, matching the beauty of the head in form. In the usage of Scripture the word "tarshish" has many meanings and is not always found with the same sense. Often it is taken to mean something condemned, and often something divine and blessed. When Jonah the prophet flees from the face of God, he looks for a ship going to Tarshish. And the great David says that the ships of Tarshish are shattered by a violent wind. By "violent wind" I think he means the wind that appeared to the disciples gathered in the upper room. It was first perceived by hearing, as the sound of a violent rushing wind, and afterward it was also made visible to the eyes, taking the shape of tongues and resembling the radiant nature of fire. By it the evil that spreads in many branches over human nature is shattered, and this evil is what the Prophet called the ships of Tarshish. These, then, are the passages in which the name signifies something bad. But the great Ezekiel, describing the vision of the theophany that came to him, uses this word to indicate the form of the divine sights, saying: And its appearance was like the appearance of tarshish. Those who have carefully examined the connotations of Hebrew words say that in this prophecy the word signifies what is colourless, intelligible and incorporeal. The word, then, carries [?] a twofold meaning. It is evident that here it has been taken in the better sense, for no one would count something blameworthy as praise. It follows that we should understand the following about the hands that are praised: they have carefully chiselled away from themselves everything superfluous and bodily, have scraped off every material and heavy attachment to things, and so pass over to what is divine and intelligible. This is what stone-carvers are said to do with a lump of emerald. With the whetstone they wear away and scrape off everything lustreless and earthy, and leave untouched only the part that has a pure gleam, green and olive-coloured at once. I think the divine Apostle explains this more clearly when he advises, in one of his sayings, that we must lay aside our attachment to visible things and direct our desires toward the invisible. For, he says, we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal. This, then, is what we have understood in the praise of the hands: chiselled free of material passion, they become pure and are [?] directed by their choice toward what is immaterial and intelligible. For his hands, it says, are chiselled work, golden, filled with tarshish.

Next we should examine the following phrase, which concerns the belly. It runs: His belly is an ivory tablet upon a sapphire stone. When the Lawgiver of nature gave Moses the law engraved on stone tablets, he called the slabs on which the divine letters were impressed "stone writing tablets." The one who spoke with Moses said of them: Come up to me on the mountain and stay there, and I will give you the stone tablets, the law and the commandments. Later, the law scraped off what was bodily and earthy through the clarity of the Gospel, and the tablet that receives the letters is no longer of stone but of bright, freshly polished ivory. What receives the commandments and laws has been called the belly, and she says it is an ivory tablet upon a sapphire stone. I think we should first make the physical image clear and then go on to the contemplation of what is said. Boxwood is a dense, whitish wood, from which people who are concerned with writing skilfully make tablets for themselves. A tablet made for writing is still loosely called a "boxwood tablet" even if it happens to be made of some other material. So when we hear "tablet," we understand a smooth object suited to receiving writing. Since "tablet" is a general name for such boards, the text here adds the kind of material to the image, saying that the tablet is made not of wood but of ivory. They say that this kind of bone is so dense and hard that it stays incorrupt and suffers no damage from time for as long as can be. The blue colour of the sapphire is meant to relieve the weariness of the eyes of those who diligently pore over the inscribed tablet, since such a gleam naturally rests the sight. This, then, is the image to which the praised belly of the Church is likened. But when I hear the prophecy commanding, in the person of God, Write the vision clearly on a tablet, I grasp what we ought to understand by the name "belly" in the Lord's praised body. If the word commands that the divine vision be written clearly on the tablet, then perhaps by the name of the belly it means the purity of the heart, on which we record the divine visions through memory. In the same way, the one who opened the mouth of the great Ezekiel and put into it the scroll of the book, full of writing on both sides, inside and out, says to him: Your mouth shall eat, and your belly shall be filled. Here he calls the thinking part of the soul, in which he stored up the divine teachings, a belly. Likewise we know that the great Jeremiah also called the heart a belly when it was pained by those

gloomy thoughts. That is why he says: My belly, my belly pains me, and the senses of my heart are in turmoil. And if we must cite from the divine voice the most authoritative of the passages that lead us to this meaning, it is what the Lord said to those who had believed, when he said that rivers of living water flow from the belly of those who believe in him. The text runs: Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. All that has been said, then, leads us to understand the name "belly" as the pure heart, which becomes a tablet of the divine law. This is the heart of those who, as the Apostle says, show the work of the law written on their hearts, not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. Such letters are engraved on the soul not on tablets of stone, the Apostle says, but on the tablet of the heart, which is pure, smooth and shining. The ruling part of the soul must be like this, so that the memory of the divine sayings may be impressed on it clearly and without confusion, as if in distinct, well-formed letters [?]. And the sapphire has fittingly been included [?] in the praise of the belly, for the sapphire's [?] is sky-coloured. Such a figure becomes a symbol of our heart setting its mind on the things above and looking toward them, where it lays up its treasure, and resting its gaze there. In this way it does not grow weary in attending to the divine precepts, because heavenly hope refreshes the sight of the soul's eyes. After the praise of the belly come the praises of the legs. It says: His legs are pillars of marble, set upon golden bases. The house of wisdom, which she built for herself, has many pillars. Many, too, are the pillars that support the tent of witness, adorned with various materials: their capitals and bases were of gold, and the middle was beautified with an overlay of silver. But the bride says that the pillars of the Church are of marble, set [?] upon golden bases. (The Church is a house, as the Apostle says: how one ought to behave in the house of God.) Anyone familiar with what is said about the tabernacle can see that the bride agrees with the wisdom of Bezalel in her description of beauty, since, like him, she adorns the head and the bases with gold. He [?] gilded the capital of each pillar and set it on a golden base. In the same way, the bride who [looks] purely at the bridegroom's beauty says here that his head is pure, unalloyed gold (this is what the word "Kephaz" indicates), and that the legs are founded on golden bases. As for what the figures of the pillars should be taken to mean, we will not miss the true sense if we follow holy Paul, who called

Peter, James and John, the leading figures among the apostles, pillars. We ought also to learn how one can become a pillar, so that we too may be worthy of such a title, so let us again listen to the wisdom of Paul, who says that a pillar is also the bulwark of the truth. Truth, then, is gold: it becomes the base of the legs, and by its own presence it also adorns the hands and the head. Anyone who takes "bulwark" to refer to the nature of marble will not be mistaken. The meaning of the passage, then, is this. The legs of the body are the marble pillars, that is, those who bear and support the common body of the Church by a bright life and sound teaching. Through them the base of faith stands firm, the race of virtue is run to its end, and the whole body is lifted aloft in the leaps of divine hope. These things are achieved through two qualities, truth and steadfastness. The gold is taken to mean truth, which, in Paul's words, both becomes and is called the foundation of the divine building. He says: No one can lay any other foundation than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ. And Christ is the truth, on which the legs, the pillars of the Church, are founded. By the marble we understand a bright life and a weighty, immovable disposition toward the good. But the pillars of the tent of witness are many, and many also support the house of wisdom, while here two are enough to hold up the whole body. Perhaps, then, we should turn the aim of the figure to some other meaning. I think it establishes the following. The guidance toward virtue that comes from the law takes many forms, and the precepts of wisdom are also many, though they look to the same goal. But the concise word of the Gospel knew how to gather the whole perfection of the virtuous life into a small and easily counted compass, as the Lord said: On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. It takes exactly the same strength to hold up a weight whether it hangs below or rests on top. The same exertion of strength is seen in both cases when someone carries a load either way: one bears it alike whether the weight hangs from one or is held up in the palm of one's hand. The Lord says that all the law and the prophets hang on these two commandments, and here the bride says that the body is supported by two pillars standing on golden foundations. So it would be well, in contemplating the figure of the legs, to take those two commandments into account. The Lord calls one of them the first and says the other is like the first. To love God with all one's heart and soul and strength is the first commandment, and to love one's neigh-

[?] … as oneself, to be of equal force with the [?]. But Paul too, preparing the great Timothy as a kind of house able to receive God, sets up these two pillars in him, naming one faith and the other conscience. By faith he signifies love for God with the whole heart and soul and strength; by good conscience, a loving disposition toward one's neighbor. Perhaps the interpretation we have now found does not contradict the earlier meaning. For through both of these it is possible to become pillars, like Peter and James and John, and anyone else like them who has been or will be worthy of such a name. For whoever is made perfect in these two commandments is fashioned into a pillar and foundation of the truth, as the Apostle puts it. So the whole body of the truth rests on these two achievements as on legs, since the golden foundation of the base of faith produces in our thoughts steadiness, immovability and firmness in every good. After these praises, as if summing up the whole beauty of the bridegroom, she says: “His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars. His throat is sweetness, and he is altogether desire. This is my kinsman, and this is my neighbor, O daughters of Jerusalem.” In this, I think, she indicates more clearly that the praise concerns the bridegroom's visible beauty; I mean that visible thing which the Apostle gives bodily form to through the individual members that make up the Church. For she says that his one appearance is the myriads of cedars with which Lebanon is covered on every side. By these words she shows that nothing small and low-growing contributes to the beauty of the body unless, like the cedar, it is lofty [?] and pressing up toward the summit. But let us first consider the comparison set out in the words. “His appearance,” she says, “is like choice Lebanon.” The choosing of anything comes about by setting it beside its opposite. Now “good” is said in two senses: of what truly is such, and of what is not, but feigns it by deceit and seems to be what it is not. The one who does not go astray in judging what is beautiful has chosen the good that has been singled out instead of the deceptive good. Since, then, she has here likened the bridegroom's appearance to choice Lebanon, the word consequently suggests that we think of two Lebanons: one wicked and rejected, which according to the prophecy is crushed like the calf together with the cedars upon it; the other choice and precious, whose beauty befits God and is like God. What is meant by these words is this. There is one King in the proper, true and primary sense: the King of all creation. Yet the world-ruler of darkness also exalts himself with the title of king. There are legions of angels with the true King, and legions of demons with the ruler of the power of darkness. Principalities and authorities and powers stand under the King of those who reign and the Lord

of those who rule; and that one too, as the Apostle says, has principalities and authorities and powers, which are being abolished, when evil is about to vanish into nonbeing. For he says, “When he abolishes every rule and authority and power.” The prophet sees the King of glory seated on a throne, high and lifted up; and that one too promises to set his own throne above the stars, so as to be like the Most High. The Master of all has vessels of election in his great house; that one too has vessels of wrath fitted for destruction. Again, the Lord of the angels supplies life and peace through angels to those who are worthy; and that one sends wrath and anger and affliction through the evil angels. Why should we list every point in which the adversary sets himself up in opposition to the nature of the good? Since, then, to the senses Mount Lebanon is a conspicuous sight, shaded and thickly covered on every side with tall cedars, Scripture divides the mountain between opposite meanings through examples drawn from its appearance, taking it appropriately in each sense. And so in the same prophets one can see the same name, according to the difference of the things signified, both praised and condemned. At one time the Lord shatters the cedars of Lebanon and grinds all Lebanon, together with its cedars, to powder, like the calf made into an idol in the wilderness. By this the prophecy shows that evil itself, and every height raised up from it against the knowledge of God, will be reduced to nothing. At another time it takes on the better meaning, when it says: “The righteous will flourish like the palm tree; like the cedar in Lebanon he will be multiplied.” For the truly righteous one (and the Lord is the righteous one), who for our sake sprang up from the earth, that palm of lofty foliage who rose up in the material of our nature, becomes a mountain, multiplied in the cedars of those who are rooted in him through faith; and these, when planted in the house of God, will blossom in the courts of our God. By the house we have understood the Church, following the Apostle's teaching, in which the planting of God's cedars takes place; by the courts, the eternal tabernacles, in which the blossoming and manifestation of our good hopes will come about at the appointed times. Since, then, the body of Christ is filled up through its individual members—for “the many become one body,” as the Apostle says—she therefore named the whole beauty of the bridegroom “choice Lebanon,” marking off by the word “choice” its difference from the rejected Lebanon. For that is the Lebanon which, according to Isaiah, will fall together with the lofty ones when the flower rises from the root of Jesse and the rod of power (Isa. 10:[?]; 11:1)

springs up, by which the nature of the lion, the leopard and the asps is changed to tameness and gentleness, so that the lion lives together with the calf, the leopard lies down with the kid, and that little child who was born to us presides over them, whose hand goes into the hole of the asps, touching the asp's offspring and blunting their venom. When these things happen, the prophet says, Lebanon too will fall with the lofty ones. What the prophecy discloses through these riddles is plain to everyone, and it would be superfluous to set it out in detail. For who does not know the child born to us, who touches the asps with his hand, under whose oversight the noxious beasts share a dwelling with the tame, forgetting their natural bitterness? Since, then, through these things Lebanon—that is, evil—falls, and with it fall the first source of evils and the heights raised against the truth, the bride therefore compares the Lord's beauty to choice Lebanon, saying in these words: “His appearance is like choice Lebanon, like

She also adds fitting praise for the throat, calling it sweetness and desire. The text runs thus: “His throat is sweetness, and he is altogether desire.” What we understand [?] about this is as follows. Ordinary usage calls the part under the chin the throat, in which, they say, sound is produced, set vibrating by the impact of the breath from the windpipe. Since, then, good words are honeycombs, and the voice is the instrument of the word, and the voice originates in the throat, anyone who takes this name to signify the ministers and interpreters of the word, in whom Christ speaks, will not go wrong. For the great John, when asked who he was, called himself a voice, since he was the forerunner of the Word; and the blessed Paul offered proof of Christ speaking in him: lending him his own voice, he became sweetness as Christ spoke through him. And all the prophets, yielding their vocal instruments to the Spirit who sounded within them, became sweetness, pouring out through their own throats the divine honey that kings and commoners alike take for their health. The enjoyment of it does not dull desire through satiety, but rather feeds longing through the sharing in what is desired. That is why she calls him altogether desire, sketching the beauty of the one sought by this word as if by a definition: “He is altogether,” she says, “desire.” How blessed are those members through which the whole becomes desire! By their perfection in every good they produce a lovely beauty blended from all of them, so that the whole is desirable not only in the eye and the hands or the locks of hair, but alike in the feet and hands and legs and throat, no member falling short in the surpassing excellence of beauty.

“This,” she says, “is my kinsman, and this,” she says, “is my neighbor, O daughters of Jerusalem.” For having set before their eyes, by the sketch her words drew, all the marks by which the one sought could be made known, she then uses words that point him out, saying: This is the one sought, who rose for us out of Judah so as to become our kinsman, and became the neighbor of the man who fell among robbers. He healed his wounds with oil and wine and bandages, lifted him onto his own beast, gave him rest at the inn, provided the two denarii for his life, and promised on his return to repay whatever had been added to the work of the commandment. It is surely plain to what each of these details refers. For the lawyer was testing the Lord: he wanted to show himself superior to others, and in his pride spurned being held equal with the rest, saying, “And who is my neighbor?” Then, in the form of a story, the Word sets out the whole loving plan of salvation. He tells of the man's descent from above, the ambush of the robbers, the stripping off of the incorruptible garment, the wounds of sin, and death advancing over half of our nature while the soul remains immortal; and the useless passing-by of the law, since neither priest nor Levite healed the wounds of the man who had fallen among robbers—for it is impossible for the blood of goats and bulls to take away sins. But he tells of the one who put on the whole of human nature through the firstfruits of the lump, in which there was a share of every nation, Jew and Samaritan and Greek and all people together: with his body, which is the beast of burden, he came to the place of man's misfortune, healed his wounds, gave him rest upon his own beast, and made for him a lodging—his loving plan of salvation, in which all who labor and are heavy laden find rest together. Whoever has come to be in him surely receives into himself the one in whom he has come to be, as the Word says: “He who abides in me, and I in him.” Having received him, then, into his own capacity, he gives lodging within himself to the One who cannot be contained, and from him he receives the two coins: one of them is love for God with the whole heart, the other love for one's neighbor as oneself, as the lawyer himself also answered. But since it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified, we must not only receive these two coins—I mean faith in the Divine and a good conscience toward our fellow men—but must also contribute something ourselves through works toward fulfilling these commandments. That is why the Lord tells the innkeeper that whatever he has done in caring for the injured man he will receive back at his second coming, in proportion to the worth of his zeal. He, then, who became our neighbor through such love for humankind, who became our kinsman by rising for us out of Judah,

this is the one whom the bride's word reveals to the maidens, this is the one whom the spotless bride makes known to the daughters of Jerusalem when she says: “This is my kinsman, and this is my neighbor, O daughters of Jerusalem.” May we too, by the marks she has made known, find him and take hold of him for the salvation of our souls, through the guidance of the Holy Spirit; to whom be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.

“Where has your kinsman gone, O fair one among women? Where has your kinsman turned his gaze, so that we may seek him with you? My kinsman has gone down into his garden, to the bowls of spice, to pasture his flock in the gardens and to gather lilies. I am my kinsman's, and my kinsman is mine, he who pastures his flock among the lilies. You are beautiful, my neighbor, as good pleasure, lovely as Jerusalem, awe-inspiring as armies drawn up in ranks. Turn your eyes away from me, for they have given me wings. Your hair is like flocks of goats that have appeared from Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, and not one among them is barren. Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is lovely. Your cheek is like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your silence. There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. One is my dove, my perfect one. She is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her.” Philip the apostle is attested to have been from the city of Andrew and Peter. This seems to me to be a commendation of Philip: that he was a fellow citizen of the brothers already admired in [?] through the account given of them. For when the Baptist pointed out who is the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, Andrew both grasped the mystery himself, following after the one pointed out and learning where he was staying, and brought his own brother the good news that the one foretold by prophecy was present. And Peter, his faith almost outrunning what he heard, attached himself with his whole soul to the Lamb, and through a change of name was transformed by the Lord into something more divine, being both named and made Peter instead of Simon. Yet to Abraham and Sarah the Lord granted the blessing that came with their names only long afterward and after many manifestations of God, appointing the one a father and the other a princess by the change of their names. Likewise Jacob too, after wrestling all night, was counted worthy of the name and the power of Israel. But the great Peter did not advance to this grace little by little through growth; all at once he heard his brother, believed in the Lamb, was made perfect through faith, and, cleaving to the rock, became Peter. This Philip, then, a worthy fellow citizen of men so many and so great, since he became the Lord's find—as the Gospel says, “Jesus finds

Philip”—was appointed a follower of the Word who said, “Follow me.” And drawing near to the true light, like a lamp he drew from it a share in the light for himself, and he shed light on Nathanael, carrying before him the torch of the mystery of godliness, when he said: “We have found him of whom Moses and the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth in Galilee.” Nathanael received the good news with careful attention, because he had been instructed with all exactness by prophecy in the mystery concerning the Lord. He knew that the first manifestation of God in the flesh would come from Bethlehem, but that because of his life among the Nazarenes he would be called a Nazarene. Looking to both, he reasoned that in David's Bethlehem, because of the plan of his birth according to the flesh, the mystery of the cave, the swaddling clothes and the manger had to take place, while Galilee would one day be called the region of the nations by the Word who loved to dwell among the nations. And so, agreeing with the one who had shown him the light of knowledge, he said, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Then Philip becomes his guide to grace, saying, “Come and see.” Through this Nathanael left behind the fig tree of the law, whose shade kept him from sharing in the light, and laid hold of the one who withers the leaves of the fig tree because it bears no good fruit. That is why the Word bears witness that he is a genuine Israelite, not a bastard one, displaying in himself the pure stamp of the patriarch in the guilelessness of his choice. “Behold,” he says, “an Israelite in whom guile [is not]

What the story in the introduction points to is surely evident to the more perceptive hearers from the reading from the Song of Songs set before us in its sequence. For as Andrew was guided to the Lamb by the voice of John, and Nathanael, enlightened by Philip and emerging from the shadow of the law that surrounded him, comes into the true light, so too the maidens, to find the good that has been proclaimed to them, take as their guide the soul that has been made perfect in beauty, saying to her: “Where has your kinsman gone, O fair one among women? Where has your kinsman turned his gaze, so that we may seek him with you?” It is fitting that the virgin souls bring their question to their teacher. First they asked what he is, in the question that came before this passage, saying: “What is your kinsman, O fair one among women?” Having been taught this through the signs she gave—that he is white and ruddy, and the rest by which she sketches the form of the one sought—they now ask where he is. So they say: “Where has your kinsman gone, or where has he turned his gaze?” Their purpose is surely that, having learned where he is, they may

worship at the place where his feet have stood, and having been taught where he looks, they may so place themselves that his glory may be seen by them as well; for his appearing becomes salvation to those who behold it, as the prophet says: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved.” And the teacher, like Philip who said, “Come and see,” leads them all to lay hold of the one they seek; instead of saying “See,” she points out the place where the one sought is, and where he looks. For she says: “My kinsman has gone down into a garden, to the bowls of spice.” Up to this point the words signify where he is. What follows shows what he sees and where he looks, as the teacher says: “to pasture his flock in the gardens and to gather lilies.” This is the guidance the words give the maidens by pointing the way, through which they learn both where he is and where he looks. But we must surely also recognize the benefit of this divinely inspired Scripture through spiritual contemplation. So when we hear that “the kinsman went down into his garden,” we learn the mystery of the Gospel from these words, each name making this mystical meaning clear to us. God, manifested in the flesh, because he rose out of Judah and shone upon the nations who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, is fittingly and aptly called by the name “kinsman” by her who was betrothed to him for eternal union, since she is a sister of the people of Judah. “He went down” shows that, because of the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, he too goes down along with the descent of the one who fell among enemies. By this it signifies the condescension from ineffable majesty to the lowliness of our nature. And through the riddle of the garden we learn that the true husbandman replants his own field, which is us human beings; for we are his field, as Paul says. He it is who in the beginning cultivated in paradise the human nature that the heavenly Father planted; and so, when the wild boar had grazed down our garden and ravaged the divine field, he came down to make the wilderness a garden once more, adorned with the planting of the virtues, channeling by his word the pure and divine spring of teaching to tend such plants. The bowls of spice, in the description of beauty, were used in praise of the cheeks, by which spiritual food is ground fine for those who are being nourished. Here, however, the words indicate that they are the bridegroom's place and dwelling, and so we learn that the bridegroom does not lodge in a soul empty of virtues, but only [?] if someone, according to the account given earlier, becomes a bowl of spice producing the perfumer's ointments. Such a person, having become a mixing bowl of wisdom, receives within himself the divine and unmixed wine, through which he becomes

…the joy to the one who has received it. The next passage teaches us on what pastures the flocks of the good shepherd are fattened. He does not drive his sheep out into deserts and thorny places to crop the grassy herbage. Food is set before them instead: the spices from the gardens. In place of grass there is the lily, which, the text says, the shepherd gathers to feed the sheep. Through these words the Word teaches us a philosophical truth. The nature and power that encompasses all beings, holding all things within itself, makes a place and room for itself in those who receive purity. In them the garden, cultivated in many ways by the virtues, is luxuriant with the blossoms of lilies and teems with the fruit of spices. The lilies are a figure of the brightness and purity of the mind, and the fragrance of the spices signifies being a stranger to every foul smell of sin. Among such things, it says, the overseer of rational flocks dwells: he pastures in the gardens, and he cuts and gathers the lilies to feed the sheep. He sets these before the sheep through the great Paul, who brings out for us from the divine storehouse the food that comes from the lilies. They are "whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is lovely, whatever is holy, whatever is commendable; if there is any virtue and if there is any praise." These, in my judgment at least, are the lilies with which the good shepherd and teacher feeds his flock. The next saying, which the pure and spotless bride makes when she says, "I am my kinsman's, and my kinsman is mine," is the rule and definition of perfection in virtue. From these words we learn that the purified soul must have nothing in itself except God and must look to nothing else. It must cleanse itself of every material thing and thought so completely that it is wholly transferred to the intelligible and immaterial, and so makes itself a most vivid image of the archetypal beauty. Someone who sees a painting on a panel accurately modeled on its archetype declares that the form of both is one. He says that the beauty in the image belongs to the prototype, and that the archetype is clearly seen in the copy. In the same way, she who said, "I am my kinsman's, and my kinsman is mine," says that she has been conformed to Christ. She has recovered her own beauty, the first blessedness of our nature, made beautiful after the image and likeness of the first beauty, which is true and alone. Think of a mirror that has been made skillfully and suited to its use. On its clean surface it will show accurately the features of the face that appears before it. So too the soul has prepared itself fittingly for its use and cast off every material stain, and it has stamped the pure form of the undefiled beauty upon itself. And so it utters

these words, this mirror endowed with will and life: "Since I look at my kinsman's face with my whole circle, the whole beauty of his form is seen in me." Paul plainly imitates these words when he says that he lives to God, having become dead to the world, and that Christ alone lives in him. The one who said, "For me to live is Christ," cries out through these words that none of the human and material passions lives in him. In him there is no pleasure, no grief, no anger, no fear, no cowardice, no alarm, no conceit, no rashness, no resentment, no envy, no vengeful disposition, no love of money, nor anything else that stains the soul through some attachment. "He alone is mine, who is none of these things. I have scraped away everything that is seen to lie outside his nature, and I have nothing in myself of the kind that is not in him. Therefore for me to live is Christ." Or, as the bride says, "I am my kinsman's, and my kinsman is mine." He is sanctification and purity and incorruption and light and truth and the like, and these things shepherd my soul, not among grass or brushwood but in the brightness of the saints. For the lily's nature, in the brightness of its color, hints at this meaning for us. That is why the one who pastures among the lilies leads his flock to the meadows of lilies: so that the brightness of the Lord our God may be upon us. Whatever is nourished always takes on the character of its food. Here is what I mean. Suppose there is a hollow vessel of glass, in which everything placed in it shows through [?], whether it is something [?] or something pure and bright. So by placing the brightness of the lilies in souls, he makes the souls bright through them, as the form within shows through to the outside. To make this thought clearer, we say that the soul is nourished by the virtues, and the text figuratively calls the virtues lilies. Whoever has been filled with them through a good way of life makes himself conspicuous, displaying in his conduct the form of each virtue through his life. Let temperance and justice and courage and prudence be a pure lily for you, together with all the things the Apostle calls true, honorable, lovely, just, holy, and commendable, "if there is any virtue and if there is any praise." When all these come to be within the soul, they are displayed in a pure life. They adorn the one who contains them, and they are themselves adorned by the one who has received them. Let us hear, then, from the sequence of the words that follows, what honors she receives from the one who glorifies those who glorify him, she who has devoted herself to her kinsman and received the beauty of the beloved into her own form. The Word says to the bride: "You are beautiful, my companion, like good pleasure; comely as Jerusa-

lem; an object of awe like ordered ranks." [?] …is sent up by the heavenly host to God in the highest for his good pleasure among men, in the hearing of the shepherds, when they saw that peace had come to be on earth. And anyone familiar with the words of the Gospels will know that the Master of all creation calls Jerusalem the city of the great King. From these things, then, one cannot fail to see what kind of beauty the Word attests in the bride by comparing her with Jerusalem and with good pleasure. For the Word clearly shows this about her: through the ascent she has accomplished, the soul has been raised so high that she stretches herself out toward the wonders of the Master. God in the highest, who is in the bosom of the Father, was mingled with blood and flesh out of good pleasure toward men, so that peace might come to be on earth. Clearly, then, she has likened her own beauty to this good pleasure and imitates Christ by her good deeds, becoming to others what Christ became to human nature. Paul, the imitator of Christ, did just this when he cut himself off from life so that by his own suffering he might obtain the salvation of Israel in exchange. He said, "I could wish to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh." With such a soul in view, the words spoken to the bride fit well: "The beauty of your soul is like the good pleasure that the Master showed on our behalf. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He gave himself as a ransom for the life of the world. Though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that we might live in his death, be made rich in his poverty, and reign in the form of his servitude." Her greatness is likewise shown by the comeliness of Jerusalem, meaning the Jerusalem above, the free one, the mother of the free, which we have learned from the Master's own voice is the city of the great King. She has made room within herself for the one who cannot be contained, so that God even walks about in her. Adorned with the comeliness of the one who dwells in her, she becomes a heavenly Jerusalem, having received its beauty upon herself. And the beauty and comeliness of the King's city is surely nothing other than the King's own beauty. For according to the psalm, he is comeliness and beauty, and the prophecy says to him: "In your comeliness and your beauty, go straight on and prosper and reign, because of truth and meekness and righteousness." For the Divine is characterized by these things, I mean by truth and righteousness and meekness. The soul formed in such beauties, then, becomes comely as Jerusalem, adorned with the King's own comeliness. These words, then, make plain the praise of the bride's beauty, which is completed by comparing her with good pleasure and with Jerusalem. Patrologia Graeca 44.

We do not doubt that the next saying is an encomium of the bride. But in what sense she who has been found worthy of this commendation is honored by this praise cannot be learned at first glance. The wording is this: "An object of awe like ordered powers." Someone following what we considered earlier might say that the Word magnifies the bride with these praises by comparing her to the nature above the world. Those are the ordered powers. There the Authorities are always in authority, and the Dominions exercise dominion completely. The Thrones stand firm, and the Principalities remain unenslaved. The Powers bless God unceasingly. The flight of the Seraphim does not stop, and their standing does not change. The Cherubim who hold up the high and lofty throne do not cease, and the ministers who do his work and hear his words do not grow weary. These authorities have been set in order by God, and the order of the intelligible powers above the world remains unconfused forever, since no evil overturns their good order.
