Therefore the soul that imitates them and does everything in order and with decorum stirs up wonder at itself like the wonder found in those ordered powers. For the word *thambos* is interpreted to mean amazement, and if we take this amazement to mean wonder, we do not miss the truth. The saying that comes next makes the speakers ambiguous, both who says it and to whom: "Turn your eyes away from me, for they have given me wings." Some think these words are spoken by the Master to the pure soul. I suspect, however, that the saying fits the bride better, for I find that the sense of what the words signify suits her. I will briefly set out what occurred to me. I have heard the divinely inspired Scripture speak in many places of God having wings. At one point the prophecy says, "In the shelter of your wings you will shelter me," and, "Under his wings you will hope." Again Moses describes this in the great song, where he says, "Spreading out his wings, he received them." And the Lord said to Jerusalem, "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a bird gathers her chicks under her wings!" Looking at what follows, one might say that these words are not foreign to the present meaning. The inspired word, for some ineffable reason, declares that there are wings about the divine nature. And the account of man's first making testifies that our nature came to be after the image and likeness of God, so that, having been made after the image, it was like its archetype in every respect. But according to

holy Scripture the prototype has wings. Therefore human nature too was made winged, so that it might bear the divine likeness in its wings as well. Clearly the word "wings" will be carried over, by a figurative interpretation, to a meaning fitting for God: the word "wings" signifies power and blessedness and incorruption and the like. These things belonged to man as long as he was like God in every respect. Afterwards, however, the inclination toward evil stripped us of such wings, for once we came outside the shelter of God's wings, we were stripped of our own wings as well. That is why the grace of God appeared, enlightening us, so that we might put away ungodliness and worldly desires and grow wings again through holiness and righteousness. If these things are not severed from the truth, then it is fitting that the bride should acknowledge the grace that came upon her from the divine eyes. For God looked upon us with the eyes of his love for humanity, and at that very moment we were given wings again, as we had them by the ancient grace. I think, then, that the Word shows through these words the same things David says to the Lord in prayer in the sixteenth psalm: "Let your eyes see uprightness"—mine, that is. "For you have tested my heart," he says; "you visited it by night; you tried me with fire, and no unrighteousness was found in me." To say, "Let your eyes see uprightness," is therefore the same as saying, "Let your eyes not behold the opposite." For whoever sees what is straight has not seen what is crooked, and whoever has not seen what is crooked has certainly beheld what is straight. So by removing the opposite, she displays the good to the divine eyes, and through them the soul that had lost its feathers through the disobedience of the first-formed receives wings again. This, then, is what we have understood from these words: "When your eyes look upon me, they are turned away from the opposite, for they will see nothing in me that is opposed to you. Therefore it comes to me from your eyes that I am given wings again and take up, through the virtues, the wings of the dove, from which I gain the power of flight, so as to fly away and be at rest"—that rest, clearly, in which God rested from his works.

After these words the description of the bride's beauty follows once more, as the Word honors each of the features that contribute to her comeliness with some fitting likeness. The beauty of her hair is praised, and the setting of her teeth, and the bloom on her lip, and the sweetness of her voice, and the blush of her cheek. The praise of each of these is completed for the bride through some suitable comparison and juxtaposition. Her hair is likened to flocks of goats that have appeared from Gilead. Flocks of shorn ewes rejoicing in twin offspring complete the praise of her teeth by the likeness. To a scarlet thread

her lip is compared, and her cheek is adorned by the rind of the pomegranate. The text reads as follows: "Your hair is like flocks of goats that have appeared from Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, and there is none barren among them. Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is lovely. Your cheek is like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your silence." All these things were examined sufficiently in the earlier homilies, so it would be superfluous [?] to burden the discourse by going over the same reflections again. But someone may want an account of them now as well, for the sake of those who did not hear the earlier reflections on these sayings, so we will briefly run through the meaning of the figures. The hairs have a nature peculiar to them, different from the rest of the body. The whole body is served by the power of sensation, without which it cannot live, for sensation is the life of the body [?]. Yet we see that the hairs alone, though they are part of the body, have no share in sensation. This peculiarity of this part is shown by the fact that hair, unlike the rest of the body, feels no pain from burning or cutting. According to Paul's words, long hair is the glory of a woman, adorning her head with its tresses. So the praise of the bride's hair teaches us that those who are seen about the head of the bride, through whom the Church is glorified, must be superior to the senses and must hide sensation through wisdom. As the Proverb says, "The wise hide perception." For them sight does not become the criterion of what is beautiful, nor is the good tested by taste, nor is the judgment of the beautiful entrusted to smell or touch or any other sense organ. Rather, with all sensation put to death, they lay hold of and long for the goods that appear to the understanding through the soul alone. In this way they glorify the woman, the Church. Honors do not puff them up, and faintheartedness does not make them shrink before afflictions. Even if they must be cut for the sake of faith in Christ, or thrown to the beasts or into the fire, or endure any other affliction, they display the insensibility of hair when they experience pain. Such was Elijah of Gilead, who rose up with his hairy and unkempt body, clothed in goatskins, [?] at every threat of the tyrant. Some imitate the prophet's greatness of soul and raise themselves above the whole world, "destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, in mountains and caves and the holes of the earth, of whom the world is not worthy." These are seen in flocks about the head of the whole body and become the glory of the Church, ascending with the Gileadite to the heavenly grace. The goat was perhaps chosen for the praise of the hair because the animal's nature

is suited to growing hair, so that this animal, naturally shaggy with hair, becomes a figure of the ornament that hair provides. Or perhaps it is because the goat walks over rocks without slipping and lives around the mountain peaks, boldly making its way through impassable and precipitous places, which fits naturally with those who succeed on the rough road of virtue. Someone might rather say that these goats contribute to the praise of the head because the lawgiver used this animal in many of the sacrifices of the Law. I also know that in the riddles of Proverbs, among the four things that go well, the he-goat leading the herd is counted as one of those that stride nobly. What we surmise about this, by way of conjecture, is as follows. Every practice begins with one person and is passed on to many. In the case of smithcraft, Scripture says that Tubal was the inventor of the art and so traces back to him the skill of all who worked iron after him. In the same way Abel led the way in shepherding and Cain in farming. Scripture calls Nimrod the founder of the art of hunting and Noah the founder of vine-growing, and it says that Enosh was the first to hope in God. Many such things can be learned from holy Scripture: when one person practiced something, the practice entered human life through imitation. Elijah led the way in divine zeal in a special way and with every preeminence. So all those after him who imitated his zeal and followed in the very footprints of the prophet's boldness have become the herd of the one who led the way in such a life. They become the glory and praise of the Church, ranked among the ornament of the hair, from which the life of sensation is separated and estranged. By similar means the text completes the praise of the teeth as well. These would be the ones who by their own efforts nourish the body of the Church. The Word wants them always to be seen clean, as if fresh from the bath, always free of superfluous hair, as if newly shorn. In bringing forth the virtues they bear twins, becoming fathers of a double purity, one seen in the soul and the other in the body, so that everything barren in what is better is banished from these teeth. The thread placed on the lip figuratively indicates the measured ministry of speech, which the Prophet called a guard and a door enclosing the mouth. This happens when the mouth of speech is opened at the right time and closed at the right time. We have learned from the prophecy of Zechariah that "thread" is a word for a measure, for the angel who spoke in him held a measuring line in his hands. Speech attains its measure most fully when it is dyed with red, which becomes a figure of the blood of the one who redeemed us. If anyone, like Paul, has Christ speaking within him, who redeemed us with his own blood, then he has the measuring line on his mouth, adorned with the blood-red dye.

The next phrase explains the riddle that came before it. It calls the scarlet thread "lovely speech," and by this it again signifies what is pure and well measured. For what is truly "in its season," and appears at its own proper time of prime, is neither unripe nor overripe. And by adorning the apple of the cheek with the rind of the pomegranate, he bears witness to a great perfection in good things in the bride. It signifies that her treasure has not been laid up in something else, but that she herself is her own treasure, holding within herself a store of [?] good. For as the edible part of the pomegranate is held within its rind, so it is shown that the treasure within her is held within the visible beauty of her life. This, then, is the hidden treasure of our hopes, the soul's own fruit, held fast by the virtuous life as by the rind of a pomegranate. The words "apart from your silence" have, I think, this meaning: "Your praise lies not so much in what is visible, in what is disclosed by speech, as in what is hidden in silence and escapes the disclosure of speech." For just as silence is understood as what lies outside speech, so one who understands speech as what lies outside silence will not go wrong. We keep silent about what we cannot report in words. If, then, silence is understood as what lies outside speech, it follows necessarily that what lies outside silence should be taken to be speech. So when he says "apart from your silence," he clearly establishes by this word that the things which can be made manifest by speech, whatever lies apart from your silence, are beautiful and great; but the things outside speech, hidden by silence, the unspeakable and unutterable, are certainly more wonderful than those that are uttered. Let us now hear the praises that follow, whose meaning is like the well in the history. A stone covered its mouth and made it impossible for the women tending the flocks to get at the water; but Jacob came, levered the stone from the mouth, filled the troughs with water, and let the flocks enjoy the streams freely. What, then, are the words we liken to such a well? "There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. My dove, my perfect one, is one. She is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her." Who, then, will roll away for us the stone of this obscurity? Who will draw up the water of these meanings, which lies so deep as to be beyond the reach of our speech? But it seems right to me to declare this solemnly in your hearing: to understand these things belongs only to those to whom the Apostle says, "In everything you were enriched, in all speech and

in all knowledge." Our poverty cannot lay hold of the treasures in the passage before us. Yet so that we may escape the condemnation of idleness, for the sake of him who commanded us to search the Scriptures, we shall not shrink from spending a little sweat on these words too. We say, then, that through the praises of the bride a rather refined doctrine is set before us, the philosophy contained in these words. The doctrine is this: beings are not created and re-created with the same sequence and order. When at the beginning the nature of creation came into existence by divine power, in each being the end was completed together with the beginning, with no interval between them; for all things brought from non-being into being, perfection arose together with the beginning. Human nature too is one of the things created, and it did not, any more than the others, advance by gradual progress toward perfection, but was formed together with perfection from its first existence. For it came to be, as the Word says, according to the image and likeness of God, and this shows the highest and most perfect of goods. What could be found higher than likeness to God? In the first creation, then, the end appeared together with the beginning, with no interval, and nature began to exist from perfection. But since it was made akin to death through its attachment to evil and fell away from abiding in the good, it does not recover its perfection all at once, as in its first constitution. Rather it advances toward the greater by a kind of road, putting off little by little, through a certain sequence and order, its passionate attachment to what is contrary. At the first fashioning nothing prevented the perfection of nature from coinciding with its coming into being, since evil did not exist. But in the second re-formation, extension in time necessarily accompanies the progression that runs back to the first good. For our mind, bound by evil to its attachment to matter, gradually thrusts away its fusion with the worse, as though a surrounding bark were being scraped off it by a nobler way of life. For this reason we have learned that there are many mansions with the Father, where recompense is prepared for all in proportion to each one's disposition toward the good and departure from the worse. One person is at the beginning of the better food, having just swum up, as from some abyss of a life of evil, to share in the truth. To another an increase of the better has already come through diligence. Another has grown still further through desire for good things. Another holds the middle of the ascent to the heights. Another has run past even the middle. There are some who have raised themselves above these; others have outrun even them; and others beyond these strain toward the upward course. In short, according to the varied difference of their choices, God receives each in his own rank, giving to all what accords with their worth,

[?] the rewards of good things for the higher and measuring them out in proportion to the lesser. We have supposed that the Word teaches this philosophy through the words before us, distinguishing in what we have read the difference among the souls that look to the bridegroom. Some it calls maidens, who surpass the very nature of number by their multitude. Others it says are concubines, and others queens. It limits the number of the concubines to eight tens and says the queens come to sixty, and then it sets above them all the perfect dove, seen as a unity, whom it also declares to be the only one of her mother and the chosen one of her who bore her. This, then, is what we are led to understand through the divine oracles. Those who have just come out of a kind of womb, the deceit lying in the depths, are as it were newborn, and have not yet taken in the Word articulated within themselves. They are seen in boundless multitude, through the rather irrational assent of faith. They have believed that the word of the mystery brings salvation, but they do not have the truth firmly established within themselves by any knowledge or by the full assurance that comes through reason. These are the ones named maidens, because they are of a youthful spiritual age. Born through the word of faith, they have not yet, by due growth, become ready to reach the prime of marriage and attain to the perfect man, to the measure of marriageable age, so as to be able to conceive by the fear of the Lord and bring forth a spirit of salvation. Instead, in the infancy and immaturity of their understanding, they still live with a somewhat irrational disposition. Nevertheless these too are among the saved, as the Prophet says: "Man and beast you will save, O Lord," calling the more irrational part of the saved "beasts." Of those who have grown in understanding through due diligence and have already left infancy behind, the Word teaches us a twofold difference. Souls of both kinds become of one body with the Word. But some cling to him with a disposition of love, as did the souls of David and of Paul. The one says, "But for me it is good to cling to God"; the other, "No one will separate us from the love of Christ: not life, not death, not things present, not things to come, nor anything else that exists." Others flee the temptations of adultery from fear of punishment. These too remain in incorruption and holiness, but they refuse evil because they are trained by fear rather than by longing alone. Those, then, who through the more perfect disposition have been blended with the purity of God by longing for incorruption are named queens, because they share in the kingdom. But those who labor at virtue through fear of the threat the Word calls concubines. For none of them is yet able to become mother of a king

and to share in his dignity. How could she, when she has not yet taken into herself the unmastered and self-governing freedom of a virtuous mind, but keeps away from fellowship with evil out of servile fear? Examples of what has been said are these. For the queens, there are those found worthy to stand on the right, to whom the King says, "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you." To the second and lower rank would belong those to whom the Lord says, "Fear him who, after killing, has authority to cast into the Gehenna of fire." It seems to me that the difference in the numbers points in a riddle to this distinction between the two ranks. What do I mean? There are six commandments through which the kingdom of God is prepared for those on the right. Let us reckon each of them to be the Master's talent, which the good and faithful servant ought to multiply tenfold by his work, so that he may enter into the joy of his Lord, found faithful over a few things and set over many. If, then, the soul comes to share in the kingdom through these six commandments, and the perfection of the work in each case is to multiply the commandment tenfold, as that good servant said, "Your one talent has made ten talents," it follows that we find the one queen expanded into sixty. She is the one received into fellowship with the kingdom through the tenfold multiplication of the six commandments, so that the one becomes many, distributed among the manifold forms of the commandments and taking a distinct shape in each of her right deeds. In this way the one is divided into sixty queens, distributed according to the kinds of commandments; and the bride becomes a sharer in the kingdom of Christ, the one having become a whole people of queens, numbered by so many dignities according to the commandments. Now if we were not unreasonable in supposing that the six commandments, cultivated tenfold in one soul, are signified in a riddle by the sixty queens, it follows that by a similar riddle the eighty point to the mystery of the Eighth Day. Looking toward it, those trained by fear are kept back from fellowship with evil. So we have learned in the psalms that have "the Eighth" set in their titles. The voices in them are plainly those of people under the lash, who through fear of what they await bend the Judge's ear to mercy. For the one who looks to the Eighth says to the fearsome Judge: "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your wrath. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled." And then follows all that he sets before the impartial Judge by way of supplication, among which he also laments that there is no remembrance of God in death.

For how could those condemned to weeping and gnashing of teeth have the gladness that comes from remembering God, since the Prophet says elsewhere that the remembrance of God brings gladness? Setting forth these and similar pleas, then, the one who fears the Eighth comes to perceive that he has a share in mercy, and says, "He has heard the voice of my weeping." Since holy Scripture speaks of many blessed fears, there may be in them too, as with the six commandments, an increase to tenfold. One who has been taught by the psalmody how the fear of the Lord is achieved, by turning away from evil and doing good, may multiply the treasure of divine fear tenfold by his work, as one would a mina or a talent. So the soul that ranks second after the queen, which accomplishes the good by fear and not by love, is expanded to the number eighty, displaying in her life each kind of right deed achieved through fear, distinctly and openly. In her case too the principle of the eighth is expanded by the tenfold increase. Drawing near the good by servile fear and not by bridal love, she becomes a concubine instead of a queen, and comes to the number eighty because of the fear of the Eighth, which she has increased tenfold in her right deeds. The account in the history also commands that she, having served a bastard, temporary and ignoble birth, should not dwell with the queen to the end, since the offspring of a slave has no equal share in the royal inheritance with the free-born son. For it says, "Cast out the slave girl and her son; for the son of the slave girl shall not inherit with the son of the free woman." If anyone thinks that this interpretation of the number set forth in the [?] is rather forced, let him remember that at the beginning we declared we could not attain the truth in these matters, but would touch on them only so far as not to pass over the riddles wholly unexamined. However, if perfect [?] love casts out fear, as it is written, and fear is transformed and becomes love, then what is saved is found to be a unity, joined to the only good, with all united to one another through the perfection of the dove. Something of this kind is what we understand from the words that follow: "My dove, my perfect one, is one. She is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her." This is explained more clearly in the Gospel by the voice of the Lord. Through his blessing he entrusts all power to his disciples, and through his words to the Father he grants the saints the other good things. Then he adds the crown of all good things: that they should no longer be split in many directions by differing choices in their judgment of the good, but that all should become one, united to the one and only good, so that

bound fast by the bond of peace through the unity of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says, they might all become one body and one spirit, through the one hope to which they were called. But it would be better to set out the divine words of the Gospel themselves, word for word: "That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one." What binds this unity together is glory. And no one who has studied the matter would deny that the Holy Spirit is called glory, if he looks at the Lord's own words: "The glory which you gave me," he says, "I have given them." For he truly gave such glory to the disciples when he said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit." And he received this glory, which he had always had before the world existed, when he clothed himself with human nature. Once that nature had been glorified by the Spirit, the glory of the Spirit is passed on to all that is akin to it, beginning from the disciples. That is why he says, "The glory which you gave me I have given them, that they may be one, as we are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one." So whoever has grown up from infancy to the perfect man and reached the measure of spiritual stature, who has risen from slave girl and concubine to the dignity of a queen, and who through freedom from passion and through purity has become able to receive the glory of the Spirit, this is the perfect dove on whom the bridegroom looks and says, "My dove, my perfect one, is one. She is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her." Nor are we at all ignorant of who the dove's mother is, for we know the tree from its fruit. When we see a human being, we do not doubt that he comes from a human being. So too, when we seek the mother of the chosen dove, we understand her to be none other than that Dove. For the nature of the parent is surely seen in the child. Since, then, what is born of the Spirit is spirit, and the child is a dove, the child's mother is surely a dove too, the one who flew down from heaven upon the Jordan, as John says and testifies. The maidens call her blessed; the concubines and queens praise her. For a common course toward such blessedness lies open to all souls of every rank. Therefore they say, "The daughters saw her and will call her blessed; concubines and queens will praise her." Every nature strains with desire toward what is blessed and praised. So if the daughters call the dove blessed, they surely desire to become doves themselves. And the praise the concubines give the dove is proof that they too are eager for what is praised, until all have become one, all looking to the same goal of desire, with no evil left in anyone, and God becomes all in all, in those who through unity with one another in the
